Base times height — same as a rectangle. The height is the straight-up distance, not the slanted side.

Example: base 8, height 5. A = 40.
Cube the side length. A cube has all sides equal.

Example: side 4. V = 4³ = 64.
Length × width × height. Measured in cubic units.

Example: 3 × 4 × 5 = 60.
Area of the circle on top × the height. Pretend it's a stack of circles.

Example: radius 3, height 10. V = π × 9 × 10 ≈ 282.74.
Four-thirds π r cubed. A sphere is round in every direction (a ball).

Example: radius 3. V = (4/3) × π × 27 ≈ 113.10.
One-third of a cylinder with the same base and height. The pointy top eats two-thirds of the space.

Example: radius 3, height 6. V = (1/3) × π × 9 × 6 ≈ 56.55.
In a right triangle, the two short sides squared and added equal the long side (hypotenuse) squared.

Example: legs 3 and 4. 9 + 16 = 25. Hypotenuse = √25 = 5. That's the famous 3-4-5 triangle.
Two right triangles show up so often they have memorized side ratios. 45-45-90: sides 1 : 1 : √2. 30-60-90: sides 1 : √3 : 2.

Example: a 45-45-90 with legs of 5 has hypotenuse 5√2. A 30-60-90 with short leg 1 has long leg √3 and hypotenuse 2.
Similar triangles have the same shape but different sizes. Their angles match, and their sides are in proportion.

Example: one triangle has sides 3, 4, 5. Another has 6, 8, 10. Same shape, doubled. They're similar.
Congruent triangles are the same shape AND the same size. You can match them up exactly by sliding, rotating, or flipping.

Prove it with SSS (all three sides match), SAS (two sides and the angle between), or ASA (two angles and the side between).
Acute = less than 90°. Right = exactly 90° (square corner). Obtuse = between 90° and 180°. Straight = exactly 180° (a flat line). Reflex = more than 180°.

A 45° angle is acute. A doorframe corner is right. A reclining lawn chair makes an obtuse angle.
The three angles inside any triangle add up to 180°. Always.

Example: if two angles are 70° and 60°, the third is 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°.
For a polygon with n sides, the interior angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°. You can split any polygon into (n − 2) triangles.

Example: quadrilateral (n=4): (4−2) × 180 = 360°. Pentagon (n=5): 540°. Hexagon (n=6): 720°.
Mnemonic for trig in a right triangle. SOH: Sine = Opposite / Hypotenuse. CAH: Cosine = Adjacent / Hypotenuse. TOA: Tangent = Opposite / Adjacent.

'Opposite' is across from the angle. 'Adjacent' is next to it (and not the hypotenuse). 'Hypotenuse' is the longest side, across from the right angle.
They're three ways to relate an angle of a right triangle to its sides. Pick any angle (not the 90°). Sine is how 'tall' the triangle is for its long side, cosine is how 'wide', tangent is tall over wide.

Calculators have sin, cos, tan buttons. Don't memorize values — memorize what they mean.
Draw a circle of radius 1 at the origin. For any angle θ measured from the positive x-axis, the point on the circle is (cos θ, sin θ). That's the whole trick.

This lets sin and cos work for any angle, not just acute ones in a right triangle. Negatives, big angles, full spins — all fine.
Worth memorizing: sin(0°)=0, sin(30°)=½, sin(45°)=√2/2, sin(60°)=√3/2, sin(90°)=1. Cosine is the reverse list: cos(0°)=1, cos(30°)=√3/2, cos(45°)=√2/2, cos(60°)=½, cos(90°)=0.

Tangent is sin/cos: tan(45°)=1, tan(0°)=0, tan(90°) is undefined.
For any triangle (not just right ones), each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same ratio.

Use it when you know two angles and a side, or two sides and an angle opposite one of them.
Generalization of the Pythagorean theorem for any triangle. If C is 90°, cos C = 0 and you're back to a² + b² = c².

Use it when you know two sides and the included angle, or all three sides and you need an angle.
Law of Sines: you have a side and its opposite angle paired up. Good for two angles + a side, or two sides + a non-included angle.

Law of Cosines: you have two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides and want an angle. No side-angle pair needed.
The mean is the average. Add all the numbers, divide by how many there are.

Example: 2, 4, 6, 8. Sum = 20. Count = 4. Mean = 5.
Median is the middle number. Sort the list, then pick the one in the middle. If there are two in the middle, take their average.

Example: 1, 3, 4, 7, 9 → median is 4. For 1, 3, 4, 7 → middle two are 3 and 4, so median is 3.5.
Mode is the number that appears most often. A list can have one mode, several, or none.

Example: 2, 4, 4, 7, 9 → mode is 4. For 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4 → modes are 2 and 3 (bimodal).
The range is the biggest number minus the smallest. It tells you how spread out the data is. Example: 3, 7, 12, 18 → range is 18 − 3 = 15.
Both measure how spread out data is from the mean. Standard deviation is the typical 'distance' from the average. Variance is just standard deviation squared.

Low stdev: everyone scores near the average. High stdev: scores all over the place. Stdev has the same units as the data; variance is in squared units.
An outlier is a number far from the rest. They yank the mean toward themselves but barely move the median.

Example: 4, 5, 6, 7, 100. Mean = 24.4 (way off). Median = 6 (still reasonable). That's why median is often better for skewed data like income.
A histogram is a bar chart for numerical data. The x-axis is grouped into intervals (bins), and each bar's height shows how many data points fall in that bin.

Use it to see the shape of a distribution — bell-shaped, skewed, two-humped, flat.
A box plot shows the median, the middle 50% of the data (the box), and the full range (the whiskers). Outliers show up as dots beyond the whiskers.

Great for comparing several groups side by side.
Correlation: two things move together. Causation: one actually causes the other. Just because A and B happen together doesn't mean A causes B — they might both be caused by something else.

Example: ice cream sales and shark attacks both go up in summer. Ice cream doesn't cause shark attacks. Hot weather causes both.
Population: everyone or everything you care about. Sample: a smaller group you actually measure. Stats is the art of using a sample to guess about a population.

Example: population = all voters. Sample = the 1,000 people the pollster called. The sample's stats estimate the population's.
Probability is the chance of something happening, on a scale from 0 (never) to 1 (always). Count the outcomes you want, divide by all possible outcomes.

Example: rolling a 4 on a fair die. One favorable outcome (a 4), six possible. P = 1/6 ≈ 0.167 or 16.7%.
The sample space is the set of every possible outcome of an experiment. For a coin flip: {heads, tails}. For a die: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
Two events are independent if one doesn't affect the other. Multiply their probabilities to find the chance both happen.

Example: flip two coins. P(both heads) = ½ × ½ = ¼.
Events are dependent if one changes the probability of the next. Common in 'without replacement' problems.

Example: draw 2 cards from a 52-card deck without replacement. P(first ace) = 4/52. P(second ace given first was an ace) = 3/51. P(both aces) = (4/52)(3/51).
AND (both happen): multiply. OR (either happens): add, then subtract the overlap so you don't double-count.

Example: rolling a die. P(even OR > 4) = P(even) + P(>4) − P(both). 3/6 + 2/6 − 1/6 = 4/6 = 2/3.
P(A|B) means 'probability of A given that B happened'. You're shrinking the sample space to just the outcomes where B is true.

Example: P(rolled a 2 | rolled an even number). Even outcomes are {2,4,6}, and 2 is one of them. P = 1/3.
Permutation: order matters (like a race podium). Combination: order doesn't (like picking a committee).

Example: from 5 people, how many ways to pick a top-3 ranked list? Permutations: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. How many unordered groups of 3? Combinations: 60 / 6 = 10 (divide by 3! to remove the orderings).
Expected value is the long-run average payoff. Multiply each outcome by its probability, then add them up.

Example: a game pays $10 with probability 1/4, otherwise $0. E = $10 × ¼ + $0 × ¾ = $2.50. If the entry fee is more than $2.50, don't play.
A prime is a whole number greater than 1 with no divisors other than 1 and itself. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13... 1 is not prime by definition. 91 looks prime but isn't (91 = 7 × 13).
Every whole number > 1 can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way. Build a factor tree: keep splitting until every leaf is prime.

Example: 60 = 2 × 30 = 2 × 2 × 15 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. Prime factorization of 60 is 2² × 3 × 5.
The GCD of two numbers is the largest number that divides both. Find prime factorizations, multiply the common primes (taking the smaller power of each).

Example: GCD(24, 36). 24 = 2³ × 3, 36 = 2² × 3². Common: 2² × 3 = 12.
The LCM is the smallest number that both numbers divide into. Useful for adding fractions (find a common denominator).

Example: LCM(4, 6). Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. Multiples of 6: 6, 12. LCM = 12.
Quick checks without dividing. By 2: last digit is even. By 3: digit sum is divisible by 3. By 5: ends in 0 or 5. By 9: digit sum is divisible by 9. By 10: ends in 0.

Example: 234. Digit sum 9 → divisible by 3 and 9. Last digit 4 → divisible by 2. Not divisible by 5 or 10.
Metric: based on 10s. Easy to convert (just slide the decimal). Used almost everywhere — meters, kilograms, liters, Celsius.

Imperial: based on whatever was handy a few centuries ago. Inches, feet, pounds, gallons, Fahrenheit. Mostly used in the US.
Metric: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm. Imperial: 1 mile = 5280 ft, 1 ft = 12 in. Bridges: 1 inch ≈ 2.54 cm, 1 meter ≈ 3.28 ft, 1 mile ≈ 1.609 km.

Example: 5 ft in cm. 5 × 12 × 2.54 ≈ 152.4 cm.
Metric: 1 kg = 1000 g. Imperial: 1 lb = 16 oz, 1 ton = 2000 lb. Bridge: 1 kg ≈ 2.205 lb, or 1 lb ≈ 0.454 kg.

Example: 150 lb in kg. 150 × 0.454 ≈ 68.1 kg.
C to F: multiply by 9/5, then add 32. F to C: subtract 32, multiply by 5/9.

Example: 100°C in F. 100 × 9/5 + 32 = 180 + 32 = 212°F (boiling). 32°F in C: (32−32) × 5/9 = 0°C (freezing).
A limit asks 'what value is f(x) heading toward as x gets close to some number?' It's about the destination, not whether you arrive.

Example: as x → 2, x² → 4. Even if f(2) were undefined or weird, the limit can still be 4 — limits care about the trip, not the endpoint.
The derivative of a function tells you its instantaneous rate of change — how fast it's rising or falling at each point. Geometrically, it's the slope of the tangent line at a point.

Example: if f(x) = x², then f'(x) = 2x. At x = 3, the function is climbing at a rate of 6 per unit of x.
Average rate of change over an interval is (Δy / Δx). The derivative is what you get when you shrink that interval down to a single instant.

Example: a car's average speed from minute 1 to minute 2 might be 60 mph. Its derivative at minute 1.5 is the exact speedometer reading right then.
Draw a curve. At any point, the tangent line just barely touches the curve. The derivative at that point IS the slope of that tangent line.

This is why derivatives tell you whether a curve is going up (positive derivative), down (negative), or flat (zero — possibly a max or min).
To differentiate x to a power: bring down the exponent as a multiplier, then subtract 1 from the exponent.

Examples: d/dx[x³] = 3x². d/dx[x⁵] = 5x⁴. d/dx[x] = 1. d/dx[constant] = 0.
Works for any real exponent — positive, negative, fractional. d/dx[1/x] = d/dx[x⁻¹] = −x⁻² = −1/x². d/dx[√x] = d/dx[x^½] = ½·x^(−½) = 1/(2√x).

For polynomials, apply the rule term by term.
Worth memorizing: d/dx[sin x] = cos x. d/dx[cos x] = −sin x. d/dx[e^x] = e^x (its own derivative). d/dx[ln x] = 1/x. d/dx[constant] = 0.

These plus the power rule cover most of intro calculus.
For a function inside a function, differentiate the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.

Example: d/dx[(x² + 1)³]. Outside: u³ → 3u². Inside: x² + 1, derivative 2x. Answer: 3(x² + 1)² × 2x = 6x(x² + 1)².
Derivative of one times the other, plus the first times the derivative of the other.

Example: d/dx[x² · sin x] = 2x · sin x + x² · cos x.
Low-D-high minus high-D-low, over the square of what's below. Or memorize the formula directly.

Example: d/dx[x / (x+1)] = ((1)(x+1) − (x)(1)) / (x+1)² = 1/(x+1)².
An antiderivative of f is a function whose derivative is f. It undoes differentiation.

Example: an antiderivative of 2x is x², because d/dx[x²] = 2x. Also x² + 5, or x² − 7 — any constant works. So we write x² + C.
A definite integral measures the (signed) area under the curve of f from x = a to x = b. Areas above the x-axis count positive, below count negative.

If you know an antiderivative F, compute it as F(b) − F(a) (the fundamental theorem).
The grand link between derivatives and integrals: to find the area under f from a to b, find any antiderivative F and compute F(b) − F(a).

This is why calculus is one subject, not two. Areas and slopes turn out to be inverse operations.
A vector has both size (magnitude) and direction. Picture an arrow. In 2D you write it as a pair like (3, 4); in 3D it's a triple.

Vectors describe things like velocity, force, or displacement — any quantity that needs a direction along with a number.
Add component-by-component. Geometrically, put the tail of the second vector at the head of the first — the sum runs from the very first tail to the very last head.

Example: (1, 2) + (3, 4) = (4, 6).
Multiply matching components, then add. The result is a single number (a scalar), not a vector.

The dot product also equals |u||v| cos(θ) where θ is the angle between the vectors. So zero dot product means they're perpendicular.
Each entry of the result is the dot product of a row from the first matrix with a column from the second. Top-left = (row 1 of A) · (column 1 of B), and so on.

Example: [[1,2],[3,4]] × [[5,6],[7,8]] = [[19,22],[43,50]]. Order matters — AB usually doesn't equal BA.
For a 2×2 matrix, the determinant is the cross-diagonal product: ad − bc. Geometrically, it's the area scaling factor of the matrix's transformation.

A zero determinant means the matrix squashes the plane onto a line — it has no inverse.
Swap a and d, negate b and c, then divide everything by the determinant. If det = 0, no inverse exists.

Example: [[1,2],[3,4]]. Det = 4 − 6 = −2. Inverse = (1/−2) × [[4, −2], [−3, 1]] = [[−2, 1], [1.5, −0.5]].
An eigenvector of a matrix is a special direction the matrix doesn't rotate — it only stretches or shrinks. The amount of stretching is the eigenvalue.

They show up everywhere: stability of systems, principal component analysis, quantum mechanics, vibrations of structures. They reveal a matrix's 'natural' axes.
A matrix is a compact way to describe a linear transformation. Rotate, scale, project, shear — all are matrix multiplications.

That's why graphics engines use matrices to move 3D models, and why neural networks are giant stacks of matrix multiplies. Linear algebra is the math of 'transform a bunch of numbers at once'.
The famous bell curve. Symmetric around the mean. Most values are near the middle; extreme values get rare fast.

68-95-99.7 rule: about 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2, 99.7% within 3. Lots of real things (heights, errors, IQ) follow it roughly.
A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean. Positive = above average, negative = below.

Example: test mean 70, stdev 10. You scored 85. z = (85 − 70) / 10 = 1.5. You're 1.5 stdevs above average — top ~7% of test-takers.
If you take lots of random samples and compute the mean of each, those sample means form a roughly normal distribution — even if the original data is wildly non-normal.

That's why bell curves keep showing up. It's also why we can use normal-curve math to make confidence statements about averages.
A range of plausible values for a population parameter, based on a sample. '95% confident' means: if we repeated the whole survey many times, 95% of the intervals we'd build would contain the true value.

Example: a poll says 52% support a candidate, ±3% margin at 95%. The interval is 49% to 55%.
Start with a 'null hypothesis' — usually 'nothing interesting is happening'. Collect data and compute how surprising it would be if the null were true.

If the result is very surprising (p-value below a threshold like 0.05), you reject the null and report evidence for the alternative. Otherwise you say 'not enough evidence' — never 'the null is true'.
A p-value answers: 'if the null hypothesis were true, how often would I see data as extreme as this just by chance?' Small p = the data would be surprising under the null.

By convention, p < 0.05 is often called 'statistically significant'. That threshold is a tradition, not a law of nature. p-values are about evidence, not proof.
A set is an unordered collection of distinct things. Written with curly braces: {1, 2, 3}. Things in a set are called elements or members.

Order doesn't matter ({1,2} = {2,1}) and duplicates are dropped ({1,1,2} is just {1,2}).
Union (A ∪ B): everything in either set. Intersection (A ∩ B): only things in both. Complement (Aᶜ): everything NOT in A (relative to the universe you're working in).

Example: A = {1,2,3}, B = {2,3,4}. A ∪ B = {1,2,3,4}. A ∩ B = {2,3}.
AND (∧): true only if both are true. OR (∨): true if at least one is true. NOT (¬): flips true and false.

Example: 'is rainy AND cold' is true only when both. 'is rainy OR cold' is true if either holds. NOT rainy is true when it's not rainy.
Flipping NOT across AND/OR swaps them. 'Not (rainy and cold)' is the same as 'not rainy or not cold'.

Useful for simplifying logic, rewriting code conditions, and dealing with set complements.
A truth table lists every possible combo of true/false inputs and shows the output. For two inputs, four rows. For three inputs, eight rows.

Example AND table: T∧T=T, T∧F=F, F∧T=F, F∧F=F. Only true when both inputs are true.
Big-O describes how a program's running time grows as the input gets bigger. O(1) = constant (doesn't depend on size). O(n) = linear (doubles when input doubles). O(n²) = quadratic (4× when input doubles). O(log n) = grows slowly.

We only care about the dominant term as n → ∞, so we drop constants and lower-order terms.
Induction proves statements for all positive integers in two steps. Base case: show it works for n = 1. Inductive step: assume it works for n = k, then show it must work for n = k + 1.

Like dominoes: knock over the first one, then guarantee each one knocks over the next. All of them fall.
A recurrence defines each term using earlier terms. Like Fibonacci: F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2), with F(1) = F(2) = 1. So 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13...

They describe how sequences grow step by step. Closed-form formulas are sometimes available but the recursion is often clearer.
Modular arithmetic is math on remainders. 17 mod 5 = 2 because 17 = 3·5 + 2. Two numbers are 'congruent mod n' if they have the same remainder.

Used everywhere: clock time, hashing, cryptography, parity checks. It's the math of cycling around.
A 12-hour clock is modular arithmetic mod 12. 5 hours after 9 is 2 o'clock, not 14 — you wrap around.

In math notation: (9 + 5) mod 12 = 2. Same idea works for days of the week (mod 7), bytes (mod 256), or any cycle.
If p is a prime and a is not divisible by p, then a raised to (p−1) leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by p.

Example: p = 5, a = 2. 2⁴ = 16. 16 mod 5 = 1. Used in primality tests and in RSA cryptography.
Fast way to find GCD. Replace the larger number with (larger mod smaller). Repeat until one number is 0; the other is the GCD.

Example: GCD(48, 18). 48 mod 18 = 12. Now GCD(18, 12). 18 mod 12 = 6. Now GCD(12, 6). 12 mod 6 = 0. GCD = 6.
RSA is public-key encryption built on number theory. You pick two huge primes, multiply them to get N. The product N is public; the original primes are secret.

It's easy to multiply primes but extremely hard to factor N back into them. Encryption uses public N. Only someone who knows the original primes can decrypt — that's the trick that secures most of the internet.
Suppose there were only finitely many primes. Multiply them all together and add 1. The result is not divisible by any prime on your list (always leaves remainder 1). So either it's a new prime, or has a new prime factor. Contradiction.

Conclusion: the list of primes never ends. Euclid wrote this proof over 2,000 years ago.
Line up the decimal points, then add or subtract column by column like normal whole numbers. Pad with zeros on the right if one number has fewer decimal places.

Example: 3.45 + 12.7. Rewrite as 3.45 + 12.70, stack with decimals aligned, add: 16.15.
An exponent says how many times to multiply a number by itself. 2⁴ means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. The bottom number is the base, the small upper number is the exponent.

Special cases: x¹ = x. x⁰ = 1 (for any nonzero x). x² is 'x squared', x³ is 'x cubed'.
A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers. Their decimal expansions either stop or repeat. Examples: 1/2 = 0.5, 1/3 = 0.333..., 7 = 7/1.

Irrational numbers can't be written as a clean fraction. Their decimals go on forever without repeating. Famous examples: π, e, √2.
Write the decimal over its place value, then simplify. One decimal place → over 10. Two places → over 100. Three places → over 1000.

Example: 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4. 0.6 = 6/10 = 3/5. 0.125 = 125/1000 = 1/8.
Drop the % sign and move the decimal point two places to the left. That's the same as dividing by 100.

Example: 25% = 0.25. 7% = 0.07. 150% = 1.50.
The midpoint is the point exactly halfway between two points. Average the x's and average the y's.

Example: midpoint of (2, 4) and (8, 10) is ((2+8)/2, (4+10)/2) = (5, 7).
The commutative property says you can swap the order of the numbers when you add or multiply, and the answer stays the same. It does NOT work for subtraction or division, where order changes everything. Picture putting 3 apples then 5 apples into a basket versus 5 then 3 — either way you end up with 8 apples. So 3 + 5 = 5 + 3, and 4 x 6 = 6 x 4.
The associative property says that when you add or multiply three or more numbers, it doesn't matter how you group them with parentheses — the total is the same. Think of paying for snacks: you can add your drink and chips first, then the candy, or add the chips and candy first, then the drink. Either way the bill is identical. So (2 + 3) + 4 = 2 + (3 + 4), and it works for multiplication too.
An identity element is a number that leaves another number unchanged when you use it in an operation. For addition, that number is zero: adding nothing keeps a value the same, so 14 + 0 = 14. For multiplication, it's one: taking a number exactly once doesn't change it, so 14 x 1 = 14. It's like a vending machine that gives back the same drink you put in.
Inverse operations are opposites that undo each other. Addition and subtraction are a pair, and so are multiplication and division. If you walk five steps forward and then five steps back, you're right where you started — that's an inverse at work. This is the secret behind solving equations: if a number was added, you subtract it to undo it; if it was multiplied, you divide.
The greatest common factor is the largest number that divides evenly into two or more numbers. To find it, list the factors of each number and pick the biggest one they share. Imagine you have 12 red marbles and 18 blue marbles and want equal bags with no leftovers — the biggest bag count that works is the GCF, which here is 6.
An even number can be split into two equal whole groups with nothing left over, and an odd number always leaves one extra. The quick test is the last digit: if it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8 it's even, otherwise it's odd. Think of pairing up socks — eight socks make four neat pairs (even), but seven leaves one lonely sock (odd).
When one number doesn't divide evenly into another, the leftover amount is called the remainder. You find the largest whole number of groups you can make, then whatever can't fill a full group is the remainder. Picture handing out 17 cookies to 5 friends: each gets 3 cookies (that's 15), and the 2 cookies left over are the remainder.
Modulo (often written 'mod') gives you just the remainder after dividing one number by another, throwing away the quotient. It's how clocks and repeating cycles work: 15 o'clock is the same as 3 on a 12-hour clock because 15 mod 12 leaves 3. Programmers love it for checking even numbers (a number mod 2 equals 0 means even) and for wrapping things around in loops.
A factor divides evenly INTO a number, while a multiple is what you get when you multiply a number OUT by whole numbers. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12 because each splits 12 cleanly. The multiples of 12 stretch outward forever: 12, 24, 36, 48, and so on. A handy way to remember: factors are 'fewer and smaller', multiples are 'many and bigger'.
A reciprocal is what you flip a number into so that multiplying the two together gives exactly 1. For a fraction you just swap the top and bottom, so the reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3. For a whole number, put it under 1 — the reciprocal of 5 is 1/5. This is the trick behind dividing fractions: you flip the second fraction and multiply.
These are nested groups of numbers that grow wider as you add more. Natural (counting) numbers are 1, 2, 3 and up — the ones you use to count objects. Whole numbers are the same list but they also include zero. Integers go even further by adding the negatives, so they cover -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, like floors above and below ground level in an elevator.
Expanded form breaks a number apart to show how much each digit is really worth based on its place. You write each digit times its place value and add them up. The number 472 becomes 400 + 70 + 2, because the 4 sits in the hundreds spot, the 7 in the tens, and the 2 in the ones. It's like unpacking a suitcase to see exactly what's inside.
Multiplication is a shortcut for adding the same number over and over again. Instead of writing 4 + 4 + 4 the long way, you say 'three groups of 4', which is 3 x 4. Picture three plates that each hold 4 cookies — you could count them one plate at a time by adding, but multiplying gets you to 12 much faster. This is also why a tall stack of equal rows is easy to total.
A unit fraction is any fraction whose top number is one, like one-half, one-fifth, or one-tenth. It represents a single equal piece of a whole that has been split into that many parts. Think of slicing a chocolate bar into equal squares: if you break it into eight squares and take one square, you are holding one-eighth, a unit fraction. Every other fraction can be built by stacking unit fractions together, so three-eighths is just three of those one-eighth pieces.
A common denominator is a bottom number that two or more fractions can share, which lets you compare or add them directly. The lowest common denominator is the smallest such number, found from the least common multiple of the original bottoms. Imagine measuring with rulers marked in halves and one marked in thirds: you cannot line them up until you switch both to sixths, the smallest size that fits both. Once the denominators match, the slices are the same size and the numerators can simply be added.
To find a fraction of a number, you divide by the bottom number and then multiply by the top number. Dividing splits the amount into equal groups, and multiplying counts how many of those groups you want. Say a bag holds twelve marbles and you want three-quarters of them: divide twelve into four equal groups to get three marbles each, then take three of those groups, which gives nine marbles. The word 'of' in math almost always tells you to multiply.
A fraction bar is a strip split into equal sections that shows a fraction as a shaded part of a whole. The bottom number tells you how many equal sections to cut the strip into, and the top number tells you how many to shade. Imagine a strip of paper folded into four equal parts: shade three of them and you can literally see three-fourths. These models make it obvious why two-fourths and one-half cover the same length, since the shaded regions match up exactly.
On a number line, a fraction marks a precise spot between two whole numbers. The bottom number tells you how many equal jumps to split the gap between zero and one into, and the top number tells you how many jumps to take from zero. Picture a hopscotch path between zero and one divided into five even squares: landing on the third square puts you at three-fifths. This view shows that fractions are real numbers with exact positions, just like whole numbers, only finer.
Cross multiplying lets you compare two fractions without finding a common denominator. You multiply the top of each fraction by the bottom of the other, then compare the two products, with the larger product belonging to the larger fraction. Imagine comparing two-thirds and three-fifths: multiply two by five to get ten, and three by three to get nine. Since ten is bigger than nine, two-thirds is the larger fraction. It works because you are effectively giving both fractions the same hidden denominator.
A proper fraction has a top number smaller than its bottom number, so it represents less than one whole, like three-fifths. An improper fraction has a top number that is equal to or larger than the bottom, so it is one whole or more, like seven-fourths. Think of slices from a pie cut into fourths: if you have seven slices, you have more than one whole pie, so seven-fourths is improper. Improper fractions are not wrong; they are just a tidy way to write amounts bigger than one.
To add mixed numbers, you add the whole-number parts and the fraction parts separately, then combine them. If the fraction parts have different bottoms, you first rewrite them with a common denominator so the pieces are the same size. Imagine combining two and one-quarter cups of flour with one and one-half cups: the wholes give three cups, and one-quarter plus two-quarters gives three-quarters, so the total is three and three-quarters cups. If the fraction part adds up to one or more, you carry it over to the whole part.
A complex fraction is a fraction that has another fraction in its top, its bottom, or both. The main fraction bar still means division, so a complex fraction is really one fraction divided by another. Picture splitting half a pizza among three friends: that is one-half divided by three, which can be written as one-half over three. To simplify it, you turn the division into multiplication by the reciprocal, just like dividing any two fractions, and here you would get one-sixth.
When multiplying fractions, you can cancel a common factor shared by any top number and any bottom number before you multiply, which keeps the numbers small. You divide that top and that bottom by the same factor, and the value of the answer stays the same. For example, in two-thirds times three-fourths, the three on the bottom of the first fraction and the three on top of the second both divide by three, leaving two-fourths times one, which simplifies to one-half. Canceling early saves you from simplifying a big messy fraction at the end.
Dividing asks how many of the divisor fit into the number, and small pieces fit in many times, which is why dividing by a fraction less than one makes the result larger. The smaller the piece, the more of them fit. Picture a loaf of bread and you slice it into half-loaves: six whole loaves contain twelve half-loaves, so six divided by one-half is twelve, not three. This is the everyday reason the rule says to flip the fraction and multiply.
The fastest way to put a fraction in lowest terms is to divide the top and bottom by their greatest common factor, the largest number that divides both evenly. Doing it in one step beats dividing by small factors over and over. Take twelve-eighteenths: the greatest common factor of twelve and eighteen is six, so dividing both by six gives two-thirds in a single move. The fraction looks different but names the same amount, the way six dimes and sixty cents mean the same money.
The complement of an event is everything except that event, and the chance of an event plus the chance of its complement always adds up to 1 (or 100%). So if you know the chance something happens, subtract from 1 to get the chance it does NOT happen. Imagine a weather app saying there is a 30% chance of rain today; the chance of no rain is just 100% minus 30%, which is 70%. This trick is handy because 'not happening' is often much easier to count than 'happening'.
Two events are mutually exclusive when they cannot both happen at the same time. Rolling a single die and getting a 2 and getting a 5 on that one roll are mutually exclusive, because the die can only land on one face. When events are mutually exclusive, you find the chance of one OR the other by simply adding their separate chances together, with no overlap to subtract. Drawing one card that is both the King of Hearts and a black card is impossible, so those describe mutually exclusive outcomes.
The addition rule finds the chance that event A OR event B happens. You add the chance of A to the chance of B, then subtract the chance they both happen, so you do not count the overlap twice. If you draw one card from a deck, the chance it is a heart or a face card adds the hearts to the face cards but subtracts the face cards that are also hearts. When two events can never happen together, there is no overlap, so you just add the two chances straight.
Probability compares the ways something can happen to ALL possible outcomes, while odds compare the ways it happens to the ways it does NOT happen. If a raffle gives you a one-in-four chance to win, the probability is one out of four total tickets, but the odds in your favor are one to three (one winning way against three losing ways). To turn odds like 'two to five' into a probability, put the favorable number over the sum of both numbers, giving two out of seven. Gamblers love odds; mathematicians usually prefer plain probability.
The law of large numbers says that the more times you repeat a random experiment, the closer your real-world results get to the true expected chance. Flip a fair coin ten times and you might see seven heads, but flip it ten thousand times and the share of heads will sit very close to one half. It does not mean a coin is 'due' for tails after a streak of heads; each flip stays fair and independent. It simply means that big piles of trials smooth out the lucky bumps you see in small ones.
The gambler's fallacy is the mistaken belief that past random results change the chances of future ones. After a roulette wheel lands on red five times in a row, it feels like black is 'due', but the wheel has no memory and the next spin is still an even contest. Each independent trial starts fresh, with the same odds it always had. Confusing this with the law of large numbers is a classic trap; averages settle over many trials, but no single upcoming trial is owed anything.
Bayes' theorem is the rule for updating what you believe when fresh evidence arrives. You start with a prior chance, then weigh how likely the new evidence would be if your belief were true versus false, and end with an updated chance called the posterior. A famous surprise is medical testing: even a very accurate test for a rare disease can give mostly false alarms, because there are so many more healthy people than sick ones to test. Bayes keeps you honest by forcing you to remember how rare the thing was to begin with.
The binomial distribution describes the chance of getting a certain number of 'successes' when you repeat the same yes-or-no trial a fixed number of times. The trials must be independent and each must have the same success chance, like flipping the same coin or shooting free throws at a steady skill level. Asking 'what is the chance of exactly three heads in five coin flips?' is a perfect binomial question. It combines how many arrangements give that count with how likely each arrangement is.
A uniform distribution is one where every possible outcome has exactly the same chance of happening. A fair six-sided die is the classic example: each face from one through six shows up one sixth of the time, with no favorite. Rolling, drawing a random name from a hat, or spinning a balanced wheel split into equal slices all follow this even, flat pattern. Because every outcome is equally likely, you can find any probability just by counting the outcomes you want and dividing by the total.
A random variable is a number whose value depends on the outcome of a random event, like a label that turns chance into math. If you roll two dice, the total of the pips is a random variable that could be anything from two to twelve. Discrete random variables take separate countable values, like the number of heads in ten flips, while continuous ones can take any value in a range, like the exact height of a randomly chosen person. Naming the outcome as a number lets you compute averages, spreads, and probabilities for it.
A tree diagram maps out a chain of events by branching at each step, with one branch per possible outcome and its probability written on the branch. To find the chance of a full path through the tree, you multiply the probabilities along that path from start to end. Picture grabbing two socks from a drawer of black and white socks: the first pick branches into black or white, and each of those branches again for the second pick. Adding up the paths that match what you want gives the total probability, which makes messy multi-step problems easy to see.
A probability distribution is the complete list of every possible outcome paired with how likely each one is. For a single roll of a fair die, the distribution gives each of the six faces an equal share, and all the shares always add up to one. Think of it as a recipe that tells you exactly how the total certainty is sliced up among the outcomes. Once you have the distribution, you can answer any question about that experiment, from the most likely result to the long-run average.
A game is fair when its expected value is zero, meaning that over many plays you neither gain nor lose on average. You find it by multiplying each prize by its chance, adding those up, and comparing the total to what you pay to play. A carnival game that charges a dollar but only pays back ninety cents on average has a negative expected value, so the longer you play, the more you tend to lose. Casinos and lotteries stay in business precisely because their games are tilted just slightly against you on every single play.
A composite number is a whole number bigger than 1 that is NOT prime, meaning it has more than two divisors. You can split it into a neat rectangle of more than one row. For example, 12 cookies can be arranged as 3 rows of 4 or 2 rows of 6, so 12 is composite. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite, because it only has a single divisor: itself.
To check if a number is prime, try dividing it by every whole number from 2 upward and see if any divide evenly. The shortcut: you only need to test divisors up to the square root of the number, because any larger factor would already pair with a smaller one you checked. For example, to test 37 you only try 2, 3, 5 (since 6 times 6 is past 37); none divide it evenly, so 37 is prime. If even one divisor works, the number is composite.
The Sieve of Eratosthenes is an ancient trick for finding every prime up to some number without dividing at all. Write all the numbers from 2 onward, then circle 2 and cross off every multiple of 2; circle the next uncrossed number (3) and cross off all its multiples; keep going. Whatever is left circled is prime. It is like a colander straining out the composites and leaving the primes behind, and it is far faster than testing each number one at a time.
A factor tree is a step-by-step way to find a number's prime factorization. Start with your number and split it into any two factors that multiply to it, then keep splitting each branch until every tip is a prime. For example, 36 splits into 6 and 6; each 6 splits into 2 and 3, so the tree ends in 2, 2, 3, 3. No matter which split you pick first, you always land on the same set of primes at the bottom.
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every whole number greater than 1 is either prime or can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way, ignoring the order. This is why primes are called the building blocks of numbers, like atoms that combine to form every molecule. For example, 90 is always 2 times 3 times 3 times 5, and you can never find a different bundle of primes that also multiplies to 90. That guarantee of uniqueness is what makes factoring so powerful.
A factor (also called a divisor) of a number is any whole number that divides it evenly, leaving no remainder. Factors always come in pairs that multiply to the original number. For example, the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12, because 1 times 12, 2 times 6, and 3 times 4 all hit 12 exactly. A handy real-world version: the factors of 12 are all the ways you could share 12 cookies into equal groups with none left over.
The Euclidean algorithm is a fast, ancient way to find the greatest common factor without listing any factors. You divide the bigger number by the smaller and keep only the remainder, then repeat with the smaller number and that remainder, again and again until the remainder hits zero; the last nonzero remainder is the GCF. For example, for 48 and 18: 48 leaves remainder 12, then 18 leaves remainder 6, then 12 leaves remainder 0, so the GCF is 6. It is dramatically quicker than factoring when the numbers are large.
Twin primes are a pair of prime numbers that sit just two apart, with a single number squeezed between them. Examples include 3 and 5, 11 and 13, and 17 and 19. As you count higher, primes spread out and twins get rarer, yet mathematicians keep finding enormous ones. Whether twin primes go on forever is still an unsolved mystery called the Twin Prime Conjecture, one of the famous open questions in math.
A perfect number is a number that exactly equals the sum of all its divisors smaller than itself. The first one is 6: its proper divisors are 1, 2, and 3, and 1 plus 2 plus 3 equals 6. The next is 28, since 1 plus 2 plus 4 plus 7 plus 14 also adds back up to 28. Perfect numbers are surprisingly rare and have fascinated mathematicians since ancient Greece, where they were seen as numbers in perfect balance with their own parts.
Any number (except zero itself) raised to the power of zero equals one. Here's the idea: each time you lower the exponent by one, you divide by the base. So going from the base squared to the base to the first power, you divide once; go down one more step to the zero power and you divide again, which lands you on one. It's like climbing down a staircase by dividing each step, and the step labeled zero always sits at one.
A negative exponent means 'flip it into a fraction' instead of multiplying. A base raised to a negative power equals one divided by that same base raised to the matching positive power. Think of the regular exponent stairs going up by multiplying, and the negative side as walking the other way by dividing. So while a positive exponent makes a number bigger, a negative one shrinks it down into the bottom of a fraction.
When you multiply two powers that share the same base, you keep the base and simply add the exponents. The reason is that each exponent counts how many copies of the base are being multiplied, so stacking two groups together just totals up the copies. Imagine three apples in one bag and two apples in another bag of the same fruit: when you pour them together you have five. Adding the exponents counts the combined number of factors.
A fractional exponent is just another way to write a root. Raising a number to the one-half power is exactly the same as taking its square root, and the one-third power is the cube root. The bottom of the fraction tells you which root to take, and the top tells you what power to raise it to. So a fractional exponent quietly packs both a power and a root into one tidy little number.
An arithmetic sequence is a list of numbers where you add the same fixed amount to get from each number to the next. That steady step is called the common difference. Picture climbing a staircase where every step is exactly the same height: counting your total height as you climb gives an arithmetic sequence. Saving the same amount of pocket money every week and tracking your total is another everyday example.
A geometric sequence is a list of numbers where you multiply by the same fixed amount to get from each number to the next, instead of adding. That multiplier is called the common ratio. Think of a rumor spreading where each person tells two new people, who each tell two more: the number of people in the know multiplies every round. Folding a piece of paper and watching the layers double each fold is the same idea in action.
The Fibonacci sequence is built by adding the two numbers before each one to get the next, starting from a pair of small numbers. So every new term is just the sum of the two that came right before it. You can see this pattern echo in nature, like the spiral of seeds in a sunflower head or the way a snail's shell coils. It shows up so often that people call the closely related ratio it produces the 'golden ratio'.
A decimal is a way of writing numbers that aren't whole by using a dot called a decimal point. The digits after the point stand for parts of one: tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths, getting ten times smaller each step. When you pay $3.50 for a sandwich, the 3 is three whole dollars and the .50 is fifty hundredths of a dollar, which is fifty cents. So a decimal lets you write 'somewhere between two whole numbers' precisely.
Each spot after the decimal point has its own value, and each one is ten times smaller than the spot to its left. The first spot is tenths, the second is hundredths, the third is thousandths. Think of money: in $0.25 the 2 sits in the tenths spot (two dimes) and the 5 sits in the hundredths spot (five pennies). That's why the same digit means more when it's closer to the point, just like dollars are worth more than cents.
Rounding shortens a decimal to fewer places while keeping it close to the original value. Look at the digit right after the place you're rounding to: if it's 5 or more, bump the previous digit up by one; if it's 4 or less, leave it alone, then drop the rest. For example, a gas price of $3.479 rounds to $3.48 because the third digit is 9, which pushes the 7 up to 8. Rounding is handy whenever exact long decimals are more detail than you need.
To see which decimal is larger, line up the decimal points and compare digits from left to right, starting with the biggest place. The first spot where they differ decides it. A common trap is thinking longer means larger, but 0.5 is bigger than 0.45 because the tenths digit 5 beats 4. Adding a zero so both have the same length, turning 0.5 into 0.50, makes the comparison crystal clear.
The golden rule is to line up the decimal points so that tenths sit under tenths and hundredths under hundredths. Then add or subtract column by column just like with whole numbers, carrying or borrowing as usual, and bring the decimal point straight down into your answer. If you buy something for $4.75 and pay with a $5 bill, you stack 5.00 over 4.75 and subtract to get $0.25 change. Writing in extra zeros keeps the columns tidy.
Multiply the numbers as if the decimal points weren't there, then put a point back in the answer. To place it, count how many digits sit after the points in both factors combined, and give your answer that many decimal places. If a sticker costs $1.20 and you buy a quantity that's 0.5 of a box, you multiply 120 by 5 to get 600, then place two decimal places for $0.60. The count of decimal places in equals the count out.
To divide by a decimal, first slide the decimal point in the divisor to the right until it becomes a whole number, then slide it the same number of spots in the number you're dividing. After that you divide normally and bring the decimal point straight up into the answer. Splitting a $6.00 lunch bill among friends, or figuring how many $0.25 candies you can buy with $2.00, both use this move. Shifting both numbers equally keeps the answer correct.
To take a percent of something, turn the percent into a decimal by moving its point two places left, then multiply. So 20% becomes 0.20, and to find 20% of a $50 meal you multiply 0.20 by 50 to get a $10 tip. A quick mental shortcut: 10% is just the number with its decimal point shifted once, and you can scale from there. This single move powers tips, sales, and taxes alike.
A discount is a percent taken off the original price, so the more the percent, the more you save. First find the percent of the price to learn the savings, then subtract it from the original. A faster way is to pay the leftover percent: a 30% off jacket means you pay 70% of the price, so multiply the price by 0.70 in one step. Both routes land on the same final cost, but the leftover trick skips the subtraction.
Percent change tells you how much something grew or shrank compared to where it started. You take the difference between the new and old amounts, divide by the original amount, then multiply by 100 to get a percent. If a plant grows from 10 cm to 13 cm, the change is 3 cm out of the original 10, which is 30% growth. The key is always dividing by the starting value, not the ending one, so the comparison is fair.
These three are just different costumes for the same value. To go from a fraction to a decimal you divide the top by the bottom, and to go from a decimal to a percent you move the point two places right and add a % sign. One-half is the fraction 1/2, the decimal 0.5, and the percent 50% all at once, like a half-eaten pizza described three ways. Knowing the conversions lets you switch to whichever form is easiest for the job.
A percent above 100 simply means you have more than one whole of something. Since 100% is one complete whole, 200% is two wholes and 150% is one and a half. If a bakery sells 150% as many cookies today as yesterday, it means today's batch equals all of yesterday's plus another half on top. These big percents show up whenever amounts grow past their original size, like investments doubling or attendance soaring.
A ratio compares two amounts of the same kind of thing, telling you how much of one you have for each of the other. You can write it as 3:2, as 3 to 2, or as the fraction 3/2. For example, if a fruit bowl holds 3 apples for every 2 oranges, the ratio of apples to oranges is 3:2. Order matters: 3:2 (apples to oranges) is not the same as 2:3 (oranges to apples).
You simplify a ratio the same way you simplify a fraction: divide both sides by the largest number that goes into each evenly (their greatest common factor). The simplified ratio describes the same relationship with smaller, cleaner numbers. For example, a class with 12 boys and 8 girls has a ratio of 12:8; both share a factor of 4, so dividing gives 3:2. That means for every 3 boys there are 2 girls, no matter how big the class gets.
A proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal, like 1:2 = 3:6. It says two comparisons describe the same relationship even though the actual numbers differ. For example, if 1 cup of rice serves 2 people, then 3 cups serve 6 people in the same proportion. Spotting that two ratios are equal is the key to scaling recipes, maps, and mixtures up or down.
When two ratios are equal and one value is unknown, you can cross-multiply to find it: multiply each top by the other ratio's bottom, set those products equal, then solve. For example, if 2 pencils cost the same per pencil as a box where 6 pencils cost the unknown price, in the proportion 2/3 = 6/x you cross-multiply to get 2 times x = 3 times 6, so 2x = 18 and x = 9. The trick works because equal fractions always have equal cross-products.
A unit rate is a rate written so the second quantity is exactly one unit, like miles per one hour or dollars per one item. You find it by dividing the first amount by the second. For example, if a car travels 150 miles in 3 hours, dividing gives 50 miles per hour, the unit rate. Unit rates make speeds, prices, and pace easy to compare at a glance.
Unit price is the cost of one single unit, so it lets you compare differently sized packages fairly. You divide the total price by the number of units to get the price per item, ounce, or pound, then pick the smallest. For example, a large bag of chips priced at four dollars for 16 ounces costs 25 cents an ounce, while a small bag at two dollars for 6 ounces costs about 33 cents an ounce, so the large bag is the better buy. Always compare the same unit on both sides.
To resize a recipe you multiply every ingredient by the same scale factor, which keeps all the ratios identical so the food still tastes right. The scale factor is the new number of servings divided by the original. For example, a recipe for 4 people that you want to make for 12 needs a factor of 12 divided by 4, which is 3, so you triple every ingredient. Scaling only one ingredient instead of all of them is what throws the balance off.
A map scale is a ratio that tells you how a distance on the map relates to the real distance on the ground, such as 1:100000 meaning one centimeter on the map equals 100000 centimeters in real life. To find a true distance, you measure the map distance and multiply by the scale. For example, on a map where 1 inch represents 50 miles, two cities that are 3 inches apart are really 150 miles apart. The same idea lets architects and model builders shrink big things down to fit on paper.
A scale factor is the number you multiply every measurement by to enlarge or shrink a shape while keeping its proportions, so it still looks like the original. A factor bigger than 1 makes things larger and a factor between 0 and 1 makes them smaller. For example, enlarging a photo with a scale factor of 2 doubles both its width and height, while a factor of one-half halves them. The angles and overall shape stay the same; only the size changes.
Two quantities are directly proportional when they grow or shrink together at a constant rate, so doubling one doubles the other and their ratio stays fixed. You can spot it because dividing one by the other always gives the same number. For example, if one notebook costs three dollars, then 2 notebooks cost six dollars and 5 cost fifteen, because the cost is always three times the count. The graph of a direct proportion is a straight line that passes through zero.
Two quantities are inversely proportional when one goes up exactly as the other goes down, so their product stays constant rather than their ratio. Doubling one halves the other. For example, if it takes 4 workers 6 hours to paint a fence, then 8 workers can do it in 3 hours, because the number of workers times the hours always equals 24 worker-hours. More speed means less time; more time means less speed.
A part-to-part ratio compares two pieces to each other, but a part-to-whole ratio compares one piece to the total, which you get by adding all the parts. To convert, add the ratio numbers to find the whole, then put each part over that total. For example, if blue and red marbles are in the ratio 3:1, the total is 4 parts, so blue marbles make up 3 out of 4, or three-quarters, of the jar. This is how ratios turn into fractions and percentages.
To split a total in a given ratio, add the ratio numbers to find how many equal shares there are, divide the total by that number to find the value of one share, then give each person their number of shares. For example, to share 20 dollars between two friends in the ratio 3:2, there are 5 shares total, so each share is worth 4 dollars; one friend gets 3 shares (12 dollars) and the other gets 2 shares (8 dollars). The amounts always add back up to the original total.
A coefficient is the number multiplied by a variable in a term. In 7x, the coefficient is 7, which means 'seven of whatever x is.' If a variable appears alone, like x, its coefficient is a hidden 1, and in -x it's a hidden -1. Think of buying apples at a fixed price: in the cost '3a' (3 dollars per apple times a apples), the 3 is the coefficient telling you how much each apple counts.
A constant term is a number on its own with no variable attached, so its value never changes no matter what the variable is. In 4x + 9, the 9 is the constant term. Picture a phone plan that costs $9 just to have it, plus $4 per gigabyte used: the $9 is fixed every month while the $4x part grows with usage.
An expression is a math phrase with no equals sign, like 3x + 5; you can simplify or evaluate it but you can't 'solve' it. An equation has an equals sign that claims two things are equal, like 3x + 5 = 20, which you can solve to find the variable. The phrase 'two more than a number' is an expression; the sentence 'two more than a number is ten' is an equation.
To evaluate an expression, you replace each variable with its given number and then do the arithmetic, following the order of operations. The variable is just a placeholder waiting for a value. For example, to evaluate 2x + 3 when x is 5, swap x for 5 to get 2 times 5 plus 3, which is 10 + 3 = 13. It's like a recipe that says 'add 2 cups per person plus 3 extra' once you know how many people are coming.
A multi-step equation needs more than one move to isolate the variable, so you first simplify each side (combine like terms, distribute) and then undo operations one at a time using inverses. Work backward through the order of operations: undo addition and subtraction first, then multiplication and division. For 3x + 4 = 19, subtract 4 from both sides to get 3x = 15, then divide both sides by 3 to find x = 5. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other to keep the scale balanced.
An inequality compares two amounts that are not necessarily equal, using signs like < (less than), > (greater than), or their 'or equal to' versions. Instead of one answer, the solution is usually a whole range of numbers. 'You must be at least 13 to ride' is the inequality age is greater than or equal to 13, which 14, 30, and 99 all satisfy. One special rule: if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, you flip the inequality sign.
To graph an inequality, draw a number line, mark the boundary number, then shade every value the solution allows. Use an open circle for < or > because the boundary itself is not included, and a closed (filled) circle for less-than-or-equal or greater-than-or-equal because it is. For x > 3, put an open circle on 3 and shade everything to the right. It's like marking 'no parking before this point' where the sign post itself may or may not count.
The coordinate plane is a flat grid made by a horizontal x-axis and a vertical y-axis crossing at the origin (0, 0). Any point is named by an ordered pair (x, y): the first number tells you how far right or left, the second how far up or down. To plot (3, 2), go 3 steps right, then 2 steps up. It works just like seats labeled by row and column, or a treasure map saying 'walk east 3, then north 2.'
Intercepts are the points where a line crosses the axes. The x-intercept is where the line crosses the x-axis, so y is 0 there; the y-intercept is where it crosses the y-axis, so x is 0 there. To find each one, set the other variable to 0 and solve. If a savings line shows your balance over time, the y-intercept is the money you started with, and the x-intercept is the moment the balance would hit zero.
Function notation writes a rule as f(x), read 'f of x,' where f is the function's name and x is the input you feed it. It does NOT mean f times x; it means 'apply rule f to the value x.' If f(x) = 2x + 1, then f(3) means put 3 in for x to get 2 times 3 plus 1, which is 7. Think of f as a vending machine: you put in x and it hands back exactly one output.
Point-slope form writes a line as y - y1 = m(x - x1), where m is the slope and (x1, y1) is one point the line passes through. It's the fastest way to build a line's equation when you know a slope and a single point, without first finding the y-intercept. If a candle burns down 2 cm per hour and is 15 cm tall at hour 1, you can write y - 15 = -2(x - 1) right away. From there you can simplify into the more familiar y = mx + b if you like.
A linear equation is a statement that two expressions are equal, where the unknown only appears to the first power (no squares, no square roots). It always has the same straight-line shape when you graph it. Think of a taxi fare: a flat fee plus a steady rate per mile is a linear equation, like cost = base + rate times miles. Solve it by undoing the operations until the variable stands alone.
A one-step equation needs just a single move to get the variable by itself. Whatever was done to the variable, you do the opposite to both sides so the equation stays balanced, like a seesaw. If you have x plus three equals ten, subtract three from both sides to find x equals seven. Adding undoes subtracting, and dividing undoes multiplying.
A two-step equation takes two reverse moves to isolate the variable, and the trick is to undo in reverse order: first peel off whatever is added or subtracted, then deal with whatever is multiplied or divided. Imagine your phone bill is a fee plus a charge times the gigabytes used; to find the gigabytes you first subtract the fee, then divide by the charge. For two times x plus five equals eleven, subtract five to get two x equals six, then divide by two to get x equals three.
An equation is like a balance scale with the equals sign as the pivot point: both sides weigh exactly the same. If you add, subtract, multiply, or divide one side, you must do the identical thing to the other side or the scale tips and the statement stops being true. Picture two bags that weigh the same; if you drop a rock in one bag, you have to drop an identical rock in the other to keep them even. This single rule is what makes every step of solving an equation legal.
When a number sits outside a set of parentheses, it multiplies every single term inside before you can keep solving. This is the distributive property, and skipping any term inside is the most common mistake. Think of buying three identical lunch combos that each have a sandwich and a drink: three combos means three sandwiches and three drinks, not just three sandwiches. So three times the group of x plus four becomes three x plus twelve.
When the unknown shows up on the left and the right of the equals sign, your first job is to gather all the variable terms onto one side and all the plain numbers onto the other. You do this by adding or subtracting a term from both sides to cancel it from one of them. Imagine two friends counting coins, each holding some loose coins plus some in identical jars; to compare you slide all the jars to one side and all the loose coins to the other. After that move it becomes an ordinary one- or two-step equation.
Once you find a value for the variable, you can prove it is right by plugging it back into the original equation and seeing if both sides come out equal. If they match, the answer is correct; if they do not, a step went wrong somewhere. It is like trying a key in the lock it was cut for: the right key turns smoothly and the wrong one just will not work. For x plus three equals ten, plugging in seven gives seven plus three equals ten, which checks out.
You solve an inequality almost exactly like an equation, using opposite operations on both sides to get the variable alone. The one special rule is that if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, you must flip the direction of the inequality symbol. Think of a budget where you want to spend less than a certain amount: solving tells you the range of how many items you can afford, not just one count. So two x less than ten becomes x less than five after dividing both sides by two.
When you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, the inequality symbol must reverse direction to stay true. The reason is that negatives turn the number line backwards: the bigger a number's size, the more negative and therefore smaller it becomes. For example five is greater than three, but multiply both by negative one and you get negative five, which is actually less than negative three. Forgetting this flip is the number one inequality mistake.
A compound inequality joins two inequality conditions into one statement, using the word and when both must be true at once or the word or when either one is enough. An and statement traps the variable between two bounds, like saying a comfortable room temperature is at least sixty-eight degrees and at most seventy-two degrees. An or statement covers two separate stretches, such as being too cold below sixty or too hot above eighty. Graphing it shows either a single band in the middle or two separate shaded regions.
An angle measures how much you turn between two lines that meet at a point, counted in degrees. A right angle is exactly 90 degrees, like the square corner of a piece of paper. An acute angle is smaller than that (sharp, like a slice of pizza), an obtuse angle is bigger than 90 but less than 180 (a wide-open laptop lid), and a straight angle is exactly 180 degrees, a flat line. Think of a clock: at 3 o'clock the hands make a right angle, and as the minute hand keeps going the angle opens up.
Two angles are complementary when they add up to 90 degrees, and supplementary when they add up to 180 degrees. So if one angle is 30 degrees, its complement is 60 and its supplement is 150. A handy memory trick: 'C' comes before 'S' in the alphabet, and 90 comes before 180. Picture cutting a square corner into two pieces, those pieces are complementary; lay an angle along a straight line and the leftover is its supplement.
The three inside angles of any flat triangle always add up to 180 degrees, no matter the shape. You can feel why with a paper triangle: tear off all three corners and place them tip-to-tip, and they line up into a perfectly straight line, which is 180 degrees. This means if you know two angles you can always find the third by subtracting from 180. It's why a triangle can have at most one right angle or one obtuse angle, never two.
Triangles are named by how many sides have equal length. An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal and all three angles equal to 60 degrees, like a road yield sign. An isosceles triangle has two equal sides and two equal base angles, like the classic shape of a slice of cheese. A scalene triangle has all three sides different lengths, with no two angles the same. You can also name triangles by their angles: right, acute, or obtuse.
A polygon is a closed flat shape made of straight sides, with no curves and no gaps. They're named by their number of sides: a triangle has 3, a quadrilateral 4, a pentagon 5, a hexagon 6, an octagon 8. You see them everywhere, a stop sign is an octagon and a honeybee's comb is built from hexagons because they tile without leaving gaps. A polygon is 'regular' when all its sides and angles are equal, like a perfect snowflake's six-pointed frame.
A quadrilateral is any four-sided polygon, and the family has special members. A rectangle has four right angles, a rhombus has four equal sides, and a square is both at once, four equal sides AND four right angles, like a floor tile. A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides that lean, like a pushed-over rectangle, and a trapezoid has just one pair of parallel sides, like a lampshade seen from the side. Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.
A circle is the set of all points the same distance from a center point. The radius is the distance from the center to the edge, and the diameter is the full distance straight across through the center, which is always exactly twice the radius. The circumference is the distance all the way around the rim, like the length of string it would take to wrap a coin. A chord is any straight line connecting two points on the edge, and the longest possible chord is the diameter.
Pi is the number you get when you divide any circle's circumference (the distance around) by its diameter (the distance across), and amazingly it's the same for every circle, about 3.14. So no matter how big or small the circle, going around is always a little more than three times going across. You can test it by wrapping a string around a can, then comparing it to three widths of the can, you'll have a bit left over. Pi never ends and never repeats, which is why we round it.
Perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside of a shape, measured in plain length units like meters. Area is the amount of flat space inside the shape, measured in square units like square meters. Imagine a garden: the perimeter is the length of fence you need to surround it, and the area is the amount of grass you'd lay inside. Two shapes can share the same perimeter but have very different areas, which is why a square encloses more space than a long skinny rectangle of the same fence length.
Two shapes are congruent when they are exactly the same size and shape, so one could be slid, turned, or flipped to land perfectly on top of the other, like two cutouts from the same cookie cutter. Two shapes are similar when they have the same shape but different sizes, like a photo and its enlarged poster, the angles match but the lengths are scaled up or down by the same factor. So all congruent shapes are also similar, but similar shapes are only congruent when the scale factor is exactly 1.
Parallel lines run in the same direction and stay exactly the same distance apart forever, so they never cross, like the two rails of a train track. Perpendicular lines cross each other to form a right angle, a perfect 90-degree corner, like the lines where a wall meets the floor. A quick test: a capital letter L shows perpendicular lines, while the two long sides of a ladder show parallel lines. Both ideas describe how straight lines relate, either side by side or meeting squarely.
A shape has reflection symmetry when you can fold it along a line and the two halves match exactly, like folding a heart down the middle. That fold line is called the line of symmetry, and some shapes have several, a square has four. A shape has rotational symmetry when you can spin it around its center and it looks the same before completing a full turn, like a pinwheel or a starfish. Butterflies, snowflakes, and faces are full of symmetry, which is part of why we find them pleasing to look at.
The interior angles are the corners inside a polygon, and their total grows in a steady pattern: a triangle's add to 180, a quadrilateral's to 360, and each extra side adds another 180 degrees. The reason is that any polygon can be sliced from one corner into triangles, and each triangle contributes its 180. The exterior angles, the turns you'd make walking around the outside, always add to a full 360 degrees no matter how many sides, just like a person walking once around a city block ends up facing their starting direction again.
Area is the amount of flat space a shape covers, measured in square units like square inches or square meters. Imagine tiling a floor with little square tiles that are each one unit on a side: the area is just how many of those tiles it takes to cover the whole surface with no gaps or overlaps. That's why area is always written with a little 2, like cm², since you are counting squares. A bigger room needs more tiles, so it has a bigger area.
The radius of a circle is the distance from the center point straight out to any spot on the edge. The diameter is the distance all the way across the circle passing through the center, which is exactly two radii laid end to end. So the diameter is always twice the radius. Picture a wheel: the radius is a single spoke from the hub to the rim, and the diameter is a full line straight across through the middle.
Volume is the amount of three-dimensional space something takes up, or how much it can hold inside, measured in cubic units like cubic centimeters. If area is about covering a flat floor with squares, volume is about filling a box with little unit cubes and counting them. That is why volume uses a little 3, like cm³. A moving truck holds more boxes than a shoebox because it has far more volume.
To find the volume of a box, also called a rectangular prism, multiply its length by its width by its height. This works because you first cover the bottom with a layer of unit cubes (that's length times width) and then stack that layer up as many times as the height. Picture filling a fish tank with sugar cubes, layer by layer, until it is full. The answer comes out in cubic units.
Surface area is the total area of all the outer faces of a solid object, the amount of skin you would need to cover it completely. For a box, you find the area of each of the six flat faces and add them all up. Picture wrapping a present: the surface area is how much wrapping paper it takes to cover the whole box. Surface area uses square units, while volume measures the space inside.
A compound or irregular shape is one made by joining simpler shapes together, like an L-shaped room. To find its area, slice it into rectangles and triangles you already know how to handle, find each piece's area, then add them up. Sometimes it is easier to picture a big rectangle and subtract the missing corner. Think of measuring an L-shaped garden by splitting it into two simple rectangles and adding the two answers.
Trigonometry is the study of how the angles and side lengths of triangles connect to each other. The big idea is that in a right triangle, once you fix one angle, the ratios between the sides are locked in no matter how big or small the triangle is. That's why a surveyor can measure the angle up to the top of a mountain and its distance away, then figure out the height without ever climbing it. Trig turns angles you can measure into lengths you can't reach.
A right triangle is any triangle with one square corner of exactly ninety degrees, the kind you see in the corner of a book. The longest side, always sitting opposite that square corner, is called the hypotenuse. The other two sides are named relative to whichever angle you're looking at: the one touching the angle is the adjacent side, and the one across from it is the opposite side. Picture leaning a ladder against a wall: the ladder is the hypotenuse, the wall is one leg, and the ground is the other.
Sine, cosine, and tangent are just three ratios you build from the sides of a right triangle, given one of its angles. Sine is the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse, cosine is the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse, and tangent is the opposite divided by the adjacent. Many people memorize this with SOH-CAH-TOA: Sine = Opposite over Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent over Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite over Adjacent. If you stand and look up at a kite, the angle of your gaze plus one known distance lets these ratios hand you the kite's height.
When you know one angle and one side of a right triangle, you can find another side by choosing the ratio that links them. First decide which sides you have and want: opposite, adjacent, or hypotenuse. Then pick sine, cosine, or tangent so those two sides appear in the formula, plug in your known values, and solve. For example, if a ramp rises at a known angle and you know how long the ramp is, sine of that angle times the ramp length gives the height it reaches.
If you know two sides of a right triangle but not the angle, you run the trig ratios in reverse using the inverse functions, written as arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent (or sin-to-the-minus-one and friends). You form the ratio of the sides you know, then ask the inverse function which angle produces that ratio. Imagine a wheelchair ramp that rises one foot over twelve feet of length: the tangent of the slope angle is one over twelve, so arctangent of that fraction tells you the ramp's angle is gentle, just under five degrees.
Degrees and radians are two different rulers for measuring angles. Degrees split a full turn into a tidy three hundred sixty parts, a habit borrowed from ancient astronomers. A radian instead measures the angle by how far you'd walk along the rim of a circle compared to its radius, so a full turn equals two pi radians, a little over six. Picture wrapping the radius along the edge of a pizza: one radius-length of crust sweeps out exactly one radian.
The Pythagorean identity says that for any angle, sine squared plus cosine squared always equals one. It comes straight from the unit circle: the point on the rim is always a distance of one from the center, and the Pythagorean theorem on its sideways and up-down legs forces those squares to add to one. Picture a person walking a circular track of radius one; no matter where they stand, their east-west distance squared plus their north-south distance squared brings them back to that fixed radius. This single rule lets you find sine if you know cosine, or vice versa.
The angle of elevation is how far you tilt your gaze upward from straight-ahead level to look at something higher, like the top of a flagpole. The angle of depression is the opposite: how far you tilt downward to look at something below you, like a boat seen from a cliff. These angles are the everyday gateway to trig, because pairing the angle with one known distance lets sine, cosine, or tangent reveal a height or distance you can't reach. A lifeguard in a tall chair uses the angle of depression to a swimmer plus the chair height to estimate how far out they are.
The law of sines extends trig to triangles that don't have a right angle. It says each side divided by the sine of the angle across from it gives the same value for all three sides. So if you know one side and its opposite angle, plus one more angle or side, you can find the rest. Surveyors use this to map a far landmark: measure the angle to it from two ends of a known baseline, and the law of sines turns those angles into the distances out to the landmark.
The law of cosines is a beefed-up Pythagorean theorem that works for any triangle, not just right ones. It says one side squared equals the sum of the other two sides squared, minus a correction term that uses the cosine of the angle between them. When that angle is a square corner, the cosine is zero and the formula collapses back into plain old Pythagoras. It's the tool you reach for when you know two sides and the angle wedged between them and want the third side, like finding the straight-line distance between two trails that split apart at a known angle.
Sine and cosine repeat forever because they track a point going around the unit circle, and every full lap brings it back to where it started. If you plot the height of that spinning point over time, you get a smooth up-and-down curve called a wave, rising to a peak, dipping to a trough, and doing it again on a fixed cycle. This is exactly how a child on a swing moves, or how the tide rolls in and out, or how a sound vibrates the air. That endless repeating shape is why trig is the language of anything that cycles.
The mean is the 'balancing point' of a set of numbers: add them all up, then divide by how many there are. It tells you the single value every item would have if you shared the total out equally.
