Say four friends scored 6, 8, 10, and 8 points in a game; the total is 32, and 32 divided by 4 friends is a mean of 8 points each. The mean uses every value, so one very big or very small number can pull it up or down.
The median is the number smack in the middle once you line all your values up from smallest to largest. If there is an odd count, it is the single middle one; if there is an even count, you average the two middle numbers. Line up the ages of five cousins as 4, 7, 9, 12, 40 and the median age is 9, the one in the center. Notice that the median barely cares about that 40-year-old outlier, which is why it often describes 'typical' better than the mean.
The mode is simply the value that shows up most often in your data. A set can have one mode, several modes, or no mode at all if nothing repeats. Imagine a shoe store noting the sizes it sold one morning: 7, 8, 8, 9, 8, 10. Size 8 appears three times, more than any other, so the mode is 8 — the size to keep stocked. The mode is the only average that also works for non-number data like favorite colors.
The range measures how spread out your numbers are: subtract the smallest value from the largest. A big range means the values are scattered widely, while a small range means they huddle close together. If the daily high temperatures one week were 60, 64, 58, 71, and 55 degrees, the range is 71 minus 55, which is 16 degrees. The range is quick to find but only looks at the two extremes, so it ignores everything in between.
A weighted average lets some values count for more than others, instead of treating every number equally. You multiply each value by its 'weight' (how much it matters), add those products, then divide by the total of the weights. Think of a class grade where the final exam counts twice as much as a quiz: if you scored high on the quiz but lower on the exam, the exam's bigger weight pulls your overall grade toward the exam score. This is exactly how report-card grades, batting averages, and stock indexes are built.
A data set is just a collection of related observations gathered to answer a question. Each entry is a 'data point,' and together they form the raw material that statistics works on. If you write down the number of pages you read each night for a month, that list of nightly counts is your data set. Before you can find a mean, median, or anything else, you first need a data set to look at.
Frequency is the count of how many times a particular value appears in your data. Tallying frequencies into a table makes patterns jump out and is the first step toward charts and finding the mode. Suppose you ask classmates their favorite fruit and apple comes up several times, banana a few times, and grape just once — those counts are the frequencies. The value with the highest frequency is the mode, so frequency and mode go hand in hand.
A percentile tells you what percentage of the data falls below a given value. Being in the 90th percentile means you scored higher than about 90 percent of everyone, not that you got 90 percent of the questions right. When a doctor says a child's height is in the 75th percentile, it means roughly three out of four kids the same age are shorter. Percentiles turn a single number into a ranking that shows where it stands in the whole group.
Standard deviation measures how far, on average, the values stray from the mean — it puts a number on the 'typical distance' from the center. A small standard deviation means the data clusters tightly around the mean; a large one means the values are spread out. Imagine two archers whose arrows both average the bullseye: one peppers arrows all over the target (big standard deviation) while the other lands them in a tight cluster (small standard deviation). It is the go-to gauge of consistency, used everywhere from test scores to weather to factory quality checks.
Data is skewed when it leans to one side, with a long tail stretching out toward the high or low end instead of being balanced. In a right-skewed set most values sit on the low side but a few big ones drag a tail to the right, pulling the mean above the median. Household incomes in a town are a classic example: most people earn modest amounts, but a handful of very high earners stretch the tail, so the average income looks higher than what a typical family actually makes. When data is skewed, the median usually describes the 'typical' value better than the mean.
An average rate spreads a total change evenly over the total time or distance, even if the real pace bounced around. For speed, you divide the total distance by the total time — not by averaging the individual speeds. If you drive 120 miles and it takes 3 hours, your average speed is 120 divided by 3, which is 40 miles per hour, whether you were crawling in traffic or zooming on the highway in between. The average rate answers 'overall, how fast?' without worrying about the ups and downs along the way.
The product rule says the log of two numbers multiplied together equals the sum of their individual logs: log(a*b) = log(a) + log(b). It works because logs measure exponents, and multiplying powers means adding the exponents underneath. This is the trick that let astronomers and navigators turn slow multiplication into quick addition for centuries. For example, log(1000) can be found as log(10) + log(100), since 1000 = 10 * 100.
The quotient rule says the log of a division equals the difference of the logs: log(a/b) = log(a) - log(b). It mirrors the product rule because dividing powers means subtracting their exponents. So if you know the logs of the top and bottom of a fraction, you just subtract to get the log of the whole thing. For instance, log(100/10) equals log(100) - log(10).
The power rule lets you bring an exponent out in front of a log as a multiplier: log(a^n) = n * log(a). It works because raising a number to a power repeats the multiplication, which repeats the addition of the exponent. This rule is what makes logs so handy for solving equations where the unknown sits up in an exponent. For example, log(8) can be written as log(2^3) = 3 * log(2).
The natural logarithm, written ln(x), is just a logarithm whose base is the special number e (about 2.718). It answers the question 'e to what power gives x?' and shows up anywhere growth or decay happens continuously, like compound interest or cooling coffee. Because e arises naturally in calculus and the real world, ln is the 'default' log in higher math. For example, ln(e) equals one, since e to the first power is e.
Most calculators only have buttons for base-10 log and natural log, but the change of base formula lets you compute a log in any base: log base b of x equals log(x) / log(b), using whichever common base you like for both. Since the same base cancels in the ratio, the answer is the same no matter which one you pick. This is how you'd find something like a base-2 log on a regular calculator. For example, log base 2 of 8 equals log(8) / log(2).
A logarithm is the inverse operation of an exponential, meaning it undoes raising to a power the way subtraction undoes addition. If b raised to the y equals x, then log base b of x equals y; the log simply hands back the exponent. This is why log base b of (b^x) gives you x, and b raised to (log base b of x) gives you back x. For example, since 2^5 = 32, the log base 2 of 32 is 5.
When the unknown is stuck up in an exponent, you take the log of both sides and use the power rule to pull the exponent down where you can solve for it. The steps are: take log of both sides, move the exponent out front, then divide. This turns an impossible-looking exponential equation into a simple division. For example, to solve 2^x = 10, take logs to get x = log(10) / log(2).
On a logarithmic scale, equal steps along the axis represent multiplying by a fixed factor rather than adding a fixed amount, so each tick might mean ten times larger. This lets you display values that span a huge range, from tiny to enormous, on a single readable chart. Scientists use it for things that grow by multiplication instead of addition. For example, on a log scale the distance from 1 to 10 is the same as the distance from 10 to 100.
The decibel scale measures sound intensity using logarithms because our ears respond to enormous ranges of power, and logs compress that range into manageable numbers. On this scale, adding a fixed number of decibels corresponds to multiplying the sound power by a fixed factor, not just adding a little. That is why a small jump in decibels can mean a big jump in actual sound energy. For example, the difference between a whisper and a jet engine is only a few dozen decibels even though the power difference is gigantic.
The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a liquid is using the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, which is why it runs roughly 0 to 14 instead of spanning huge raw numbers. Because it is logarithmic, each whole step on the scale means a tenfold change in acidity, not just a small change. So a drop of one pH unit means the liquid became ten times more acidic. For example, lemon juice near pH 2 is far more than twice as acidic as water near pH 7.
Earthquake magnitude scales are logarithmic, so each whole-number increase in magnitude represents about ten times more ground shaking measured by a seismograph. This compresses earthquakes that range from barely detectable to catastrophic onto one tidy number line. It also explains why a seemingly small jump in magnitude is actually a massive jump in motion. For example, a magnitude 6 quake produces about ten times the amplitude of a magnitude 5 quake.
Two log values come up constantly: the log of 1 in any base is always 0, and the log of the base itself is always 1. The first is true because any base raised to the power 0 equals 1, and the second because any base raised to the power 1 is just itself. Knowing these instantly speeds up a lot of log work. For example, log base 5 of 1 is 0, and log base 5 of 5 is 1.
Logarithmic growth describes a quantity that rises quickly at first and then slows down more and more, the mirror image of fast-accelerating exponential growth. Its curve keeps climbing but flattens out, because reaching the next level requires a much bigger input each time. You see it whenever early progress is easy but further gains get harder. For example, the amount of practice needed to improve a skill often grows logarithmically: the first gains come fast, then later gains take far more effort.
To add or subtract mod n, you do the normal operation and then take the remainder mod n. The handy part is that you can reduce the inputs first or the answer at the end and get the same result. For example, mod 12, the time 9 + 7 = 16, and 16 mod 12 = 4, so 7 hours after 9 o'clock is 4 o'clock. Subtraction wraps the same way: 2 - 5 mod 12 = -3 mod 12 = 9.
Multiplication mod n works like ordinary multiplication, except you keep only the remainder after dividing by n. A useful shortcut is that you may reduce each factor mod n before multiplying, which keeps the numbers small. For example, mod 7, the product 4 times 5 is 20, and 20 mod 7 = 6. This is the workhorse behind hashing and cryptography, where the same operation runs on huge numbers.
Modular exponentiation finds a number raised to a power, then takes the remainder mod n, without ever computing the giant power directly. The trick is to reduce mod n after each multiplication, and to square repeatedly so you reach big exponents in only a handful of steps. For example, mod 5, three squared is 9, and 9 mod 5 = 4. This is what lets RSA encryption raise numbers to enormous exponents quickly.
The modular inverse of a number a mod n is the number that multiplies with a to give a remainder of 1. It plays the role that dividing plays in ordinary math, since there is no direct division in modular arithmetic. An inverse exists only when a and n share no common factor other than 1. For example, mod 7, the inverse of 3 is 5, because 3 times 5 is 15, and 15 mod 7 = 1.
Two numbers are congruent mod n when they leave the same remainder after dividing by n, which is the same as saying their difference is a multiple of n. We write this with a special three-line equals sign, but the everyday meaning is that the two numbers land on the same spot when you wrap around the cycle. For instance, 17 and 5 are congruent mod 12 because both point to the 5 on a clock face. Congruence sorts every whole number into one of n groups by remainder.
A residue class mod n is the whole set of numbers that share one particular remainder when divided by n. There are exactly n of these classes, usually labeled by the remainders from 0 up to n minus 1. Mod 3, for example, every integer falls into the class of remainder 0, remainder 1, or remainder 2, so numbers like 2, 5, 8, and 11 all belong to the same class. Doing arithmetic mod n really means doing arithmetic on these classes rather than on individual numbers.
The Chinese Remainder Theorem says that if you know a number's remainders for several moduli that share no common factors, there is exactly one matching value within their product. It lets you stitch separate remainder clues back into a single answer. A classic riddle asks for a number leaving remainder 2 when divided by 3 and remainder 3 when divided by 5; the value 8 fits both. Computers use it to break one huge calculation into smaller independent ones run in parallel.
Euler's theorem says that if a number a shares no common factor with n, then a raised to the totient of n leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by n. The totient counts how many numbers below n are coprime to it, and this generalizes Fermat's little theorem to moduli that are not prime. For example, the totient of 10 is 4, and 3 raised to the 4th power is 81, which leaves remainder 1 mod 10. This is the property that makes RSA decryption undo encryption.
Euler's totient of n counts how many whole numbers from 1 up to n share no common factor with n other than 1. For a prime p the answer is simply p minus 1, because every smaller number is coprime to a prime. For 12, the coprime numbers are 1, 5, 7, and 11, so the totient of 12 is 4. This count appears anywhere you need to know how many invertible elements exist mod n.
A quadratic residue mod n is any remainder you can get by squaring a number and reducing mod n. Not every remainder is reachable this way, which is why some numbers have a square root mod n and others do not. Mod 5, squaring 1, 2, 3, and 4 gives remainders 1, 4, 4, and 1, so 1 and 4 are residues while 2 and 3 are non-residues. This split matters in cryptography and in tests for whether a number is a perfect square.
A primitive root mod n is a number whose powers cycle through every nonzero remainder before repeating. It acts like a generator that can reach the whole group of invertible remainders one step at a time. Mod 7, the number 3 is a primitive root because its powers run through 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, and 1, hitting all six nonzero remainders. Primitive roots underpin Diffie-Hellman key exchange, where the cycling makes the secret hard to reverse.
The discrete logarithm asks which exponent you must raise a base to, mod n, in order to land on a given target remainder. It is the modular cousin of the ordinary logarithm, but with a wrapping number line instead of a smooth one. Mod 7, raising 3 to the power 4 gives 81, which is 4 mod 7, so the discrete log of 4 to base 3 is 4. Finding it is believed to be very hard for large n, and that difficulty is the lock behind several encryption schemes.
The familiar divisibility shortcuts are really statements in modular arithmetic. Because 10 leaves remainder 1 mod 9, every power of 10 also leaves remainder 1, so a number and its digit sum are congruent mod 9; that is why adding the digits tests divisibility by 9. The same idea, called casting out nines, lets you spot arithmetic mistakes by checking remainders. For 1234, the digits add to 10, which is 1 mod 9, so 1234 also leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9.
Stars and bars counts how many ways to distribute identical items into distinct groups. To split n identical items among k groups, you imagine n stars in a row and slide in k-1 dividers (bars); each arrangement of stars and bars is one way. The count is the number of ways to choose where the bars go among the n + k - 1 total positions, written C(n + k - 1, k - 1). For example, handing out 7 identical candies to 3 kids (allowing zero) is C(7 + 3 - 1, 3 - 1) = C(9, 2) ways.
When you arrange objects in a circle, rotations that look the same shouldn't be counted twice, so there are fewer arrangements than in a straight line. For n people around a round table, fix one person's seat as a reference and arrange the rest, giving (n - 1)! distinct arrangements instead of n!. For example, 4 friends around a table can be seated in (4 - 1)! = 3! = 6 ways. If the circle can also be flipped over (like beads on a necklace), you divide by 2 more because a mirror image counts as the same.
When some items are identical, swapping two copies doesn't make a new arrangement, so you must divide out the duplicates. To arrange n items where one value repeats a times, another b times, and so on, the count is n! divided by (a! times b! times ...). For example, the word LEVEL has 5 letters with L twice and E twice, so it has 5! / (2! times 2!) = 120 / 4 = 30 distinct arrangements. This is why a word with all different letters has more anagrams than one with repeats.
The pigeonhole principle says that if you put more items into fewer categories than there are items, at least one category must hold two or more items. More generally, if you place n items into k boxes, some box ends up with at least the ceiling of n divided by k items. For example, in any group of 13 people at least two share a birth month, because there are only 12 months. It feels obvious, but it proves surprising facts, like the certainty that two people in a large city have the exact same number of hairs.
Inclusion-exclusion counts items in overlapping groups without double-counting the overlaps. For two sets you add their sizes and subtract the overlap: |A or B| = |A| + |B| - |A and B|. For three sets you add the singles, subtract every pair overlap, then add back the triple overlap. For example, if 30 students take art, 25 take music, and 10 take both, the number taking at least one is 30 + 25 - 10 = 45, not 55.
A derangement is an arrangement where no item ends up in its original position. The classic story is a hat-check that returns hats randomly: how many ways can everyone get the wrong hat? The count of derangements of n items, written !n, can be found from a formula or built up step by step, and remarkably the fraction of permutations that are derangements settles near 1 over e (about 37 percent) as n grows. For example, the 3 derangements of 1,2,3 are 2-3-1, 3-1-2, and... checking each spot differs from its label gives exactly 2 valid ones for n = 3.
Catalan numbers count many things that involve nesting or matching without crossing, like valid arrangements of parentheses. The nth Catalan number equals C(2n, n) divided by (n + 1), giving the sequence 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 and onward. For example, there are 5 ways to fully parenthesize a product of 4 factors, and 5 distinct shapes of a binary tree with 3 internal nodes. The same number counts paths that stay above a diagonal and ways to cut a polygon into triangles, which is why mathematicians find it everywhere.
The binomial theorem expands a power of a sum, (a + b)^n, into a tidy sum of terms. Each term looks like C(n, k) times a^(n-k) times b^k, and the coefficients C(n, k) are exactly the entries in Pascal's triangle. The combinatorics reason is that expanding the product means choosing b from k of the n factors, and there are C(n, k) ways to choose them. For example, (a + b)^3 = a^3 + 3a^2 b + 3ab^2 + b^3, where 1, 3, 3, 1 is row 3 of Pascal's triangle.
Pascal's triangle is a triangle of numbers where each entry is the sum of the two numbers directly above it, with 1s down both edges. Row n (counting from 0) holds the combination values C(n, 0) through C(n, n), so the triangle is a lookup table for how many ways to choose k things from n. For example, row 4 reads 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, telling you C(4, 2) = 6 ways to choose 2 items from 4. The addition rule that builds it mirrors a real choice: an item is either in your group or not, splitting each count into the two above it.
The multiplication principle says that if one choice can be made in m ways and a second independent choice in n ways, the two together can be made in m times n ways, and this extends to any number of stages. It is the engine behind almost every counting formula. For example, a menu with 3 mains, 4 sides, and 2 drinks offers 3 times 4 times 2 = 24 different meals. The key condition is that each later choice has the same number of options no matter what you picked earlier.
The hockey stick identity says that summing a diagonal of combination values in Pascal's triangle gives the single value just below and to the side, so the sum bends like a hockey stick. In symbols, C(r, r) + C(r+1, r) + ... + C(n, r) = C(n+1, r+1). For example, C(2, 2) + C(3, 2) + C(4, 2) = 1 + 3 + 6 = 10, which equals C(5, 3) = 10. It is handy for collapsing a long sum of choose-values into one term.
A k-permutation is an ordered selection of k items chosen from n, written P(n, k) or nPr. Because order matters and items aren't reused, you multiply the shrinking pool: n choices for the first slot, n-1 for the second, down through k factors, which equals n! divided by (n - k)!. For example, awarding gold, silver, and bronze to 8 runners gives P(8, 3) = 8 times 7 times 6 = 336 outcomes. Dividing a k-permutation count by k! removes the ordering and turns it into a combination.
A bijection is a perfect one-to-one matching between two sets, and if such a matching exists the sets must have exactly the same size. Combinatorialists use this to count a hard-to-count set by pairing each of its items with an item in an easier set. For example, the number of subsets of a 3-element set equals the number of length-3 strings of yes/no, because each subset matches the string saying whether each element is included, giving 2 times 2 times 2 = 8. A related trick, double counting, finds the size of one set by counting the same collection two different ways and setting the answers equal.
A one-sided limit asks what value a function approaches as you slide toward a point from only one direction: the left-hand limit comes from smaller x-values, the right-hand limit from larger ones. The two-sided limit exists only when the left and right limits agree. Think of walking toward a doorway from inside the room versus from the hallway: if you'd arrive at the same spot either way, the overall limit exists; if not, it doesn't.
Limit laws let you break a complicated limit into easier pieces: the limit of a sum is the sum of the limits, the limit of a product is the product of the limits, and the limit of a constant times a function is that constant times the limit. They only apply when each individual limit actually exists. It's like splitting a grocery bill into separate items, totaling each, then adding them up rather than wrestling with the whole receipt at once.
For many friendly functions, you can find a limit just by plugging the target x-value straight into the formula. This works whenever the function is continuous there, meaning it has no break, jump, or hole at that point. Polynomials always allow this, and most everyday functions do too away from trouble spots. It's like reading a thermometer right at noon because the temperature changes smoothly with no sudden jumps.
An indeterminate form shows up when direct substitution gives an expression like zero divided by zero or infinity minus infinity, which doesn't tell you the answer by itself. The form is 'indeterminate' because the true limit could turn out to be anything depending on how the pieces shrink or grow. You have to do more work, such as factoring or simplifying, to reveal it. It's like being told two runners are 'tied' without knowing whether both are sprinting or both are crawling.
When substitution gives zero over zero, try factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling a shared factor. The cancellation removes the troublesome term that was forcing the zero in the bottom, leaving a simpler expression you can then plug into. The original function had a hole at that point, but the limit still exists because the function gets arbitrarily close to that value nearby. It's like untangling a knot in a string before measuring the length you actually care about.
When a limit involves a square root and substitution gives zero over zero, multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate, which is the same expression with the opposite sign in the middle. Multiplying by the conjugate turns the difference of roots into a difference of squares, clearing the root and exposing a factor you can cancel. After simplifying, substitute the value as usual. It's like rationalizing to clear a stubborn radical out of a fraction before you can work with it.
A limit at infinity asks what value a function settles toward as x grows without bound in the positive or negative direction, describing the function's long-run end behavior. For a rational function, compare the degrees of top and bottom: the limit follows whichever part grows faster, often approaching a horizontal asymptote. A common trick is dividing every term by the highest power of x so most terms shrink toward zero. It's like asking what your average speed approaches over a road trip that never ends.
A horizontal asymptote is a horizontal line that a graph hugs as x heads toward positive or negative infinity, and it is defined precisely by the function's limits at infinity. If the limit as x grows large equals some fixed value, the line at that height is a horizontal asymptote. A function can approach the same asymptote on both ends or different ones on each side. Think of a cooling cup of coffee leveling off toward room temperature but never quite reaching it.
An infinite limit happens when a function grows without bound as x approaches a certain value, usually because the denominator shrinks toward zero while the numerator does not. We say the limit is positive or negative infinity to describe the runaway behavior, even though no actual number is reached. These points produce vertical asymptotes, where the graph shoots up or down along a vertical line. It's like the screech of feedback as a microphone gets closer and closer to its speaker.
The squeeze theorem says that if a function is trapped between two other functions that both approach the same limit at a point, then the squeezed function must approach that limit too. It's handy when a function wiggles too wildly to evaluate directly but can be bounded above and below by tamer functions. Because the upper and lower bounds meet, there's nowhere else for the trapped function to go. It's like a younger sibling walking between two parents who arrive at the same door, so the child must arrive there as well.
A function is continuous at a point when three things all hold: the function is defined there, the limit exists there, and that limit equals the function's actual value. In plain terms, the curve has no hole, jump, or break at that spot, so you could trace it without lifting your pencil. If any of the three conditions fails, the function is discontinuous there. It's like a smoothly paved road versus one with a missing slab you'd have to hop over.
A removable discontinuity is a single missing point, a hole, where the limit exists but the function is either undefined there or defined to the wrong value. Because the limit exists, you could 'remove' the gap simply by redefining the function at that one point to match the limit. These often appear after a factor cancels in a fraction. It's like a knitted scarf with one dropped stitch: the pattern clearly tells you what belongs there, so the fix is a single point.
The epsilon-delta definition makes 'approaching' precise: a limit equals L if, for every tiny tolerance epsilon you demand around L, there is a small distance delta around the target x so that staying within delta keeps the output within epsilon of L. In short, no matter how strict the output target, you can always find a tight enough input window to meet it. The challenger names a tolerance and you must respond with a matching closeness. It's like promising a thermostat can hold the room within any tightness someone asks, as long as they let you set the dial close enough.
Implicit differentiation finds a derivative when y is tangled up with x and you cannot easily solve for y by itself, like a circle equation x^2 + y^2 = r^2. The trick is to differentiate both sides with respect to x while treating y as a hidden function of x, so every time you differentiate a y term you tack on a dy/dx by the chain rule. Then you collect all the dy/dx pieces on one side and solve for dy/dx algebraically. It is like knowing how fast a balloon's height changes even though height and width are baked into one stretched-shape equation rather than written as height equals something.
The second derivative is just the derivative of the derivative: you differentiate once to get the rate of change, then differentiate that result again. It measures how the rate itself is changing, so a positive second derivative means the curve bends upward like a smile and a negative one means it bends downward like a frown. In a moving car, the first derivative of position is speed and the second derivative is acceleration, telling you whether your speed is rising or falling. So when your foot presses the gas harder, the second derivative is positive even before you reach top speed.
A critical point is an input where the derivative is either zero or undefined, and these are the spots where a function can switch from rising to falling or the other way around. Because the derivative is the slope, a slope of zero means the curve has momentarily flattened out, which is exactly what happens at the top of a hill or the bottom of a valley. To hunt for the highest or lowest value of a function, you first solve where the derivative equals zero to get your candidate locations. Think of tossing a ball: at the instant it reaches its peak height, its upward speed is zero, and that peak is the critical point.
The first derivative test decides whether a critical point is a local maximum, a local minimum, or neither by checking the sign of the derivative just before and just after that point. If the derivative is positive then negative, the function rose and then fell, so you sat at a peak; if it goes negative then positive, you bottomed out in a valley. If the sign does not flip, the point is just a flat pause, not a true high or low. It is like walking a trail: if the ground tilts up then tilts down, the spot in between was a summit.
The second derivative test offers a shortcut for classifying a critical point where the first derivative is zero: just plug that point into the second derivative. If the second derivative is positive the curve is bending upward like a bowl, so you have a local minimum, and if it is negative the curve bends downward like a dome, giving a local maximum. When the second derivative is zero the test is inconclusive and you fall back on the first derivative test. Picture a marble: it settles in a bowl-shaped dip (positive concavity, a minimum) but rolls off a dome-shaped bump (negative concavity, a maximum).
An inflection point is where a curve changes its concavity, switching from bending upward to bending downward or the reverse, which shows up as the second derivative changing sign. It is not about the curve being highest or lowest, but about the moment its bend reverses direction. You find candidates by setting the second derivative to zero and then confirming the sign actually flips on either side. Think of an S-shaped slide: there is a point in the middle where it stops curving one way and starts curving the other, and that turning of the bend is the inflection point.
Related rates problems link two or more quantities through an equation and ask how fast one changes given how fast another changes. You differentiate the connecting equation with respect to time, which pulls in a rate (a per-second term) for every changing variable, then plug in the known rate to solve for the unknown one. The key insight is that the chain rule ties each variable's change to the clock. A classic example is a ladder sliding down a wall: because the ladder length is fixed, knowing how fast the foot slides outward lets you compute how fast the top slides down.
A partial derivative measures how a function of several variables changes when you nudge just one input while holding all the others frozen. You differentiate normally with respect to the chosen variable and treat every other variable as if it were a fixed constant. This lets you isolate the influence of a single ingredient in a recipe with many. Imagine the temperature in a room depending on both your distance from the heater and the time of day: the partial derivative with respect to distance tells you how temperature changes as you step closer, pretending the clock has stopped.
You can multiply numbers in any order and the answer stays the same. Picture 4 rows of 3 dots (12 dots) versus 3 rows of 4 dots (also 12 dots) — same grid, just turned sideways. So 4 x 3 = 3 x 4 = 12. This is handy because you can pick the easier order to multiply.
The associative property says that when you add (or multiply) three or more numbers, how you group them with parentheses does not change the answer. (2 + 3) + 4 gives 5 + 4 = 9, and 2 + (3 + 4) gives 2 + 7 = 9. Same with multiplying. It lets you regroup numbers to make the math easier.
Multiplying any number by 1 gives back that same number, since one group of something is just the something. That makes 1 the multiplicative identity. So 8 x 1 = 8 and 1 x 256 = 256. It works for fractions too: 3/4 x 1 = 3/4.
Dividing asks 'how many groups of this size fit?' 12 divided by 3 asks how many 3s fit in 12 (answer 4). But 12 divided by 0 asks how many 0s fit in 12 — and zeros never add up to 12 no matter how many you use. There is no sensible answer, so dividing by zero is left undefined.
Multiplication is just a shortcut for repeated addition, so it represents a bundled-up group that should be counted as one chunk first. In 5 + 2 x 3, the 2 x 3 means 'two threes,' a single bundle worth 6. We add that bundle to 5 to get 11. Doing it the other way would break what the expression really means.
When operations are at the same level — like multiplication and division, or addition and subtraction — you work them from left to right, like reading. For 12 / 2 x 3, you do 12 / 2 = 6 first, then 6 x 3 = 18. Doing 2 x 3 first would give the wrong answer, so the left-to-right rule keeps things consistent.
Addition and subtraction are inverse operations — they undo each other. If 8 + 5 = 13, then 13 - 5 = 8 and 13 - 8 = 5. This is why you can check a subtraction by adding back: to test 20 - 7 = 13, add 13 + 7 and see if you get 20. You do, so it's correct.
Division and multiplication are inverse operations. If 6 x 7 = 42, then 42 / 7 = 6 and 42 / 6 = 7. So you can check a division by multiplying back: to test 56 / 8 = 7, compute 7 x 8 and see if it returns 56. It does, so the answer is right. Knowing your times tables makes division much easier.
A remainder is what's left over when something can't be split evenly. Sharing 17 cookies among 5 friends gives each friend 3 cookies (5 x 3 = 15), with 2 cookies left over. So 17 / 5 = 3 remainder 2. The remainder is always smaller than the number you're dividing by, or you could give out more.
To turn an improper fraction into a mixed number, divide the top by the bottom. The whole-number quotient is your whole part, the remainder becomes the new top, and the bottom stays the same. For 11/4, divide 11 by 4 to get 2 remainder 3, so 11/4 = 2 and 3/4. It's just asking how many whole groups fit.
To turn a mixed number into an improper fraction, multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and put it over the same denominator. For 3 and 1/2: multiply 3 x 2 = 6, add 1 to get 7, keep the 2 on the bottom, so 3 and 1/2 = 7/2. This makes mixed numbers easier to multiply and divide.
A common denominator is a shared bottom number for two fractions, which you need to add, subtract, or compare them. The easiest choice is the least common multiple of the denominators. For 1/4 and 1/6, the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12, so rewrite as 3/12 and 2/12. Now both fractions speak the same 'twelfths' language.
Multiplying by a fraction less than one means taking a part of something, so the result is smaller than the start. Half of 10 is 5, and a quarter of 8 is 2. The word 'of' in math often means multiply: 1/2 of 6 is 1/2 x 6 = 3. This surprises people who expect multiplying to always make things bigger.
To divide by a fraction, flip the second fraction upside down (its reciprocal) and multiply. So 1/2 / 1/4 becomes 1/2 x 4/1 = 4/2 = 2. This makes sense: how many quarters fit in a half? Two. The 'keep, change, flip' phrase helps: keep the first, change divide to multiply, flip the second.
Any whole number can be written as a fraction by putting it over 1, since dividing by 1 changes nothing: 5 = 5/1. Also, a fraction whose top equals its bottom equals one whole: 4/4 = 1, 7/7 = 1. This helps when you multiply or divide a whole number by a fraction, because everything is now a fraction.
After the decimal point, each place is ten times smaller than the one before. The first place is tenths (1/10), the second is hundredths (1/100), the third is thousandths (1/1000). In 0.642, the 6 means six tenths, the 4 means four hundredths, and the 2 means two thousandths. Reading these places helps you compare decimals.
Adding zeros at the end of a decimal doesn't change its value. 0.5, 0.50, and 0.500 are all the same amount — five tenths — because the extra zeros mean zero hundredths and zero thousandths, which add nothing. This trick is useful when you want decimals to have the same number of places so you can line them up and compare or add.
Multiply decimals as if they were whole numbers, then count how many digits are after the decimal points in both factors and put that many in your answer. For 0.3 x 0.4: ignore the points and do 3 x 4 = 12; there are two decimal digits total, so the answer is 0.12. The point placement keeps the size of the answer correct.
After multiplying decimals as whole numbers, count the total decimal digits in both numbers you multiplied, then place the point that many spots from the right of your answer. For 1.25 x 1.2: 125 x 12 = 1500; there are 3 decimal digits total (two in 1.25, one in 1.2), so move the point three places left to get 1.500, which is 1.5.
To divide by a decimal, slide the decimal point in the divisor to make it a whole number, then slide the point in the dividend the same number of places. For 6.4 / 0.8, move both points one place right to get 64 / 8 = 8. This works because you're really multiplying top and bottom by the same power of ten, which keeps the answer the same.
Multiplying by 10, 100, or 1000 moves the decimal point to the right (1, 2, or 3 places); dividing moves it to the left the same way. So 4.7 x 100 = 470, and 53 / 10 = 5.3. The number of zeros tells you how many places to slide the point. This is a fast shortcut that needs no long multiplication or division.
A repeating decimal has a digit or group of digits that goes on forever. When you divide and the remainder keeps coming back, the decimal repeats. 1/3 = 0.3333... and 2/11 = 0.181818... We mark the repeating part with a bar over it or with dots (...). Repeating decimals come from fractions whose bottoms have factors other than 2 and 5.
A terminating decimal stops after a certain number of digits instead of repeating forever. 1/4 = 0.25 and 3/8 = 0.375 both end. A fraction terminates when its simplified bottom number is made only of 2s and 5s (the factors of ten), because then it can be rewritten as something over 10, 100, or 1000.
Money uses decimals because a dollar splits into 100 cents, just like the hundredths place. So 3.45 dollars is 3 dollars and 45 cents. The first decimal place is dimes (tenths of a dollar) and the second is pennies (hundredths). When you add prices, line up the decimal points so dollars match dollars and cents match cents.
Round decimals to easy whole numbers to estimate and check your work. To estimate 4.8 + 3.1, round to 5 + 3 = 8, so the real answer (7.9) should be near 8. If you got 79, the misplaced decimal point would stand out right away. Estimation is your safety net for catching decimal-point mistakes.
Think of a number line: adding a positive moves right, adding a negative moves left. So 5 + (-3) means start at 5 and step 3 to the left, landing on 2. And -2 + (-4) steps left twice, reaching -6. Adding a negative is the same as subtracting that amount: 5 + (-3) equals 5 - 3.
Subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive — two minuses make a plus. So 4 - (-2) becomes 4 + 2 = 6. Picture it as removing a debt: taking away something you owed leaves you better off. The double negative flips direction, so 'minus a negative' moves you to the right on the number line.
When multiplying, count the negative signs. A positive times a negative is negative: 4 x (-3) = -12. A negative times a negative is positive: (-4) x (-3) = 12, because the second negative flips the first. The rule: same signs give a positive answer, different signs give a negative answer.
Division follows the same sign rule as multiplication. Different signs give a negative answer: -12 / 3 = -4 and 12 / -3 = -4. Same signs give a positive answer: -12 / -3 = 4. Just divide the numbers normally, then decide the sign by checking whether the two signs are the same (positive) or different (negative).
Integers are whole numbers and their negatives, plus zero: ...-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3... They have no fractions or decimals. Whole numbers are just the non-negative integers (0 and up), so integers add in the negatives. Temperatures, scores, and floors above and below ground are all real-world integers.
A cube number comes from multiplying a number by itself three times. 2 cubed is 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, written 2^3. It's called cubing because that many small cubes can be stacked into a bigger cube: 8 little cubes form a 2-by-2-by-2 cube. The first cube numbers are 1, 8, 27, 64, 125.
Any number to the first power is just itself: 7^1 = 7. And any nonzero number to the zero power equals 1: 5^0 = 1. The zero rule comes from a pattern: 2^3=8, 2^2=4, 2^1=2, and each step divides by 2, so 2^0 = 1. It seems strange, but it keeps the exponent rules working smoothly.
To change a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and simplify. 40% becomes 40/100, which reduces to 2/5. 75% becomes 75/100 = 3/4. Since percent means 'out of 100,' the 100 is your starting denominator every time. Then just simplify with the greatest common factor.
To find 10% of any number, just move the decimal point one place to the left. 10% of 80 is 8, and 10% of 45 is 4.5. From there you can build other percents: 20% is double the 10% (16), 5% is half of it (4), and 15% is 10% plus 5%. This makes tips and discounts easy to do in your head.
A percent increase tells how much something grew compared to its starting size. Find the increase, then compare it to the original. If a price goes from 20 to 25, the increase is 5; 5 out of 20 is 5/20 = 0.25 = 25% increase. The key is always comparing the change to the starting amount, not the new amount.
A percent decrease tells how much something shrank compared to its starting size. Find the drop, then compare it to the original. If a price falls from 50 to 40, the drop is 10; 10 out of 50 is 10/50 = 0.20 = 20% decrease. Like percent increase, you always compare the change to the original amount.
A discount is a percent taken off the original price. To find the sale price, figure the discount amount and subtract it. A 30% discount on a 40 dollar item: 30% of 40 is 12, so you save 12 and pay 40 - 12 = 28. A shortcut: paying after a 30% discount means paying 70%, so 0.70 x 40 = 28 directly.
A rate is a ratio that compares two different kinds of things, like miles and hours. A unit rate tells how much per ONE — like miles per hour. If a car goes 120 miles in 2 hours, divide to get the unit rate: 120 / 2 = 60 miles per hour. Unit rates make it easy to compare deals, like cost per item.
A proportion says two ratios are equal. If 2 apples cost 1 dollar, then 6 apples cost 3 dollars, because 2/1 = 6/3. You can solve proportions by scaling: 2 apples to 6 apples is times 3, so the cost is also times 3. Proportions help with recipes, maps, and figuring out 'if this, then how much of that.'
Doubling and halving makes multiplying easier: cut one number in half and double the other, keeping the product the same. To do 16 x 5, halve 16 to 8 and double 5 to 10, giving 8 x 10 = 80. It works because you multiply by 1/2 and by 2, which cancel. Use it when one number is even and the other is awkward.
Friendly numbers are easy combinations you can spot to make mental math faster. Look for pairs that add to round numbers. To add 8 + 7 + 2, notice 8 + 2 = 10 first, then add 7 to get 17. Or break a number apart: 47 + 25 is 47 + 3 + 22 = 50 + 22 = 72. Rearranging into round numbers makes the math smooth.
Division can mean repeatedly subtracting the same number until you reach zero, counting how many times you did it. 12 / 3 asks how many 3s you can take from 12: 12 - 3 - 3 - 3 - 3 = 0, that's four subtractions, so the answer is 4. It can also mean sharing 12 things equally into 3 groups — same answer.
Benchmark fractions like 0, 1/2, and 1 are reference points you compare other fractions to. To tell if 5/8 is big or small, notice 4/8 is 1/2, so 5/8 is a little more than half. And 2/9 is less than half because half of 9 is 4.5 and 2 is below that. Benchmarks let you estimate and compare without exact math.
To subtract mixed numbers, subtract the fraction parts and the whole parts. Sometimes the top fraction is too small — then borrow one whole and turn it into a fraction. For 3 and 1/4 minus 1 and 3/4: borrow one whole from the 3, making it 2 and 5/4, then subtract to get 1 and 2/4 = 1 and 1/2. Borrowing works just like with whole numbers.
A fraction is really a division problem: the line means 'divided by.' So 3/4 means 3 divided by 4. If 3 friends share 4 cookies... wait, flip it: 4 cookies shared by 5 people is 4/5 of a cookie each. This is why dividing the top by the bottom turns any fraction into a decimal.
When fractions have the same top number, the one with the smaller bottom is bigger. That's because a bigger bottom means the whole is cut into more, smaller pieces. So 1/3 is bigger than 1/4 — cutting a pizza into 3 pieces gives bigger slices than cutting it into 4. Same goes for 2/5 versus 2/7: fifths are bigger than sevenths.
A few fraction-decimal pairs are worth knowing by heart because they pop up everywhere: 1/2 = 0.5, 1/4 = 0.25, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2, 1/10 = 0.1, and 1/3 = 0.333... Memorizing these lets you switch between forms instantly, which speeds up percents, money, and measuring problems.
Rounding to a bigger place uses the same rule: look at the digit just to the right of that place. To round 462 to the nearest hundred, look at the tens digit (6); since it's 5 or more, round up to 500. To round 4,231 to the nearest thousand, look at the hundreds digit (2); it's 4 or less, so round down to 4,000.
Front-end estimation uses just the leftmost digits to get a quick rough answer. To estimate 412 + 365, add the front digits: 400 + 300 = 700, so the answer is around 700 (it's 777). It's faster than full rounding and great for a fast sanity check, though it tends to underestimate a little since it ignores the smaller places.
Breaking apart (decomposing) splits a number into easy chunks by place value to make adding simpler. To add 47 + 36, split into tens and ones: 40 + 30 = 70 and 7 + 6 = 13, then 70 + 13 = 83. You can recombine however you like as long as you use all the parts. It turns one hard sum into a few easy ones.
To multiply a two-digit number by 11, add its two digits and place the sum between them. For 11 x 36: add 3 + 6 = 9, put it between the 3 and 6, giving 396. If the digit sum is 10 or more, carry the extra: 11 x 57 is 5, then 5+7=12 (write 2, carry 1 to the 5 making 6), giving 627. A fun shortcut for any two-digit number.
To multiply by 5 fast, multiply by 10 (add a zero) and take half — because 5 is half of 10. For 5 x 48: 48 x 10 = 480, then half of 480 is 240. Or halve first: half of 48 is 24, times 10 is 240. Either way you turn a times-5 into an easy times-10 and a halving.
A fact family is a group of related addition and subtraction (or multiplication and division) facts using the same three numbers. The numbers 3, 5, and 8 make: 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 3 = 8, 8 - 3 = 5, 8 - 5 = 3. Learning one fact gives you the whole family, since they're just the same relationship seen different ways.
A number bond shows how a number splits into two parts that add back to the whole. The number 10 can bond as 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, and so on. Knowing the bonds of 10 makes mental addition fast: to add 8 + 5, take 2 from the 5 to complete 10 (8 + 2), then add the leftover 3 for 13.
Partial products multiply each place value separately, then add. For 23 x 4, split 23 into 20 and 3: do 20 x 4 = 80 and 3 x 4 = 12, then add to get 92. This is the distributive property in action and shows clearly where each piece of the answer comes from, which makes the standard algorithm easier to understand.
The area model draws a rectangle split into boxes to multiply by place value. For 12 x 13, make a 2-by-2 grid splitting into 10 and 2 across, 10 and 3 down. Fill the boxes: 100, 30, 20, 6. Add them all: 100 + 30 + 20 + 6 = 156. The picture shows why multiplying multi-digit numbers needs every part-times-every-part.
To estimate a multiplication, round each factor to an easy number, then multiply. For 38 x 21, round to 40 x 20 = 800, so the real answer (798) is close. Estimating products helps you check that you didn't misplace a digit — if your calculator showed 79.8 or 7,980, the estimate of 800 would flag the error.
In PEMDAS, exponents come right after parentheses and before any multiplying or dividing. For 2 + 3 x 2^2: first the exponent 2^2 = 4, then multiply 3 x 4 = 12, then add 2 to get 14. Doing the exponent late would give the wrong answer, so always handle powers early — just after anything inside parentheses.
Parentheses group part of an expression so it's done first, even overriding the normal order. Without them, 2 + 3 x 4 = 14, but with them, (2 + 3) x 4 = 5 x 4 = 20. They let you change the meaning on purpose. Inside parentheses you still follow the order of operations, then bring the result out to finish.
Zero holds a place open so the other digits keep their correct value. In 308, the 0 shows there are no tens, keeping the 3 in the hundreds spot and the 8 in the ones. Without the placeholder zero, 308 would collapse to 38, a totally different number. That's why our number system needs zero to write big numbers clearly.
The signs > (greater than) and < (less than) compare two numbers. The open, wide side faces the bigger number and the point faces the smaller one — like a hungry mouth eating the larger amount. So 7 > 3 reads 'seven is greater than three,' and 2 < 9 reads 'two is less than nine.' The = sign means the two are equal.
There are neat patterns when adding odd and even numbers. Even + even = even (4 + 6 = 10). Odd + odd = even (3 + 5 = 8). Even + odd = odd (4 + 3 = 7). The same idea works for multiplying: an answer is even unless every number multiplied is odd. These rules help you predict and check answers quickly.
Rounding money to the nearest dollar uses the cents: if cents are 50 or more, round up; if 49 or less, round down. So 7.62 rounds to 8 dollars and 4.30 rounds to 4 dollars. To round to the nearest dime, look at the pennies the same way: 3.47 becomes 3.50. Rounding money helps you estimate a shopping total fast.
To find change, subtract the cost from the money paid. If something costs 6.40 and you pay with a 10, the change is 10.00 - 6.40 = 3.60. A cashier trick is 'counting up': start at 6.40 and add coins and bills to reach 10 — 60 cents gets to 7, then 3 dollars gets to 10, so the change is 3.60.
An average (mean) evens out a set of numbers into one typical value. Add all the numbers, then divide by how many there are. For the scores 8, 6, and 10: add to get 24, divide by 3 numbers, and the average is 8. It's like sharing the total equally among the items. Averages summarize a group with a single number.
When you must borrow but the next column is a zero, keep moving left until you find a digit you can borrow from, turning the zeros into 9s along the way. For 300 - 124: you can't take 4 from 0, and the next column is also 0, so borrow from the 3. It becomes 2, the middle 0 becomes 9, and the last 0 becomes 10. Now subtract to get 176.
To estimate a division, change the numbers to a nearby fact you know. For 423 / 7, think of the close basic fact 420 / 7 = 60, so the answer is about 60 (it's 60 remainder 3). Picking compatible numbers — ones that divide cleanly — gives a quick estimate to check your real answer and to spot a misplaced digit.
In long division, if the number you're dividing into is too small at a step, you write a 0 in the answer and bring down the next digit. For 618 / 6: 6 into 6 is 1, then 6 into 1 doesn't fit so write 0, bring down the 8 to make 18, and 6 into 18 is 3. The answer is 103. The zero keeps every digit in its right place.
To multiply three numbers, multiply two of them first, then multiply that result by the third. For 2 x 3 x 5: do 2 x 3 = 6, then 6 x 5 = 30. Thanks to the associative and commutative properties, you can choose any order or grouping — picking 2 x 5 = 10 first, then x 3, also gives 30, and is often easier.
This mental trick rounds a number to something easy, does the math, then fixes the result. To add 198 + 47, round 198 up to 200, add to get 247, then subtract the 2 you added back, giving 245. To subtract 53 - 19, take 20 (53 - 20 = 33) then add back 1 to get 34. You compensate for the rounding at the end.
A hundredths grid is a 10-by-10 square with 100 small boxes, where the whole grid is 1. Shading boxes shows decimals: shade 30 boxes for 0.30, and 7 boxes for 0.07. A whole column of 10 boxes is one tenth (0.1). Grids make it easy to see that 0.30 is bigger than 0.07 and that 0.5 fills exactly half the grid.
Commas split big numbers into groups of three digits, and each group has a name: ones, thousands, millions. To read 4,827,015, say the millions group then the thousands group then the ones: 'four million, eight hundred twenty-seven thousand, fifteen.' Reading each three-digit chunk and adding its group name makes huge numbers manageable.
To make more or less of a recipe, multiply every ingredient by the same number. To double a recipe that needs 3/4 cup of flour, compute 3/4 x 2 = 6/4 = 1 and 1/2 cups. To halve it, multiply by 1/2: 3/4 x 1/2 = 3/8 cup. The key is using the same factor on every ingredient so the proportions stay correct.
To compare numbers written in different forms, change them all to the same form — decimals are usually easiest. To compare 1/2, 0.4, and 45%, convert: 1/2 = 0.5, 0.4 stays, 45% = 0.45. Now ordering is clear: 0.4 < 0.45 < 0.5, so the order is 0.4, then 45%, then 1/2. One common form makes comparing simple.
To multiply a fraction by a whole number, multiply the whole number by the top and keep the bottom. For 3 x 2/5: 3 x 2 = 6 over 5, giving 6/5, which is 1 and 1/5. It makes sense as repeated addition: 2/5 + 2/5 + 2/5 = 6/5. Simplify or convert to a mixed number at the end if you like.
To divide a whole number by a fraction, write the whole over 1, flip the fraction, and multiply. For 4 / (1/2): that's 4/1 x 2/1 = 8. This makes sense — how many halves are in 4 wholes? Eight. Dividing by a fraction smaller than one gives an answer BIGGER than you started with, which surprises a lot of people.
If you know a fraction of a whole, you can work backward to the whole. If 3/4 of a group is 12, then 1/4 is 12 / 3 = 4, so the whole (4/4) is 4 x 4 = 16. The trick is to find one unit piece first by dividing, then build up to the full whole. This reverses 'finding a fraction of a number.'
Use the benchmarks 0, 1/2, and 1 to estimate fraction sums quickly. For 7/8 + 1/12, notice 7/8 is close to 1 and 1/12 is close to 0, so the sum is about 1. For 5/9 + 4/7, both are near 1/2, so the sum is about 1/2 + 1/2 = 1. Estimating tells you if your exact answer is reasonable.
You can only add fractions when the pieces are the same size. 1/2 + 1/3 isn't 2/5, because halves and thirds are different-sized pieces — like adding apples and oranges. Switching both to sixths (3/6 + 2/6) makes the pieces equal, so you can count them: 5/6. The common denominator gives every piece a matching size.
Measurements use decimals to show parts of a unit. On a metric ruler, the space between centimeters is split into 10 millimeters, so each millimeter is 0.1 cm. A length of 4 cm and 7 mm is written 4.7 cm. The decimal places match how finely the unit is divided, which is why measuring tools and decimals fit together so well.
On a number line, numbers get bigger as you move right and smaller as you move left. This makes ordering easy: whatever is farther right is greater. It works for negatives too — -1 sits to the right of -5, so -1 is bigger. Plotting numbers on a line gives a clear picture of which is largest and how far apart they are.
To split a cost evenly, divide the total by the number of people. If lunch costs 36 dollars and 4 friends share it, each pays 36 / 4 = 9 dollars. If it doesn't divide evenly, you can round to the nearest cent and let one person cover any tiny leftover. This is everyday division with money.
Since an hour has 60 minutes, you can write minutes as a fraction of an hour over 60. 30 minutes is 30/60 = 1/2 hour, 15 minutes is 15/60 = 1/4 hour, and 20 minutes is 20/60 = 1/3 hour. Simplifying makes time easy to picture: a quarter hour, a half hour. This links fractions to clocks and schedules.
A tip is a percent of the bill. The easy way: find 10% by moving the decimal one place left, then build up. On a 40 dollar bill, 10% is 4 dollars, so a 20% tip is double that, 8 dollars, and a 15% tip is 4 plus half of 4 (2), which is 6 dollars. Round the bill first if you want an even tidier number.
To say a fraction, read the top as a regular number and the bottom as an ordinal (like 'third' or 'fifth'), adding an 's' if the top is more than one. So 1/4 is 'one fourth' and 3/4 is 'three fourths.' Special cases: 1/2 is 'one half' and anything over 2 is 'halves.' This naming reflects how many equal parts make the whole.
Dividing by 10, 100, or 1000 makes a number smaller by shifting digits to smaller places, which can create a decimal. 500 / 10 = 50, 500 / 100 = 5, and 50 / 100 = 0.5. Each power of ten moves the decimal point one place left. If there aren't enough digits, a decimal point and zeros appear, like 7 / 100 = 0.07.
A longer decimal isn't always bigger — you must compare place by place. 0.5 versus 0.45 looks like 0.45 has more digits, but add a zero to line them up: 0.50 versus 0.45. In the tenths place, 5 beats 4, so 0.5 is larger. Never judge by how many digits there are; compare the actual place values from the left.
Zero is a real number that means 'none' or 'empty,' and it has special powers in math. Adding zero changes nothing (5 + 0 = 5), multiplying by zero gives zero (5 x 0 = 0), and you can never divide by zero. Zero also marks the boundary between positive and negative numbers and acts as a placeholder in big numbers.
When you make a series of independent choices, multiply the number of options at each step to count all possibilities. With 3 shirts and 2 pairs of pants, the number of outfits is 3 x 2 = 6. With 4 ice cream flavors and 2 cone types, that's 4 x 2 = 8 treats. Multiplying works because each first choice can pair with every second choice.
Rounding is for when an exact number isn't needed or possible. You round to estimate a grocery total, to report a crowd size ('about 5,000 people'), or to give a sensible measurement (a board 'about 2 meters'). The rule of thumb: round when a close-enough answer is more useful or honest than false precision. For money you pay, though, use the exact amount.
After a decimal calculation, estimate with whole numbers to make sure the point is in the right place. If 3.1 x 4.2 came out as 13.02, check: 3 x 4 = 12, so 13 makes sense. But if you got 1.302 or 130.2, the estimate of 12 would flag the misplaced point right away. Estimating is the fastest guard against decimal-point slips.
A fraction is bigger than one whole when its top number is larger than its bottom — that's an improper fraction. 7/4 means you have seven of the quarter-pieces, but only four make a whole, so 7/4 is one whole plus 3/4 more, or 1 and 3/4. Seeing the top beat the bottom is a quick sign the value is more than one.
One meaning of division is sharing a total equally into a known number of groups. To share 20 stickers among 5 kids, divide 20 / 5 = 4, so each kid gets 4. The other meaning is grouping: how many groups of 5 fit in 20 (also 4). Both give the same answer but picture the problem differently — sharing fills known groups, grouping counts how many groups form.
To add money, line up the decimal points so dollars stack on dollars and cents on cents, then add like decimals. For 3.75 + 2.40: line them up and add to get 6.15. Bring the decimal point straight down. Since both numbers have two decimal places (cents), this is just careful decimal addition with a dollar sign.
Estimating before or after solving gives you a target so you can catch big mistakes. If you're adding 312 + 489 and expect about 800 (from 300 + 500), an answer of 80 or 8,001 instantly looks wrong. Estimation won't catch tiny errors, but it reliably flags misplaced digits, dropped numbers, and decimal-point slips. Always have a ballpark in mind.
To order a list, compare them two at a time and arrange smallest to largest (or the reverse). First sort by number of digits, then compare matching place values from the left. For 45, 9, 132, 50: the one-digit 9 is smallest, then 45 and 50 (compare tens: 45 < 50), then the three-digit 132 is largest, giving 9, 45, 50, 132.
Borrowing works because of place value: each spot to the left is worth ten times more. When you borrow from the tens column, you take one ten (worth 10 ones) and add it to the ones column. In 42 - 7, borrowing one ten from the 4 (leaving 3 tens) gives the ones 10 + 2 = 12, so 12 - 7 = 5, and the answer is 35. You never lose value — you just trade one ten for ten ones.
To say a mixed number, read the whole number, say 'and,' then read the fraction. So 2 and 3/4 is 'two and three fourths,' and 5 and 1/2 is 'five and one half.' The word 'and' marks where the whole number stops and the fraction begins — the same way 'and' marks the decimal point when you read decimals aloud.
When the whole is exactly 100, the percent IS the count — no math needed. If 100 kids are surveyed and 37 like pizza, that's 37%. This is the heart of what percent means: out of 100. When the total isn't 100, you scale to compare, but starting with 100 shows percents most clearly. It's why test scores out of 100 already read as percents.
Decimals that add to 1.0 are like puzzle pieces filling a whole. 0.7 needs 0.3 more to reach 1, and 0.25 needs 0.75. Think of it as making change from a dollar: 0.6 plus what equals 1.00? 0.40. This skill helps with subtraction from a whole and with mental money math at the cash register.
A remainder can be written as a fraction by putting it over the number you divided by. For 13 / 4 = 3 remainder 1, the remainder 1 over the divisor 4 gives 3 and 1/4. This makes sense when the leftover can be shared, like 13 cookies among 4 kids: each gets 3 whole cookies plus 1/4 of the last one. It turns a remainder into an exact mixed number.
Before multiplying fractions, you can cancel a common factor between any top and any bottom to keep numbers small. For 2/9 x 3/4: the 2 and 4 share a factor of 2 (becoming 1 and 2), and the 3 and 9 share 3 (becoming 1 and 3), leaving 1/3 x 1/2 = 1/6. Canceling early means no big reducing at the end — you simplify the same total, just sooner.
A thermometer is a vertical number line where zero is the freezing point and negatives go below it. If it's 5 degrees and drops 8 degrees, you pass through zero down to -3. The change is 5 - 8 = -3. Counting the difference between -4 and 6 (which is 10 degrees) is a classic way to see how far apart numbers are across zero.
Halving an odd number leaves a half left over, giving a decimal or fraction. Half of 7 is 3.5 (or 3 and 1/2), because 7 splits into 3 whole pairs with 1 left to cut in half. Half of 25 is 12.5. Even numbers split cleanly, but odd numbers always leave that extra half, which is why the answer ends in .5.
You can make a division easier by dividing both numbers by a common factor first, just like reducing a fraction. For 48 / 12, both divide by 12... but try a friendlier split: divide both by 4 to get 12 / 3 = 4. For 60 / 15, divide both by 5 to get 12 / 3 = 4. Shrinking both numbers by the same factor keeps the answer the same.
To reach a money amount, start with the biggest coins and work down, adding smaller ones to fill the gap. To make 0.85 with quarters (0.25), dimes (0.10), and nickels (0.05): three quarters is 0.75, then one dime is 0.85. Using larger coins first uses the fewest coins. This is real-world decimal addition with money values.
Simplifying doesn't change a fraction's value — 4/8 and 1/2 are the same amount — but the simplest form is easier to read, compare, and picture. '1/2' tells you 'half' instantly, while '4/8' makes you stop and think. Teachers usually want the simplest form as the final answer because it's the clearest way to write the value.
Many statistics are decimals because they come from dividing. A batting average of 0.300 means a player got a hit 3 out of every 10 at-bats (3/10 = 0.3, often written .300). A 0.500 record means winning half the games. These decimals are just fractions turned into a common form so different players or teams can be compared on the same scale.
Making ten is a fast way to add near-ten numbers. To add 8 + 6, borrow 2 from the 6 to turn 8 into 10, then add the leftover 4: 10 + 4 = 14. To add 9 + 5, give 1 to the 9 to make 10, then add 4 more for 14. Tens are easy to add, so reshaping a sum to include a ten speeds up the mental math.
In a fraction word problem, first find what the 'whole' is — the thing being split. 'Maya ate 2/3 of a pizza' makes one pizza the whole. The word 'of' signals multiplication: 2/3 of 12 slices is 2/3 x 12 = 8 slices. Spotting the whole and watching for 'of' turns confusing wording into a clear fraction calculation.
Angles are sorted by how open they are, measured in degrees. Acute is less than 90 degrees (sharp, like a slice of pizza). A right angle is exactly 90 degrees (a perfect corner). Obtuse is between 90 and 180 degrees (wide open). A straight angle is exactly 180 degrees (a flat line). A reflex angle is more than 180 but less than 360 degrees (it bends the long way around).
Two angles are complementary when they add up to exactly 90 degrees. They fit together to make a right angle (a square corner). To find the complement of an angle, subtract it from 90.

Example: the complement of a 30 degree angle is 90 - 30 = 60 degrees. So 30 and 60 are complementary.
Two angles are supplementary when they add up to exactly 180 degrees. Together they form a straight line. To find the supplement of an angle, subtract it from 180.

Example: the supplement of a 110 degree angle is 180 - 110 = 70 degrees. So 110 and 70 are supplementary.
When two straight lines cross, they make an X shape with four angles. The angles that are directly across from each other (the opposite pairs) are called vertical angles, and they are always equal.

Example: if two lines cross and one angle is 70 degrees, the angle straight across from it is also 70 degrees. The other two angles are each 110 degrees.
All the angles sitting on one side of a straight line add up to 180 degrees. So if you know all but one of them, you can find the missing angle by subtracting from 180.

Example: two angles share a point on a line and one is 130 degrees. The other must be 180 - 130 = 50 degrees.
If several angles meet at a single point and go all the way around, they add up to 360 degrees (a full turn). Find a missing angle by subtracting the known ones from 360.

Example: three angles meet at a point: 120, 90, and one unknown. The unknown is 360 - 120 - 90 = 150 degrees.
The three inside angles of any triangle always add up to 180 degrees, no matter the shape. So if you know two angles, subtract their sum from 180 to find the third.

Example: a triangle has angles of 50 and 60 degrees. The third is 180 - 50 - 60 = 70 degrees.
The four inside angles of any four-sided shape (quadrilateral) add up to 360 degrees. That is because you can split any quadrilateral into two triangles, and 180 + 180 = 360.

Example: three angles of a quadrilateral are 90, 90, and 100. The fourth is 360 - 90 - 90 - 100 = 80 degrees.
For a polygon with n sides, the inside angles add up to (n - 2) times 180 degrees. The idea: you can cut any polygon into (n - 2) triangles, and each triangle holds 180 degrees.

Example: a pentagon has 5 sides, so the sum is (5 - 2) x 180 = 3 x 180 = 540 degrees.
An exterior angle is made by extending one side of a polygon. For any convex polygon, all the exterior angles together add up to 360 degrees, no matter how many sides it has. Imagine walking around the outside and turning at each corner: you turn a full circle in total.

Example: a regular pentagon has 5 equal exterior angles, so each one is 360 / 5 = 72 degrees.
A regular polygon has all sides and all angles equal. To find one interior angle, first find the total angle sum, (n - 2) x 180, then divide by the number of angles, n.

Example: a regular hexagon has 6 sides. Sum = (6 - 2) x 180 = 720. Each angle = 720 / 6 = 120 degrees.
Triangles get names based on how many sides are equal. Equilateral: all three sides equal (and all angles 60 degrees). Isosceles: exactly two sides equal (the two angles opposite them are also equal). Scalene: all three sides different lengths.
Triangles also get names from their angles. Acute triangle: all three angles are less than 90 degrees. Right triangle: one angle is exactly 90 degrees. Obtuse triangle: one angle is more than 90 degrees. A triangle can have at most one right or obtuse angle.
For three lengths to form a triangle, the two shorter sides added together must be longer than the longest side. If they are equal or shorter, the sides just lie flat and no triangle closes up.

Example: 3, 4, 5 works because 3 + 4 = 7 is greater than 5. But 2, 3, 6 fails because 2 + 3 = 5 is less than 6.
A rectangle is a four-sided shape where every corner is a right angle (90 degrees) and opposite sides are equal and parallel. Its two diagonals are equal in length and cut each other in half. A square is a special rectangle with all four sides equal.
A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. Opposite sides are equal in length and opposite angles are equal. Angles next to each other add up to 180 degrees. The diagonals cut each other exactly in half. Rectangles, rhombuses, and squares are all special parallelograms.
A rhombus is a parallelogram with all four sides equal in length (like a tilted square or a diamond shape on a playing card). Opposite angles are equal, and its two diagonals cross at right angles, each cutting the other in half.
A trapezoid (called a trapezium in some countries) is a four-sided shape with exactly one pair of parallel sides. The parallel sides are called the bases, and the slanted sides are the legs. In an isosceles trapezoid the two legs are equal, making it symmetrical.
A geometric kite is a four-sided shape with two pairs of equal sides that are next to each other (not opposite). It looks like the kite you fly. The diagonals cross at right angles, and one diagonal cuts the other exactly in half.
All four-sided shapes are quadrilaterals. Within that family, some are more special. A square is the most special: it is a rectangle (right angles) AND a rhombus (equal sides) AND a parallelogram. A rectangle and a rhombus are both parallelograms. A trapezoid has only one pair of parallel sides, so it sits outside the parallelogram group.
Perimeter is the total distance all the way around the edge of a flat shape. To find it, add up the lengths of every side. Think of walking around the outside of a yard: the perimeter is how far you walked.

Example: a rectangle 5 cm by 3 cm has perimeter 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm.
A square has four equal sides, so its perimeter is just four times the length of one side: 4 x side.

Example: a square with sides of 7 cm has perimeter 4 x 7 = 28 cm.
Area is the amount of flat space inside a shape, measured in square units (like square centimeters). Imagine covering the shape with little squares and counting them. Area tells you how much surface something covers, such as the carpet needed for a floor.

Example: a 3 by 4 grid of unit squares has 12 little squares, so the area is 12 square units.
A square has equal sides, so its area is one side multiplied by itself: side x side, which is the side squared.

Example: a square with sides of 5 cm has area 5 x 5 = 25 square cm.
A circle has special parts. The center is the middle point. The radius is the distance from the center to the edge. The diameter goes straight across through the center and is twice the radius. The circumference is the distance all the way around the edge. A chord connects two edge points, and an arc is part of the curved edge.
Pi (written as the Greek letter pi) is the number you get when you divide the distance around any circle by its diameter. It is always the same, about 3.14159, for every circle. Because its decimals go on forever without repeating, we usually round it to 3.14. Pi shows up in every circle and sphere calculation.
A semicircle is exactly half of a circle, cut along the diameter. An arc is a portion of the curved edge of a circle, like a slice of the crust. A sector is a 'pizza slice' shaped piece, bounded by two radii and an arc. A quarter circle is a sector that is one-fourth of the whole circle.
A cube is a 3D shape with 6 square faces, all the same size. It has 12 equal edges and 8 corners (called vertices). A dice and a sugar cube are cubes. Every face meets its neighbors at right angles.
A cuboid (also called a rectangular prism) is a box shape with 6 rectangular faces. Like a cube it has 12 edges and 8 vertices, but its faces can be rectangles of different sizes. Cereal boxes and bricks are cuboids.
These 3D shapes have curved surfaces. A sphere is perfectly round like a ball, with no flat faces, edges, or corners. A cylinder is like a can: two circular flat ends joined by a curved tube. A cone has one circular flat base and a curved surface that meets at a single point (the apex), like an ice cream cone.
A prism has two identical ends (the bases) joined by flat rectangular sides; its cross-section stays the same all the way through, like a Toblerone bar (triangular prism). A pyramid has one base and triangular sides that rise to a single point at the top, like the Egyptian pyramids (square base) or a triangle-based tetrahedron.
3D shapes are described by three features. A face is a flat (or curved) surface. An edge is the line where two faces meet. A vertex is a corner point where edges meet (the plural is vertices). 

Example: a square-based pyramid has 5 faces (1 square + 4 triangles), 8 edges, and 5 vertices.
For any solid shape with flat faces (a polyhedron), the number of faces plus the number of vertices is always two more than the number of edges: Faces + Vertices = Edges + 2.

Example: a cube has 6 faces and 8 vertices. 6 + 8 = 14, and edges + 2 = 12 + 2 = 14. It matches!
A net is what you get when you unfold a 3D shape flat onto paper. If you cut along the edges of a cube and open it up, you get a flat pattern of 6 connected squares. Folding the net back up rebuilds the solid. Nets are handy for finding surface area because you can see every face at once.
Surface area is the total area of all the outside faces of a 3D shape added together. Think of how much wrapping paper you would need to cover a present with no gaps. You find the area of each face and add them all up.

Example: a cube with side 2 has 6 faces, each 2 x 2 = 4. Total surface area = 6 x 4 = 24 square units.
A cube has 6 identical square faces, so its surface area is 6 times the area of one face: 6 x side x side.

Example: a cube with side 5 cm has surface area 6 x 5 x 5 = 6 x 25 = 150 square cm.
A cuboid has three pairs of matching rectangular faces. Add the area of each different face and double it: 2 x (length x width + length x height + width x height).

Example: a box 4 by 3 by 2 has surface area 2 x (4x3 + 4x2 + 3x2) = 2 x (12 + 8 + 6) = 2 x 26 = 52 square units.
Volume is the amount of space a 3D shape takes up, measured in cubic units (like cubic centimeters). Imagine filling a box with little 1x1x1 cubes and counting them. Volume tells you how much something can hold, like water in a tank.

Example: a box 2 by 3 by 4 holds 2 x 3 x 4 = 24 little cubes, so its volume is 24 cubic units.
To find the volume of a box (cuboid), multiply length times width times height: length x width x height. This counts how many unit cubes fit inside.

Example: a box 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm has volume 5 x 3 x 2 = 30 cubic cm.
Any prism has the same shape all the way through, so its volume is the area of one end (the cross-section) times the length: cross-sectional area x length.

Example: a triangular prism whose triangular end has area 6 square cm and length 10 cm has volume 6 x 10 = 60 cubic cm.
Perimeter and area measure different things. Perimeter is the distance around the edge, measured in regular units like cm (the length of the fence). Area is the space inside, measured in square units like square cm (the grass inside the fence). Two shapes can share a perimeter but have different areas.
Area measures flat space, the surface of a 2D shape, in square units (square cm). Volume measures the space inside a 3D object, in cubic units (cubic cm). Area is for flat things like a wall; volume is for things that hold space like a box. A useful clue: square units mean area, cubic units mean volume.
Length measures distance. In the metric system the units, from small to big, are millimeters (mm), centimeters (cm), meters (m), and kilometers (km). 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, and 1000 m = 1 km. To go from a big unit to a smaller one you multiply; from small to big you divide.
Because metric units jump by powers of ten, converting just moves the decimal point. To change a smaller unit to a bigger one (like cm to m) divide; to go from bigger to smaller multiply. 1 m = 100 cm, so multiply meters by 100 to get cm.

Example: 3.5 m = 3.5 x 100 = 350 cm. And 250 cm = 250 / 100 = 2.5 m.
