Mass measures how much matter is in something. Common metric units are milligrams (mg), grams (g), kilograms (kg), and tonnes (t). 1000 mg = 1 g, 1000 g = 1 kg, and 1000 kg = 1 tonne. A paperclip is about 1 gram; a textbook is about 1 kilogram.
Capacity measures how much liquid a container holds. Metric units are milliliters (mL) and liters (L), with 1000 mL = 1 L. A teaspoon is about 5 mL, a water bottle about 500 mL, and a big soda bottle is 2 L. One liter of water also takes up 1000 cubic centimeters of space.
Time is measured in seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, and years. 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour, 24 hours = 1 day, 7 days = 1 week, and about 365 days = 1 year. To convert minutes to seconds you multiply by 60; to convert seconds to minutes you divide by 60.

Example: 3 minutes = 3 x 60 = 180 seconds.
A compound shape is made of simpler shapes stuck together, often forming an L or T. To find its perimeter, carefully walk around the whole outside edge and add up every straight piece, including the steps. Missing side lengths can usually be found by comparing the longer sides on the opposite walls.
A scale drawing shows something big at a smaller size, keeping the same proportions. A scale like 1:100 means 1 unit on the drawing stands for 100 real units. To find a real length, multiply the drawing length by the scale number; to find a drawing length, divide.

Example: at scale 1:50, a wall drawn 4 cm long is really 4 x 50 = 200 cm = 2 m.
A map scale tells you how distances on the map compare to real distances. A scale of 1:25000 means 1 cm on the map equals 25000 cm in real life (which is 250 m). To find a real distance, measure on the map and multiply by the scale number, then convert to a sensible unit.
The two axes split the coordinate plane into four regions called quadrants, numbered with Roman numerals counterclockwise from the top right. Quadrant I (+, +) is top right; Quadrant II (-, +) top left; Quadrant III (-, -) bottom left; Quadrant IV (+, -) bottom right. The signs of x and y tell you which quadrant a point lies in.
To find how far apart two points are, you can use the Pythagorean theorem on the horizontal and vertical gaps. Find the difference in x and the difference in y, square each, add them, then take the square root.

Example: from (1, 2) to (4, 6): across is 3, up is 4. Distance = square root of (3x3 + 4x4) = square root of 25 = 5.
The midpoint is the exact middle of a line segment. To find it, take the average of the two x-coordinates and the average of the two y-coordinates: add the pair and divide by 2.

Example: the midpoint of (2, 4) and (6, 8) is ((2+6)/2, (4+8)/2) = (4, 6).
When a straight line (a transversal) crosses two parallel lines, special equal angles appear. Corresponding angles sit in the same position at each crossing and are equal (they form an F shape). Alternate angles are on opposite sides between the lines and are equal (a Z shape). Co-interior angles are between the lines on the same side and add to 180 (a C shape).
A line of symmetry is a line you could fold a shape along so both halves match perfectly, like a mirror. A shape can have zero, one, or many lines of symmetry. A square has 4 lines of symmetry, a rectangle has 2, and a circle has infinitely many.
A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks exactly the same when you turn it around its center, before a full 360 degree spin. The order of rotational symmetry is how many times it matches itself in one full turn. A square has order 4 because it looks the same every 90 degrees.
A translation slides a shape to a new spot without turning or flipping it. Every point moves the same distance in the same direction. We often describe it with how far to move right or left and up or down.

Example: translating the point (2, 3) by '4 right and 1 up' moves it to (6, 4). The shape stays exactly the same size and direction.
A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line, creating a backwards copy. Each point and its reflection are the same distance from the mirror line, on opposite sides. The size and shape stay the same, but it faces the other way.

Example: reflecting the point (3, 2) over the y-axis gives (-3, 2).
A rotation turns a shape around a fixed point called the center of rotation, by a certain angle and direction (clockwise or counterclockwise). The shape keeps its size and form, just spun to a new position. Common turns are 90, 180, and 270 degrees.

Example: rotating a shape 180 degrees about the origin turns the point (2, 3) into (-2, -3).
An enlargement makes a shape bigger or smaller while keeping the same proportions. The scale factor tells you how many times larger each length becomes. A scale factor of 2 doubles every side; a scale factor of 1/2 halves them. The shape stays the same kind, just a different size.

Example: enlarging a 3 cm by 2 cm rectangle by scale factor 3 makes it 9 cm by 6 cm.
Two shapes are congruent if they are exactly the same size AND the same shape, even if one is flipped or turned. If you could pick one up and lay it perfectly on top of the other, they are congruent. All matching sides and angles are equal.
Two shapes are similar if they are the same shape but different sizes, like a photo and its enlargement. Their angles are equal and their matching sides are all in the same ratio (the scale factor). Every pair of squares is similar; every pair of circles is similar.
In a right triangle, the longest side (the hypotenuse, across from the right angle) is linked to the other two sides by a rule: the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. So a x a + b x b = c x c.

Example: legs 3 and 4 give 9 + 16 = 25, and the square root of 25 is 5, so the hypotenuse is 5.
A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers that fit the Pythagorean theorem perfectly, making a right triangle with no leftover decimals. The most famous is 3, 4, 5. Multiply any triple by a number and you get another, like 6, 8, 10. Other triples include 5, 12, 13 and 8, 15, 17.
The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle. It is always the side directly across from the right angle (the 90 degree corner), and it never touches the right angle itself. The other two shorter sides are called the legs.
A full circle is divided into 360 degrees. A half circle (straight line) is 180 degrees, a quarter circle (right angle) is 90 degrees. The number 360 is handy because it divides evenly by so many numbers (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12 and more), making fractions of a turn easy.
A protractor measures angles in degrees. Place its center hole on the angle's corner (the vertex) and line up one arm of the angle with the zero line. Then read where the other arm crosses the scale. Be careful: use the scale that starts at zero on your baseline, since a protractor has two sets of numbers.
A bearing is a way to describe direction using degrees, always measured clockwise from North and written with three digits. North is 000, East is 090, South is 180, and West is 270. A bearing of 045 points northeast.

Example: to face directly southeast, you would use a bearing of 135 degrees.
An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, and the two angles at the bottom (base angles) opposite those equal sides are also equal. Since all three angles add to 180, if you know the top angle you can find each base angle: subtract from 180 and split the rest in half.

Example: top angle 40, so base angles are (180 - 40) / 2 = 70 each.
An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal, which means all three angles are equal too. Since the angles must add up to 180 degrees, each one is 180 / 3 = 60 degrees.
A right angle is an angle of exactly 90 degrees, the kind you see in the corner of a square, a book, or a window. It is a quarter of a full turn. We mark a right angle with a small square in the corner instead of a curved line.
A diagonal is a straight line joining two corners of a shape that are not already connected by a side. A triangle has none. A quadrilateral has 2 diagonals. The number for an n-sided shape is n x (n - 3) / 2.

Example: a pentagon (5 sides) has 5 x (5 - 3) / 2 = 5 x 2 / 2 = 5 diagonals.
Polygons are named by their number of sides. 3 = triangle, 4 = quadrilateral, 5 = pentagon, 6 = hexagon, 7 = heptagon, 8 = octagon, 9 = nonagon, 10 = decagon, 12 = dodecagon. The names come from Greek number words, so 'oct' (eight) appears in octagon and octopus alike.
A regular polygon has all sides the same length AND all angles equal, like a perfect honeycomb hexagon or a stop sign. An irregular polygon has sides or angles that are not all equal, like a random four-sided lot. Both can have the same number of sides; it is the equal-ness that makes one 'regular'.
A convex shape has all its corners pushing outward, so no angle is bigger than 180 degrees and no part caves in, like a regular hexagon. A concave shape has at least one corner that points inward (a 'dent'), making one interior angle a reflex angle (more than 180). An arrow shape is concave.
These are the basic building blocks of geometry. A point marks an exact location and has no size, shown as a dot. A line is straight, goes on forever in both directions, and has no thickness. A plane is a perfectly flat surface that stretches forever in all directions, like an endless tabletop.
A line segment is a straight piece with two endpoints, so it has a definite length. A ray starts at one endpoint and goes on forever in one direction, like a beam of light from a flashlight. A full line goes on forever in both directions with no endpoints.
A perpendicular bisector is a line that cuts a line segment exactly in half AND crosses it at a right angle (90 degrees). Every point on this line is the same distance from both ends of the segment, which makes it useful for finding the middle of things fairly.
An angle bisector is a line or ray that splits an angle into two equal smaller angles. If you bisect a 60 degree angle, you get two 30 degree angles. Every point on the bisector is the same distance from both arms of the angle.

Example: bisecting a 90 degree angle creates two 45 degree angles.
Lines interact with a circle in different ways. A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle (the diameter is the longest chord). A tangent just touches the circle at exactly one point and never goes inside. A secant cuts right through, crossing the circle at two points.
There is a neat circle rule: if you draw a triangle where one side is the diameter and the opposite corner touches the edge of the circle, that corner angle is always exactly 90 degrees. This is sometimes called Thales' theorem.
A tessellation is a pattern of shapes that fit together with no gaps and no overlaps, covering a surface like floor tiles. Shapes tessellate when the angles meeting at each point add up to exactly 360 degrees. Squares, equilateral triangles, and regular hexagons all tessellate on their own.
Each interior angle of a regular hexagon is 120 degrees. Where hexagons meet, three corners come together: 120 + 120 + 120 = 360 degrees, a full turn with no gap. That perfect fit, plus hexagons holding lots of space with little wall, is why bees build hexagonal honeycombs.
A sector is a pie-slice of a circle. Its area is a fraction of the whole circle's area, where the fraction is the slice's angle out of 360 degrees. So sector area = (angle / 360) x pi x radius x radius.

Example: a quarter slice (90 degrees) of a circle with radius 4 has area (90/360) x 3.14 x 16 = (1/4) x 50.24 = about 12.56 square units.
An arc is part of the circle's edge. Its length is a fraction of the full circumference, where the fraction is the arc's angle out of 360 degrees. So arc length = (angle / 360) x pi x diameter.

Example: a 90 degree arc on a circle with diameter 10 has length (90/360) x 3.14 x 10 = (1/4) x 31.4 = about 7.85 units.
A pyramid holds one-third the volume of a prism (box) with the same base and height. So its volume is (1/3) x base area x height.

Example: a pyramid with a square base 6 by 6 (area 36) and height 5 has volume (1/3) x 36 x 5 = (1/3) x 180 = 60 cubic units.
Liquid capacity and cubic space are connected. 1 milliliter takes up exactly 1 cubic centimeter, and 1 liter equals 1000 cubic centimeters (which is the size of a 10 cm cube). So if you know a container's volume in cubic cm, you instantly know its capacity in mL.
To read a ruler, measuring jug, or scale, first work out what each small mark is worth by counting the gaps between two labeled numbers. If 5 gaps fill the space from 0 to 100, each gap is 100 / 5 = 20. Then count the marks to the pointer.

Example: marks every 50 mL, pointer 3 marks above 200, reads 200 + 150 = 350 mL.
Area units do not convert the same way as lengths, because area uses two dimensions. Since 1 m = 100 cm, a square meter is 100 cm x 100 cm = 10000 square cm, not just 100. So you square the length conversion factor when converting area.

Example: 2 square meters = 2 x 10000 = 20000 square cm.
Volume uses three dimensions, so the length conversion factor is cubed. Since 1 m = 100 cm, a cubic meter is 100 x 100 x 100 = 1,000,000 cubic cm. That is why a small mistake in unit conversion can be huge with volume.

Example: 3 cubic meters = 3 x 1,000,000 = 3,000,000 cubic cm.
These three are linked: speed = distance / time. Rearranged, distance = speed x time, and time = distance / speed. A handy triangle has distance on top, with speed and time below; cover the one you want to find.

Example: traveling 120 km in 2 hours gives speed = 120 / 2 = 60 km per hour.
Density tells how packed something is: density = mass / volume. Rearranged, mass = density x volume, and volume = mass / density. Dense things like metal pack a lot of mass into a small space; light things like foam do not.

Example: 200 g packed into 100 cubic cm has density 200 / 100 = 2 g per cubic cm.
Clockwise is the direction the hands of a clock turn: from 12 to 3 to 6 to 9 and back to 12. Counterclockwise (also called anticlockwise) is the opposite direction, going backwards around the clock. These words describe which way to turn or rotate.
If you unroll a cylinder (like a soup can), you get three flat pieces: two circles for the top and bottom, and one rectangle for the curved side. The rectangle's width is the same as the circle's circumference, because that side wrapped all the way around the circle.
A cylinder's surface is two circles plus the curved side. The two circles together are 2 x pi x radius x radius, and the curved part (a rolled-up rectangle) is the circumference times the height: 2 x pi x radius x height. Add them.

Example: radius 2, height 5: circles 2 x 3.14 x 4 = 25.12, side 2 x 3.14 x 2 x 5 = 62.8, total about 87.9 square units.
A vertex is a corner point where lines or edges meet (the plural is vertices). In a 2D shape it is where two sides meet, like the three corners of a triangle. In a 3D shape it is where edges meet, like the 8 corners of a cube. An angle's tip is also called its vertex.
Adjacent angles are two angles that sit right next to each other, sharing a common arm (side) and the same corner (vertex), but not overlapping. They are like two slices of pizza side by side. If their outer arms form a straight line, the two adjacent angles add to 180 degrees.
When finding the area of a triangle or parallelogram, the base is any chosen side and the height is the straight-up distance from that base to the opposite point or side, measured at a right angle (not along a slanted side). The base and its height must be perpendicular to each other.
At each corner of a polygon, the interior angle is inside the shape, and the exterior angle is the angle made by extending a side outward. The two sit on a straight line, so they always add up to 180 degrees. If an interior angle is 110, its exterior angle is 180 - 110 = 70.
A square number, like 4, 9, or 16, gets its name because that many dots can be arranged into a perfect square. 3 squared is 9, which is a 3 by 3 grid of 9 dots. This is the same idea as the area of a square: side times side.
A cube number, like 8, 27, or 64, is called that because you can stack that many little cubes into one big cube. 3 cubed is 27, a 3 by 3 by 3 stack. This matches the volume of a cube: side times side times side.
If you put a dot at the center of a regular polygon and draw lines to each corner, you split it into equal triangles. Each central angle is 360 degrees divided by the number of sides.

Example: a regular pentagon (5 sides) has central angles of 360 / 5 = 72 degrees each.
A regular polygon has all sides equal, so its perimeter is just the number of sides times the length of one side: n x side.

Example: a regular pentagon with each side 6 cm has perimeter 5 x 6 = 30 cm.
A flat shape has two dimensions: length and width (so we call it 2D). A solid object adds a third, height (or depth), making it 3D. A line is 1D (just length), a sheet of paper is roughly 2D, and a box is 3D. Each new dimension lets the object spread in a new direction.
Unfolding a square-based pyramid gives a flat net of one square (the base) with a triangle attached to each of its four sides, folding up to meet at the top point. A triangle-based pyramid (tetrahedron) unfolds into four triangles. Nets help you find surface area by showing every face flat.
Some shapes are full of right angles. A rectangle and a square each have 4 right angles, one at every corner. A right-angled triangle has exactly 1. An L-shaped hexagon can have several. Spotting right angles (square corners) helps you recognize and measure shapes quickly.
A reflex angle is more than 180 degrees. To find one, measure the smaller angle on the other side, then subtract from 360 (since the two together make a full turn).

Example: if the inside angle is 110 degrees, the reflex angle going the long way around is 360 - 110 = 250 degrees.
A rhombus is a slanted square with equal sides. One easy way to find its area uses the two diagonals: multiply them and divide by 2, since the diagonals cross at right angles. So area = (diagonal1 x diagonal2) / 2.

Example: diagonals 6 and 8 give area (6 x 8) / 2 = 48 / 2 = 24 square units.
A kite's diagonals cross at right angles, so just like a rhombus, its area is half the product of the two diagonals: (diagonal1 x diagonal2) / 2.

Example: a kite with diagonals 8 and 6 has area (8 x 6) / 2 = 48 / 2 = 24 square units.
If you have a fixed amount of fencing (perimeter), the shape that encloses the most area is a circle. Among rectangles with a fixed perimeter, a square wins. So a square garden holds more space than a long thin one using the same fence, and a circle beats them all.
A polygon is a flat, closed 2D shape made only of straight sides that join end to end with no gaps. Triangles, squares, and pentagons are polygons. A shape with a curved side (like a circle) or one that does not close up is not a polygon.
Not every arrangement of faces folds into the solid. A net is valid only if folding the faces leaves no gaps and no overlaps, and every face ends up in the right place. A cube has 11 different valid nets; many other six-square arrangements look fine flat but overlap when folded.
A 2D shape is flat, like a drawing on paper, with only length and width; examples are circles, squares, and triangles. A 3D shape is solid and takes up space, with length, width, and height; examples are cubes, spheres, and cones. 2D shapes have area; 3D shapes have volume and surface area.
A coefficient is the number multiplied by a variable. In 7x, the coefficient is 7 — it tells you how many x's you have. If a variable has no number written, the coefficient is 1 (x means 1x), and -x means -1x.

Example: in 5y the coefficient is 5; in -3ab the coefficient is -3. Knowing this matters when you combine terms or factor.
A constant is a number on its own with no variable attached — its value never changes. In 2x + 9, the 9 is the constant. Constants combine with other constants but not with variable terms.

Example: in 3a + 4 + 7, the constants 4 and 7 add to 11, giving 3a + 11. The 3a part can't merge with them.
An expression is a math phrase with no equals sign — you can only simplify or evaluate it. An equation has an equals sign and claims two things are equal — you can solve it for the variable.

Example: 3x + 2 is an expression (simplify it). 3x + 2 = 11 is an equation (solve it, x = 3). The equals sign is the key difference.
The distributive property says a(b + c) = ab + ac. You multiply the outside number by every term inside the parentheses. This works with subtraction too.

Example: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. With a minus: 5(2y - 3) = 10y - 15. Watch the signs: -2(x - 6) = -2x + 12 because -2 times -6 is +12.
Factoring is distribution in reverse. Find the greatest common factor of all terms and pull it outside parentheses, leaving what's left inside.

Example: 6x + 9. The GCF of 6 and 9 is 3, so 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3). With variables: 4x^2 + 8x has GCF 4x, giving 4x(x + 2). Check by distributing back.
When an equation has parentheses, distribute first to clear them, then combine like terms, then solve the normal way.

Example: 3(x + 2) = 18. Distribute: 3x + 6 = 18. Subtract 6: 3x = 12. Divide: x = 4. If both sides have parentheses, distribute both before moving terms around.
A literal equation has several letters and you solve for one of them in terms of the others, using the same inverse-operation rules as numbers.

Example: solve A = lw for w. Divide both sides by l: w = A/l. For y = mx + b solved for x: subtract b (y - b = mx), then divide by m (x = (y - b)/m). The letters just stand in for numbers.
A compound inequality joins two inequalities with 'and' or 'or'. 'And' means both must be true (the overlap). 'Or' means at least one is true (the combination).

Example: 1 < x < 5 means x is between 1 and 5. Solve a sandwich like 2 < x + 1 < 6 by subtracting 1 from all three parts: 1 < x < 5. An 'or' like x < 0 or x > 3 covers two separate regions.
Absolute value measures distance from zero, so |x| = 5 has two answers: x = 5 and x = -5. To solve, isolate the absolute value, then split into two cases (positive and negative).

Example: |x - 2| = 3. Case 1: x - 2 = 3, so x = 5. Case 2: x - 2 = -3, so x = -1. Both are solutions. If the absolute value equals a negative number, there's no solution.
A function is a rule that takes an input and gives exactly one output. Think of it as a machine: put in a number, get one number out. Each input maps to only one output (but different inputs can share an output).

Example: the rule 'double it' is a function: input 3 gives 6, input 5 gives 10. A rule that gave two different outputs for the same input would NOT be a function.
f(x) is read 'f of x' and names a function f with input x. It does NOT mean f times x. The whole f(x) stands for the output. To evaluate, plug the input into the rule.

Example: if f(x) = 2x + 1, then f(3) = 2(3) + 1 = 7. f(0) = 1. You can use other letters too, like g(x) or h(t).
The domain is the set of all allowed inputs (x-values). The range is the set of all possible outputs (y-values). Domain answers 'what can go in?', range answers 'what comes out?'

Example: for f(x) = x^2, the domain is all real numbers (any x works), but the range is y >= 0 because squaring never gives a negative. Watch for inputs that break things, like dividing by zero.
The vertical line test checks if a graph is a function. If any vertical line crosses the graph more than once, it's NOT a function, because that x-value would have two outputs.

Example: a straight line or a parabola passes the test (one output per input). A sideways parabola or a full circle fails — a vertical line hits it twice.
A function table lists inputs in one column and the matching outputs in another. To find the rule, look at how each input changes into its output.

Example: inputs 1, 2, 3 give outputs 4, 5, 6 — each output is input + 3, so the rule is y = x + 3. If inputs 1, 2, 3 give 2, 4, 6, the rule is y = 2x.
Slope measures how steep a line is — how much y changes for each step in x. It's 'rise over run': the vertical change divided by the horizontal change. Positive slope goes up, negative goes down, zero is flat.

Example: going from (0, 1) to (2, 5), the rise is 4 and the run is 2, so slope = 4/2 = 2. The line climbs 2 units for every 1 unit right.
Slope-intercept form is y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis). It's the quickest way to graph a line: start at b, then use the slope to step.

Example: y = 2x + 3 has slope 2 and y-intercept 3. Start at (0, 3), go up 2 and right 1 to plot the next point.
The y-intercept is where a line or curve crosses the y-axis, which always happens when x = 0. In y = mx + b, the y-intercept is simply b. To find it from an equation, set x = 0 and solve for y.

Example: y = 3x - 5. Set x = 0: y = -5, so the y-intercept is (0, -5). It often represents a starting value in word problems.
The x-intercept is where a graph crosses the x-axis, which happens when y = 0. To find it, set y to 0 and solve for x. X-intercepts are also called zeros or roots of a function.

Example: y = 2x - 6. Set y = 0: 0 = 2x - 6, so x = 3. The x-intercept is (3, 0).
Standard form is Ax + By = C, where A, B, and C are usually integers. It's useful for finding both intercepts quickly and for systems of equations. You can convert to slope-intercept form by solving for y.

Example: 2x + 3y = 12. Find x-intercept (y=0): x = 6. Find y-intercept (x=0): y = 4. To get slope form: y = (-2/3)x + 4.
With two points, slope = (change in y) / (change in x) = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1). Subtract the y's on top and the x's on bottom, keeping the order consistent.

Example: points (1, 2) and (4, 11). Slope = (11 - 2)/(4 - 1) = 9/3 = 3. The line rises 3 for every 1 across.
Parallel lines never meet, and the reason is they have the exact same slope. They climb at the identical rate but cross the y-axis at different spots.

Example: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x - 4 are parallel — both have slope 2. To write a line parallel to a given one, copy its slope and use a new point to find the intercept.
Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, and their slopes are negative reciprocals — flip the fraction and change the sign. The product of the two slopes is -1.

Example: a line with slope 2 is perpendicular to a line with slope -1/2. Slope 3/4 pairs with slope -4/3. A horizontal line (slope 0) is perpendicular to a vertical line.
A horizontal line has the form y = a number; every point shares that y-value, and its slope is 0. A vertical line has the form x = a number; every point shares that x-value, and its slope is undefined.

Example: y = 4 is a flat line through all points with y = 4. x = -2 is a straight up-down line through all points with x = -2.
A linear function makes a straight-line graph and has a constant rate of change (constant slope). Its equation looks like f(x) = mx + b. Each step in x changes y by the same amount.

Example: f(x) = 3x + 2 adds 3 to the output every time x goes up by 1: f(0)=2, f(1)=5, f(2)=8. The equal jumps are the signature of linear.
A nonlinear function does not make a straight line — its rate of change varies. Squares, cubes, square roots, and curves are all nonlinear. In a table, the differences between outputs are not constant.

Example: f(x) = x^2 gives outputs 0, 1, 4, 9 for x = 0,1,2,3 — the jumps (1, 3, 5) keep growing, so it curves. A linear function would have equal jumps.
Rate of change tells how fast one quantity changes compared to another. For a line it's the slope: change in output over change in input. Real life calls it speed, cost per item, growth per year, and so on.

Example: if a plant grows from 4 cm to 10 cm over 3 days, the rate of change is (10 - 4)/3 = 2 cm per day. Same idea as slope, just with units.
Composing functions means feeding the output of one function into another. f(g(x)) means do g first, then put its result into f. Work from the inside out.

Example: f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x. f(g(3)): first g(3) = 6, then f(6) = 7. The order matters — g(f(3)) would give 8 instead.
An inverse function undoes what the original did. If f turns 3 into 7, its inverse turns 7 back into 3. To find it: swap x and y, then solve for y. The inverse is written f^-1(x).

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1. Write y = 2x + 1, swap: x = 2y + 1, solve: y = (x - 1)/2. So f^-1(x) = (x - 1)/2. Composing them returns the original input.
A piecewise function uses different rules for different intervals of x. You pick which rule to use based on where the input falls.

Example: f(x) = x + 1 if x < 0, and f(x) = 2x if x >= 0. For x = -3 (negative), use the first rule: f(-3) = -2. For x = 4 (not negative), use the second: f(4) = 8. Parking fees and tax brackets work this way.
A function is increasing where its graph goes up as you move right (outputs grow), and decreasing where it goes down (outputs shrink). Reading left to right is key.

Example: y = x^2 decreases for x < 0 (falling toward the bottom) and increases for x > 0 (rising). A line with positive slope is increasing everywhere; negative slope is decreasing everywhere.
A quadratic function has an x-squared term as its highest power: f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c. Its graph is a U-shaped curve called a parabola. If a is positive it opens up; if negative it opens down.

Example: f(x) = x^2 - 4 is a parabola opening up with its lowest point at (0, -4). The x^2 term is what makes it curve instead of going straight.
The vertex is the turning point of a parabola — the lowest point if it opens up, or the highest if it opens down. For f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c, the vertex x-value is at x = -b/(2a), then plug in to get y.

Example: f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5. Here a=1, b=-6, so x = 6/2 = 3. f(3) = 9 - 18 + 5 = -4. The vertex is (3, -4).
The axis of symmetry is the vertical line that splits a parabola into two mirror-image halves. It passes through the vertex, so its equation is x = -b/(2a).

Example: f(x) = x^2 + 4x + 1 has a = 1, b = 4, so the axis is x = -4/2 = -2. Points the same distance left and right of x = -2 have equal y-values.
Vertex form is f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k, where (h, k) is the vertex. It instantly reveals where the parabola turns and which way it opens (a's sign). Watch the sign: x - h means h is positive.

Example: f(x) = 2(x - 3)^2 + 1 has vertex (3, 1) and opens up. f(x) = -(x + 4)^2 - 2 has vertex (-4, -2) and opens down.
To factor x^2 + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. Those numbers go into two binomials.

Example: x^2 + 5x + 6. Find numbers multiplying to 6 and adding to 5: that's 2 and 3. So it factors to (x + 2)(x + 3). Check by multiplying back out. Watch signs: x^2 - x - 6 = (x - 3)(x + 2).
A difference of squares is a^2 - b^2, and it factors neatly into (a + b)(a - b). Spot it when you have a perfect square minus another perfect square.

Example: x^2 - 9 = (x + 3)(x - 3) because 9 is 3 squared. Also 4x^2 - 25 = (2x + 5)(2x - 5). Note: a SUM of squares (x^2 + 9) does not factor over real numbers.
A perfect square trinomial factors into the same binomial twice: a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = (a + b)^2, and a^2 - 2ab + b^2 = (a - b)^2. Recognize it by two perfect-square end terms and a middle term equal to 2 times their roots.

Example: x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2 because 3^2 = 9 and 2(3) = 6. Likewise x^2 - 10x + 25 = (x - 5)^2.
Completing the square turns x^2 + bx into a perfect square. Take half of b, square it, and add it. This rewrites a quadratic in vertex form or helps solve it.

Example: x^2 + 6x. Half of 6 is 3, squared is 9. So x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2. To solve x^2 + 6x = 7, add 9 to both sides: (x + 3)^2 = 16, so x + 3 = +-4, giving x = 1 or x = -7.
The discriminant is b^2 - 4ac, the part of the quadratic formula under the square root. It tells how many real solutions a quadratic has without fully solving. Positive means two solutions, zero means one, negative means none (real).

Example: x^2 + 2x + 1: discriminant = 4 - 4 = 0, so one solution. x^2 + x + 5: discriminant = 1 - 20 = -19, so no real solutions.
The zero product property says if a product equals zero, then at least one factor must be zero. This is how you solve factored quadratics: set each factor equal to zero.

Example: (x - 2)(x + 5) = 0. So either x - 2 = 0 (x = 2) or x + 5 = 0 (x = -5). The solutions are x = 2 and x = -5. It only works when one side equals zero.
When you multiply powers with the same base, add the exponents: x^a times x^b = x^(a+b). The base stays the same — you're just counting how many factors total.

Example: x^3 times x^4 = x^7 (three x's times four x's is seven x's). With numbers: 2^2 times 2^3 = 2^5 = 32. This only works for matching bases.
When you divide powers with the same base, subtract the exponents: x^a / x^b = x^(a-b). You're cancelling matching factors top and bottom.

Example: x^7 / x^3 = x^4. With numbers: 5^6 / 5^2 = 5^4 = 625. If the bottom exponent is bigger, you'll get a negative exponent, which means a fraction.
To raise a power to another power, multiply the exponents: (x^a)^b = x^(a times b). The base stays; you stack the repeated multiplication.

Example: (x^2)^3 = x^6, because x^2 used three times is x to the six. With numbers: (2^3)^2 = 2^6 = 64. Don't confuse this with the product rule, which adds.
Any nonzero number raised to the zero power equals 1. The reason comes from the quotient rule: x^3 / x^3 = x^0, but anything divided by itself is 1, so x^0 = 1.

Example: 7^0 = 1, (-5)^0 = 1, and (3x)^0 = 1. The only catch is 0^0, which is left undefined.
A fractional exponent is a root. The denominator is the root, the numerator is a power: x^(1/n) is the nth root of x, and x^(m/n) is the nth root of x raised to m.

Example: 9^(1/2) = square root of 9 = 3. 8^(1/3) = cube root of 8 = 2. And 8^(2/3) = (cube root of 8)^2 = 2^2 = 4.
To simplify a square root, pull out perfect-square factors. Break the number into a perfect square times something else, then take the root of the perfect square.

Example: square root of 12 = square root of (4 x 3) = square root of 4 times square root of 3 = 2 times square root of 3. Square root of 50 = 5 times square root of 2.
A radical equation has the variable under a square root. To solve, isolate the radical, then square both sides to remove it, then solve normally. Always check answers — squaring can create extra ones.

Example: square root of (x + 1) = 3. Square both sides: x + 1 = 9, so x = 8. Check: square root of 9 = 3. It works.
Rationalizing means clearing a square root out of the bottom of a fraction by multiplying top and bottom by that root. The fraction's value stays the same because you multiplied by a form of 1.

Example: 1/square root of 2. Multiply top and bottom by square root of 2: square root of 2 / 2. Now the denominator is a clean whole number.
To solve a system of two equations by substitution, solve one equation for a variable, then plug that into the other equation so only one variable is left.

Example: y = x + 1 and 2x + y = 7. Substitute the first into the second: 2x + (x + 1) = 7, so 3x = 6, x = 2. Then y = 2 + 1 = 3. The solution is (2, 3).
Elimination adds or subtracts the two equations to cancel one variable. Line them up, then make one variable's coefficients opposite so they vanish when added.

Example: x + y = 10 and x - y = 4. Add them: 2x = 14, so x = 7. Plug back: 7 + y = 10, y = 3. The solution is (7, 3). Sometimes you multiply an equation first to set up the cancel.
Graph both lines and the solution is the point where they cross — the (x, y) that satisfies both equations at once. Parallel lines (same slope) never cross, so there's no solution; identical lines overlap, giving infinitely many.

Example: y = x + 1 and y = -x + 5 cross at (2, 3). That single point is the system's solution.
When solving, if the variable disappears and you get a false statement (like 5 = 8), there's no solution. If you get a true statement (like 4 = 4), it's true for all values — infinitely many solutions.

Example: 2x + 3 = 2x + 7 leads to 3 = 7 (false): no solution. But 2x + 4 = 2(x + 2) gives 4 = 4 (true): all numbers work.
For an inequality like y < 2x + 1, first graph the boundary line. Use a dashed line for < or > and a solid line for <= or >=. Then shade the side that makes the inequality true — test a point like (0, 0).

Example: y < 2x + 1. Draw a dashed line y = 2x + 1. Test (0,0): 0 < 1 is true, so shade the side containing (0, 0).
Direct variation means two quantities grow together at a constant rate: y = kx, where k is the constant of variation. As x doubles, y doubles. Its graph is a straight line through the origin.

Example: if y = 3x, then k = 3. When x = 2, y = 6; when x = 4, y = 12. To find k, divide y by x for any matching pair.
Inverse variation means as one quantity goes up, the other goes down so their product stays constant: y = k/x, or xy = k. Its graph is a curve, not a line.

Example: y = 12/x. When x = 2, y = 6; when x = 4, y = 3 — x doubled and y halved, but xy = 12 each time. Speed and travel time vary inversely for a fixed distance.
In a proportional relationship y = kx, the number k is the constant of proportionality — it tells how much y changes per unit of x. Find it by dividing y by x for any pair.

Example: a table shows x: 2,3,4 and y: 6,9,12. Each y/x = 3, so k = 3 and the rule is y = 3x. It's the same idea as unit rate or slope.
Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor each step instead of adding. It looks like y = a times b^x with b greater than 1. Growth starts slow then explodes.

Example: a population that doubles each year: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. The rule is y = 1 times 2^x. Compare to linear, which would add the same amount each time, not multiply.
Exponential decay multiplies by a factor between 0 and 1 each step, so the amount shrinks fast at first then levels off. The form is y = a times b^x with 0 < b < 1.

Example: medicine that halves each hour starting at 100 mg: 100, 50, 25, 12.5. The rule is y = 100 times (1/2)^x. The factor 1/2 makes it decay.
The zeros of a function are the inputs that make the output equal zero — exactly where the graph crosses the x-axis. To find them, set f(x) = 0 and solve. They're also called roots or x-intercepts.

Example: f(x) = x^2 - 9. Set it to zero: x^2 - 9 = 0, so x = 3 or x = -3. Those are the two zeros, where the parabola hits the x-axis.
End behavior describes what a graph does at its far left and far right — does it shoot up, fall down, or level off as x goes to very large or very small values?

Example: f(x) = x^2 rises on both ends (both arms point up). f(x) = -x^2 falls on both ends. A line with positive slope falls on the left and rises on the right.
Adding outside the function moves the graph up or down; changing inside moves it left or right (and inside works backwards). For f(x): f(x) + k shifts up k, f(x) - k shifts down. f(x - h) shifts right h, f(x + h) shifts left.

Example: y = x^2 + 3 lifts the parabola up 3. y = (x - 2)^2 slides it right 2. Inside shifts feel reversed, so x - 2 means move right.
A negative sign flips a graph over an axis. -f(x) flips it over the x-axis (upside down). f(-x) flips it over the y-axis (left-right mirror).

Example: y = x^2 opens up; y = -x^2 flips to open down. For y = square root of x, replacing x with -x mirrors it across the y-axis. The minus sign placement decides the axis.
Multiplying a function by a number changes its steepness. a times f(x) with a > 1 stretches it taller (steeper); with 0 < a < 1 it squishes it shorter (wider).

Example: y = 2x^2 is a narrower, steeper parabola than y = x^2. y = (1/2)x^2 is a wider, flatter one. The bigger the multiplier, the steeper the curve.
The absolute value function f(x) = |x| makes a V-shape because it turns every output positive. The point of the V (the vertex) sits where the inside equals zero.

Example: f(x) = |x| has its vertex at (0, 0) and both arms go up at slope 1 and -1. f(x) = |x - 3| moves the V's point to (3, 0).
The square root function f(x) = square root of x makes a curve that starts at a point and rises slowly, like half a sideways parabola. Its domain is x >= 0 because you can't take the square root of a negative (in real numbers).

Example: f(x) = square root of x passes through (0,0), (1,1), (4,2), (9,3). The outputs grow but slower and slower.
A cubic function has x-cubed as its highest power: f(x) = ax^3 + ... Its basic graph (y = x^3) makes an S-shaped curve that falls on the left and rises on the right, passing through the origin.

Example: f(x) = x^3 gives -8, -1, 0, 1, 8 for x = -2,-1,0,1,2. Unlike a parabola, it keeps going down on one side and up on the other.
A polynomial is a sum of terms made of numbers and variables raised to whole-number powers. No variables in denominators, under roots, or with negative exponents. The pieces are monomial (1 term), binomial (2), trinomial (3).

Example: 3x^2 + 2x - 5 is a polynomial (a trinomial). But 4/x or x^(1/2) are NOT polynomials because of the negative/fractional powers.
The degree of a polynomial is the highest exponent on the variable. It controls the shape and the most an expression can be. The term with that exponent is the leading term.

Example: 4x^3 + 2x^2 - x + 7 has degree 3 (from x^3). A plain number like 8 has degree 0. The degree tells you the maximum number of solutions a polynomial equation can have.
To add polynomials, combine like terms — add the coefficients of terms that share the same variable and power. Line them up by power to stay organized.

Example: (3x^2 + 2x + 1) + (x^2 + 5x + 4). Add x^2 terms: 4x^2. Add x terms: 7x. Add constants: 5. Result: 4x^2 + 7x + 5.
To subtract polynomials, distribute the minus sign to every term in the second polynomial (flip all its signs), then combine like terms.

Example: (5x^2 + 3x) - (2x^2 - x). Flip the second: -2x^2 + x. Now add: (5x^2 - 2x^2) + (3x + x) = 3x^2 + 4x. Forgetting to flip every sign is the most common mistake.
FOIL is a way to multiply two binomials: First, Outer, Inner, Last. Multiply those four pairs, then combine like terms.

Example: (x + 2)(x + 3). First: x times x = x^2. Outer: x times 3 = 3x. Inner: 2 times x = 2x. Last: 2 times 3 = 6. Combine: x^2 + 5x + 6.
Distribute the single term to every term inside the parentheses, multiplying coefficients and adding exponents on matching variables.

Example: 2x(3x + 4). Multiply: 2x times 3x = 6x^2, and 2x times 4 = 8x. Result: 6x^2 + 8x. Remember the exponent rule: x times x = x^2.
You can only add or subtract radicals that have the same root inside (like radicals), the same way you combine like terms. Add the numbers in front and keep the radical.

Example: 2 times square root of 3 plus 4 times square root of 3 = 6 times square root of 3. But square root of 2 + square root of 3 can't combine — different radicands. Simplify first so hidden like radicals appear.
To multiply square roots, multiply what's inside and keep one radical: square root of a times square root of b = square root of (a times b). Then simplify if you can.

Example: square root of 2 times square root of 8 = square root of 16 = 4. And square root of 3 times square root of 12 = square root of 36 = 6. Simplifying after multiplying often gives a clean number.
The index is the little number tucked into a radical sign that tells which root to take. No number means 2 (square root). A 3 means cube root, a 4 means fourth root, and so on.

Example: cube root of 27 = 3 because 3 times 3 times 3 = 27. Fourth root of 16 = 2 because 2^4 = 16. The index asks 'what number, used that many times, gives this?'
A proportion sets two ratios equal: a/b = c/d. Solve it by cross multiplying — multiply diagonally and set the products equal, then solve for the unknown.

Example: x/4 = 6/8. Cross multiply: 8x = 24, so x = 3. Proportions solve scaling problems like recipes, maps, and similar shapes.
Turn key words into operations: 'sum/more than' is +, 'difference/less than' is -, 'product/times' is x, 'quotient/per' is divide. 'Is/equals' becomes =. Pick a letter for the unknown.

Example: 'five more than twice a number' becomes 2n + 5. 'A number decreased by 7 is 12' becomes n - 7 = 12. Watch order: 'less than' flips it (3 less than n is n - 3).
Consecutive integers go in a row, so name them n, n+1, n+2. For consecutive even or odd integers, step by 2: n, n+2, n+4. Then write an equation from the clue.

Example: three consecutive integers sum to 36. Write n + (n+1) + (n+2) = 36, so 3n + 3 = 36, 3n = 33, n = 11. The integers are 11, 12, 13.
Squaring a binomial means multiplying it by itself: (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2. Don't just square each term — the middle 2ab is essential. A common mistake is writing a^2 + b^2.

Example: (x + 3)^2 = x^2 + 2(x)(3) + 9 = x^2 + 6x + 9. And (x - 4)^2 = x^2 - 8x + 16.
A relation is any set of ordered pairs linking inputs to outputs. A function is a special relation where each input has exactly one output. So every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function.

Example: {(1,2), (3,4), (5,6)} is a function — no repeated inputs. But {(1,2), (1,5)} is only a relation, because input 1 has two outputs.
An inverse undoes a number back to the identity. The additive inverse (opposite) of a is -a, since a + (-a) = 0. The multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of a is 1/a, since a times 1/a = 1.

Example: the opposite of 6 is -6 (6 + -6 = 0). The reciprocal of 4 is 1/4 (4 times 1/4 = 1). These power the rules for solving equations.
A rational expression is a fraction with polynomials. To simplify, factor the top and bottom, then cancel any common factors — just like reducing a numeric fraction.

Example: (x^2 - 9)/(x + 3). Factor the top: (x + 3)(x - 3). Cancel the (x + 3): you're left with x - 3. You can only cancel whole factors, never individual terms.
A fraction is undefined when its denominator equals zero, because dividing by zero has no meaning. For a rational expression, find which x-values make the bottom zero and exclude them.

Example: in 5/(x - 2), the expression is undefined at x = 2 (that makes the bottom zero). For 1/(x^2 - 9), it's undefined at x = 3 and x = -3.
You can graph a line fast using just its two intercepts. Set y = 0 to get the x-intercept, set x = 0 to get the y-intercept, plot both points, and connect them.

Example: 2x + 3y = 12. x-intercept (y=0): x = 6, point (6,0). y-intercept (x=0): y = 4, point (0,4). Draw the line through (6,0) and (0,4).
A parent function is the simplest form of a function family, before any shifts or stretches. Learning the parent's shape lets you predict every transformed version. Common ones: y = x (line), y = x^2 (parabola), y = |x| (V), y = square root of x (curve), y = x^3 (S-curve).

Example: y = (x - 3)^2 + 1 is the parent y = x^2 moved right 3 and up 1. Knowing the parent shape makes graphing fast.
In real-world linear relationships, the slope is a unit rate — how much one thing changes per single unit of another. It carries units like dollars per hour or miles per gallon.

Example: if a job pays $45 for 3 hours, the slope (pay per hour) is 45/3 = $15 per hour. The equation y = 15x predicts pay for any hours x.
Given two points, first find the slope, then use one point to find the y-intercept. Plug into y = mx + b.

Example: points (1, 3) and (3, 7). Slope = (7 - 3)/(3 - 1) = 2. Use (1, 3): 3 = 2(1) + b, so b = 1. The equation is y = 2x + 1.
A recursive formula builds each term from the one before (you need the previous term). An explicit formula computes any term directly from its position number. Explicit is faster for far-out terms.

Example: for 3, 5, 7, 9... recursive is 'next = previous + 2'. Explicit is a(n) = 2n + 1, so the 10th term is 2(10) + 1 = 21 without listing them all.
An arithmetic sequence adds the same number (the common difference) each step. Its explicit rule is a(n) = a1 + (n - 1)d, where a1 is the first term and d is the difference. They graph as evenly spaced points on a line.

Example: 4, 7, 10, 13... has d = 3, a1 = 4. The rule a(n) = 4 + (n - 1)3. The 6th term: 4 + 5(3) = 19.
A geometric sequence multiplies by the same number (the common ratio) each step. Its explicit rule is a(n) = a1 times r^(n-1). Geometric sequences grow or shrink exponentially.

Example: 3, 6, 12, 24... has ratio r = 2, a1 = 3. Rule: a(n) = 3 times 2^(n-1). The 5th term: 3 times 2^4 = 48.
To classify a sequence, check the pattern between terms. If you ADD the same amount each time, it's arithmetic (common difference). If you MULTIPLY by the same amount, it's geometric (common ratio).

Example: 5, 10, 15, 20 adds 5 each time (arithmetic). But 5, 10, 20, 40 multiplies by 2 each time (geometric). Look at whether successive differences or successive ratios are constant.
Split an absolute value inequality into two parts. For |x| < c (less-than), it becomes -c < x < c (a sandwich). For |x| > c (greater-than), it becomes x < -c OR x > c (two outer pieces).

Example: |x| < 4 means -4 < x < 4. But |x| > 4 means x < -4 or x > 4. Less-than is 'and' (between), greater-than is 'or' (outside).
For a curve, the average rate of change between two points is the slope of the line connecting them: (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a). It tells the overall climb between those inputs, even if the curve wiggles.

Example: f(x) = x^2 from x=1 to x=3. f(1)=1, f(3)=9. Average rate = (9 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 8/2 = 4. On a straight line this just equals the constant slope.
To rewrite an equation in y = form, isolate y on one side using inverse operations. This makes it easy to graph or find the slope and intercept.

Example: 2x + y = 8. Subtract 2x: y = -2x + 8 (slope -2, intercept 8). With 3x - 2y = 6: subtract 3x, then divide by -2: y = (3/2)x - 3.
Every parabola has one turning point at its vertex. If it opens up (positive a), the vertex is the minimum. If it opens down (negative a), the vertex is the maximum. The y-value of the vertex is that extreme value.

Example: f(x) = -x^2 + 4x. It opens down, so it has a maximum. Vertex x = -4/(2 times -1) = 2, and f(2) = 4. The maximum value is 4.
Interval notation describes a range of numbers with brackets and parentheses. Square brackets [ ] include the endpoint; parentheses ( ) exclude it. Infinity always gets a parenthesis.

Example: x >= 2 is [2, infinity). 1 < x <= 5 is (1, 5]. All real numbers is (-infinity, infinity). It's a compact alternative to inequality notation.
To solve a quadratic by factoring, first get one side equal to zero, factor the other side, then set each factor equal to zero (zero product property) and solve.

Example: x^2 + x - 6 = 0. Factor: (x + 3)(x - 2) = 0. So x + 3 = 0 (x = -3) or x - 2 = 0 (x = 2). The two solutions are -3 and 2.
Factoring by grouping works on four-term polynomials. Group them into two pairs, factor the GCF from each pair, and if the leftover binomials match, factor that out.

Example: x^3 + 2x^2 + 3x + 6. Group: x^2(x + 2) + 3(x + 2). Both have (x + 2), so factor it out: (x + 2)(x^2 + 3).
The leading coefficient is the number in front of the term with the highest power. It controls a graph's overall direction and steepness. For a polynomial, write it in order of powers first, then read the front number.

Example: in -2x^3 + 5x - 1, the leading coefficient is -2. Its negative sign makes a cubic fall on the right, and its size makes the curve steep.
Any radical can be written as a fractional exponent: the nth root of x to the m power is x^(m/n). The root becomes the denominator, the power becomes the numerator. This lets you use exponent rules on radicals.

Example: square root of x is x^(1/2). The cube root of x^2 is x^(2/3). Now square root of x times square root of x = x^(1/2) times x^(1/2) = x^1 = x.
The sign of slope tells the direction a line travels left to right. Positive slope rises (goes uphill). Negative slope falls (goes downhill). Zero slope is flat, and undefined slope is straight up and down.

Example: y = 2x + 1 climbs (positive). y = -3x + 4 drops (negative). The bigger the number, the steeper the climb or fall.
Geometry formulas are literal equations you can solve for any variable. Use inverse operations the same as with numbers, treating the other letters as constants.

Example: area of a triangle A = (1/2)bh. Solve for h: multiply both sides by 2 (2A = bh), then divide by b (h = 2A/b). Now you can find a height from a known area and base.
To get a linear equation from a table, find the slope (the constant change in y per step in x), then find b by reading the y-value when x = 0 (or back-solving).

Example: x: 0,1,2 and y: 4,7,10. Each y rises by 3, so slope = 3. At x = 0, y = 4, so b = 4. Equation: y = 3x + 4.
A one-step inequality needs a single inverse operation to isolate the variable, just like a one-step equation. The catch: flip the sign if you multiply or divide by a negative.

Example: x + 4 < 9. Subtract 4: x < 5. And -2x >= 6: divide by -2 and flip: x <= -3. Adding or subtracting never flips the sign.
Phrases map to inequality symbols: 'at least' and 'no less than' mean >=, 'at most' and 'no more than' mean <=, 'more than' is >, 'less than' is <. Pick a variable and translate.

Example: 'You must be at least 13 to sign up.' Let a be age: a >= 13. 'No more than 20 students' becomes s <= 20. The 'at least/at most' phrases include the boundary.
If both sides of an exponential equation can be written with the same base, set the exponents equal and solve. Rewrite numbers as powers first.

Example: 2^x = 8. Since 8 = 2^3, the equation is 2^x = 2^3, so x = 3. Another: 3^(x+1) = 27 = 3^3, so x + 1 = 3, x = 2.
Spot the family by the pattern in a table or the equation's form. Linear adds a constant (constant first differences). Quadratic has constant second differences. Exponential multiplies by a constant ratio.

Example: y: 2,4,6,8 adds 2 (linear). y: 1,4,9,16 has first differences 3,5,7 and constant second differences 2 (quadratic). y: 2,6,18,54 multiplies by 3 (exponential).
A one-to-one function never repeats an output — each y comes from only one x. You can test it with the horizontal line test: if no horizontal line hits the graph more than once, it's one-to-one. Only one-to-one functions have true inverses.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1 is one-to-one (a slanted line passes the test). But f(x) = x^2 is not, because both x = 2 and x = -2 give 4.
Slope is rise over run. A vertical line has two points with the same x-value, so the run (change in x) is zero. Since dividing by zero is undefined, the slope is undefined — not zero.

Example: line through (3, 1) and (3, 6). Slope = (6 - 1)/(3 - 3) = 5/0, which is undefined. The line just goes straight up, so 'steepness as a number' doesn't exist.
A minus sign in front of parentheses flips the sign of every term inside, because it's really multiplying by -1.

Example: -(x - 4) = -x + 4 (both signs flip). And 5 - (2x - 3) = 5 - 2x + 3 = -2x + 8. Forgetting to flip the second term's sign is one of the most common algebra slips.
When a function has a variable in the denominator, the domain excludes any x that makes the denominator zero, since division by zero is undefined. Find those forbidden x-values by setting the denominator to zero.

Example: f(x) = 1/(x - 5). The denominator is zero at x = 5, so the domain is all real numbers except 5. For 1/(x^2 - 4), exclude x = 2 and x = -2.
A complex fraction has fractions inside its top or bottom. Simplify by remembering a fraction bar means division: divide the top by the bottom, which means multiply by the reciprocal.

Example: (1/2)/(3/4). This is 1/2 divided by 3/4, so flip and multiply: 1/2 times 4/3 = 4/6 = 2/3. Treat the big bar as 'divided by'.
To graph y = mx + b, plot the y-intercept b first as a point on the y-axis. Then use the slope as rise over run to step to another point, and draw the line.

Example: y = (2/3)x - 1. Start at (0, -1). Slope 2/3 means up 2, right 3, landing at (3, 1). Connect the two points and extend.
Solve a two-step inequality just like a two-step equation: undo addition/subtraction first, then multiplication/division. Flip the sign only if you divide or multiply by a negative.

Example: 3x - 5 < 7. Add 5: 3x < 12. Divide by 3: x < 4. But -2x + 1 > 9: subtract 1 (-2x > 8), divide by -2 and flip (x < -4).
When a product is raised to a power, the exponent applies to each factor: (xy)^n = x^n times y^n. The same goes for numbers and coefficients inside.

Example: (3x)^2 = 3^2 times x^2 = 9x^2. And (2ab)^3 = 2^3 a^3 b^3 = 8a^3 b^3. Don't forget to raise the number out front to the power too.
When a fraction is raised to a power, raise both the top and bottom to that power: (x/y)^n = x^n / y^n.

Example: (x/3)^2 = x^2 / 9. And (2/y)^3 = 8 / y^3. It's the quotient version of the power-of-a-product rule, applied to numerator and denominator separately.
The V-shaped graph of f(x) = |x - h| + k has its corner (vertex) at (h, k). The inside number moves it left/right (backwards), the outside number moves it up/down.

Example: y = |x - 2| + 3. The vertex is at (2, 3) — right 2 and up 3 from the basic V. A negative inside like |x + 1| moves it left 1.
A monomial is a single term: a number, a variable, or numbers and variables multiplied together with whole-number exponents. No plus or minus signs joining pieces, no division by a variable.

Example: 5, x, 3x^2, and -7ab are all monomials. But x + 2 (two terms) and 4/x (variable in denominator) are not. Monomials are the building blocks of polynomials.
To divide monomials, divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents of matching variables (the quotient rule).

Example: 12x^5 / 4x^2. Divide numbers: 12/4 = 3. Subtract exponents: x^(5-2) = x^3. Result: 3x^3. If the variable cancels completely (same exponent), it becomes x^0 = 1.
To solve an equation with fractions, multiply every term by the least common denominator. This clears all fractions, leaving a simpler whole-number equation.

Example: x/2 + 1/3 = 5/6. The LCD is 6. Multiply each term by 6: 3x + 2 = 5. Then 3x = 3, x = 1. Multiplying the WHOLE equation keeps it balanced.
An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at the same speed and direction, unless a force acts on it. This is why you lurch forward when a car brakes suddenly — your body wants to keep moving even though the car has stopped.

The tendency to resist a change in motion is called inertia, and more massive objects have more of it.
Force equals mass times acceleration. A heavier object needs more force to accelerate the same amount; a smaller object accelerates more from the same force. Push a shopping cart vs a car with the same force and you'll feel the difference.
For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with the same force. Rockets work this way: hot gas shoots down, and the rocket gets pushed up.

The two forces always act on different objects, which is why they don't just cancel out.
Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. The faster something moves, the more energy it has — and doubling the speed quadruples the energy (it's squared). A car going 60 mph has four times the crash energy of one going 30 mph.
When you lift something up, you store energy in it. That stored energy is gravitational potential energy, and it depends on mass, gravity, and height. Drop the object and that PE turns back into kinetic energy.
Momentum is mass in motion — how hard it is to stop something. A slow-moving truck and a fast-moving bike can have similar momentum. In any collision, total momentum stays the same (conservation of momentum), which is how Newton's cradle and billiards work.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transformed from one form to another. A roller coaster trades potential energy at the top for kinetic energy at the bottom. Some always sneaks off as heat or sound, but the total is the same.

This is one of the most fundamental laws in all of physics.
In a closed system with no outside forces, the total momentum before a collision equals the total after. This is why a cue ball stops when it hits another billiard ball dead-on — its momentum transfers to the other ball.

Rockets, jet engines, and recoil from a gun all follow this rule.
In physics, work means force applied over a distance — and it equals the energy transferred. Pushing a box 3 meters with 10 N of force does 30 joules of work. Holding a heavy box still does zero physics-work, even though it feels exhausting.
Power is how fast you do work — energy per unit time. Two engines might do the same total work, but the more powerful one finishes faster. A 100-watt bulb uses 100 joules of energy every second.
To keep something moving in a circle, you need a force pulling it inward — that's centripetal force. For a car turning a corner, it's friction; for the moon, it's gravity; for a yo-yo on a string, it's tension.
A pendulum's swing time depends almost entirely on its length, not on the weight at the end. A longer pendulum swings more slowly. This is why grandfather clocks are tall.
Friction is a force that resists motion between surfaces. Static friction holds things in place until you push hard enough; kinetic friction slows things that are already sliding (and is usually weaker than static). Rolling friction — for wheels and balls — is much weaker than either.

Fluid friction (or drag) is what slows you down in water or air.
Falling objects accelerate until air resistance pushing up equals gravity pulling down. At that point they stop speeding up — that steady speed is terminal velocity. A skydiver hits about 53 m/s (120 mph) belly-down, or much higher if streamlined.
Angular momentum is conserved — it depends on how mass is distributed and how fast you're rotating. Pull your mass closer to the spin axis and you must spin faster to keep the same angular momentum.

This is also how a collapsing star can spin into a fast-rotating neutron star.
The electric force between two charges is proportional to the charges and falls off with the square of the distance. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract. The constant k ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
Voltage equals current times resistance. Push harder (more volts) and more current flows; add resistance and the current drops. This relationship works for most ordinary conductors.
Current flowing through resistance produces heat — that's why toasters glow and laptops warm up. The power dissipated grows with the square of the current, which is why long-distance power lines use very high voltage (low current) to minimize losses.
An electric field is the invisible region around an electric charge where another charge would feel a force. It points from positive to negative, and its strength falls off with distance squared. The unit is volts per meter (or newtons per coulomb).
A magnetic field is the region around a magnet or moving charge where magnetic forces act. It loops from a magnet's north pole around to its south pole. The unit is the tesla (T); Earth's field at the surface is about 50 microtesla.
A changing magnetic field through a wire loop creates a voltage — Faraday's discovery. Spin a magnet near a coil and current flows. This is how every electric generator works, from bicycle dynamos to gigawatt power plants.

Transformers, electric motors (in reverse), and induction stoves all rely on it.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light — what differs is wavelength (and energy). From longest to shortest: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

Visible light is a thin slice in the middle, from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red).
Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength. For a given medium, the speed is fixed — so if frequency goes up, wavelength must go down. This is true for sound, light, and water waves alike.
When a source of waves moves toward you, the waves bunch up — higher frequency. When it moves away, they stretch out — lower frequency. That's why an ambulance siren drops in pitch as it passes.

Astronomers use the same effect with light: galaxies moving away from us are redshifted, which is how we learned the universe is expanding.
When light passes from one material to another, it bends. The amount depends on the materials' indices of refraction. This is why a straw looks broken in a glass of water.

The formula: n₁ sin(θ₁) = n₂ sin(θ₂).
Sunlight contains all colors. When it hits air molecules, the shorter (bluer) wavelengths scatter more than the longer (redder) ones — this is called Rayleigh scattering. The blue scatters in every direction, so the whole sky glows blue.

At sunset, light passes through more atmosphere, blue gets scattered away entirely, and only reds and oranges reach you.
Lenses bend (refract) light to focus it. A convex (bulging) lens converges light to a point — used in magnifying glasses, cameras, and your eye. A concave (caved-in) lens spreads light out — used in glasses for nearsightedness.

The focal length tells you how strongly a lens bends light.
PV = nRT relates pressure, volume, amount of gas (in moles), and temperature. Squeeze a gas and pressure goes up; heat it and pressure or volume rises. R is the gas constant (8.314 J/mol·K).
To raise the temperature of something, you have to add energy. The amount depends on mass, the specific heat (a property of the substance), and the temperature change. Water has an unusually high specific heat — that's why oceans moderate climate.
First law: energy is conserved — you can change forms but you can't make new energy. Second law: entropy (disorder) of a closed system always increases — heat flows from hot to cold, not the other way. Third law: as temperature approaches absolute zero, entropy approaches a minimum.

There's also a zeroth law: if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they're in equilibrium with each other.
Entropy is a measure of disorder or the number of ways a system can be arranged. A shuffled deck has higher entropy than a sorted one. In nature, isolated systems tend toward higher entropy — ice cubes melt in warm rooms, perfume diffuses, hot coffee cools.

This is why time has a direction — entropy never spontaneously decreases.
Light comes in packets called photons. Each photon carries energy proportional to its frequency — blue photons have more energy than red, X-rays much more, gamma rays even more. Planck's constant h ≈ 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
A photon is a particle (quantum) of light — the smallest packet of electromagnetic energy. Photons have no mass and always travel at c (299,792,458 m/s in vacuum). Their energy depends on frequency: E = h × f.
Every particle has wave-like properties — the heavier and faster it moves, the shorter its wavelength. For everyday objects the wavelength is so tiny we never notice. For electrons, it's big enough to use in electron microscopes.
Light and matter both behave sometimes like waves, sometimes like particles. The famous double-slit experiment shows even single electrons or photons create an interference pattern — as if each one passed through both slits at once.

Quantum mechanics says particles don't have definite paths; they have probabilities, and only measurement forces a single answer.
You cannot know both the exact position and exact momentum of a particle at the same time. The more precisely you measure one, the fuzzier the other becomes. This isn't a measurement problem — it's a fundamental feature of nature.

It only matters at quantum scales; for baseballs the uncertainty is unimaginably small.
Two particles can become linked so that measuring one instantly determines the state of the other, no matter how far apart they are. Einstein called it 'spooky action at a distance.' It doesn't let us send messages faster than light, but it's real and now used in quantum computing.
Einstein showed that time runs slower for fast-moving objects. Astronauts on the ISS age microseconds less than people on Earth. At 90% the speed of light, a clock would tick at about 43% the normal rate.

GPS satellites have to correct for both special and general relativity, or they'd drift kilometers off in a day.
From a stationary observer's view, a fast-moving object appears shorter in the direction of motion. At 0.87 c, lengths shrink to half. We never see this in daily life because nothing we encounter goes anywhere close to light speed.

It's the spatial counterpart to time dilation — both come from the constancy of the speed of light.
Mass and energy are two forms of the same thing. A small amount of mass holds an enormous amount of energy because c² is huge (~9 × 10¹⁶ m²/s²). This is what powers stars and nuclear weapons.

1 kg of matter holds about 9 × 10¹⁶ J — enough to power a city for a year.
If you compressed mass below this radius, it would form a black hole — the size of its event horizon. For the Sun it's about 3 km; for Earth, only about 9 mm.

The formula: r = 2GM/c², where G is the gravitational constant.
Einstein's theory of gravity says mass and energy curve spacetime, and objects move along the straightest paths through that curvature. The Sun warps spacetime, and Earth's orbit follows that warp.

It predicts time dilation in gravity (clocks tick slower at sea level than on a mountaintop), light bending around mass, and gravitational waves.
Ripples in spacetime caused by massive accelerating objects, like merging black holes. They travel at the speed of light. LIGO first detected them in 2015 from two black holes merging over a billion light-years away, opening a new window onto the universe.
Sound travels about 343 m/s in air at 20°C — roughly a kilometer in three seconds. It moves much faster in water (1500 m/s) and faster still in steel (5000 m/s), because the molecules are packed closer.

In a vacuum, sound can't travel at all — there's no medium to vibrate.
The upward force on an object in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. If that's more than the object weighs, it floats. Steel ships float because their hull shape displaces a huge volume of water — enough to outweigh the steel.
Pressure is force spread over area. The same force on a small area creates higher pressure — that's why snowshoes work (spread weight) and knives cut (concentrate force).
Density is mass packed into volume. A bowling ball and a beach ball have similar size but very different densities. Whether something floats in water depends on whether its density is less than water's (1000 kg/m³).
A mole is just a count, like a dozen — except a mole is 6.022 × 10²³ things. Chemists use it because atoms are so small that gram-amounts of any substance contain trillions of trillions of atoms.

One mole of carbon-12 weighs exactly 12 grams. The same logic gives you the molar mass for every element on the periodic table.
Molarity is the concentration of a solution — how many moles of solute per liter of solution. A 1 M (one-molar) saltwater solution has 1 mole of NaCl in every liter.
When you dilute a solution, the moles of solute don't change — only the volume. So the starting concentration times starting volume equals the ending concentration times ending volume.
pH measures how acidic or basic a solution is: pH = -log[H⁺]. A pH of 7 is neutral; lower is acidic, higher is basic. Each step is 10×: pH 4 is ten times more acidic than pH 5.

The log scale exists because hydrogen ion concentrations span an enormous range — from about 1 M in strong acid to 10⁻¹⁴ M in strong base.
pOH is the basic-side cousin of pH, measuring hydroxide ion concentration: pOH = -log[OH⁻]. In water at 25°C, pH + pOH = 14, so they're always linked.
Arrhenius: acids release H⁺ in water, bases release OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry: acids donate protons, bases accept them — broader and more useful. Lewis: acids accept electron pairs, bases donate them — most general of all.

Each definition covers more cases than the last, but Brønsted-Lowry is the everyday workhorse.
Across a period (left to right), atoms get smaller, electronegativity rises, and ionization energy rises — nuclear charge pulls electrons in tighter. Down a group, atoms get larger and these properties weaken — electrons sit in outer shells, farther from the nucleus.

Fluorine is the most electronegative element; cesium has one of the lowest ionization energies.
Ionic bonds form when atoms transfer electrons — usually a metal and a nonmetal (like Na⁺Cl⁻). Covalent bonds share electrons — usually between nonmetals (H₂O, CO₂). Metallic bonds let electrons flow freely through a lattice — that's why metals conduct.

Hydrogen bonds are weaker attractions between molecules (think water sticking to itself, or DNA strands holding together).
A weak attraction between a hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom (N, O, or F) and another electronegative atom nearby. Hydrogen bonds give water its surface tension and high boiling point, hold DNA's two strands together, and shape proteins.
The main categories: synthesis (A + B → AB), decomposition (AB → A + B), single replacement (A + BC → AC + B), double replacement (AB + CD → AD + CB), combustion (fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O), and redox (electrons transfer between species).

Most reactions fit more than one category — combustion is also a redox reaction, for example.
Solid, liquid, gas, plasma — and exotic ones like Bose-Einstein condensates. As you add energy, particles move faster: melting (solid→liquid), vaporization (liquid→gas), and ionization (gas→plasma). Cooling reverses each step.

Sublimation skips the liquid phase entirely (dry ice does this).
Water is one of the few substances where the solid form is less dense than the liquid. Hydrogen bonds force water molecules into an open, hexagonal crystal when they freeze — taking up more space than liquid water.

If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up, and aquatic life couldn't survive winter.
Radioactive isotopes decay at a steady statistical rate. After one half-life, half of the original sample remains; after two half-lives, a quarter; and so on. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years, which is how we date organic artifacts.
Atoms aren't created or destroyed in a chemical reaction, so the same number of each element must appear on both sides. You balance by adjusting the coefficients (the big numbers in front of formulas), never the subscripts inside formulas.

Start with the element that appears in the fewest compounds, and save free elements (like O₂ or H₂) for last.
Oxidation is losing electrons; reduction is gaining them. They always happen together — what one species loses, another gains. Mnemonic: 'LEO says GER' — Lose Electrons, Oxidation; Gain Electrons, Reduction.

Rusting iron, burning wood, and batteries all involve redox reactions.
A catalyst speeds up a reaction by giving it an easier pathway — lower activation energy — without being used up itself. Catalytic converters in cars use platinum, palladium, and rhodium to turn toxic exhaust into less harmful gases.

Living things use enzymes (protein catalysts) for essentially every reaction in the body.
When you disturb a chemical equilibrium — by changing concentration, pressure, or temperature — the reaction shifts to partly undo the change. Add more reactant, and the reaction makes more product. Cool an exothermic reaction, and it makes more product (releasing more heat).
Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) are small, simple cells with no nucleus — their DNA floats free in the cell. Eukaryotes (plants, animals, fungi, protists) have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles like mitochondria.

Eukaryotes likely evolved when ancient cells engulfed bacteria that became mitochondria and chloroplasts.
The nucleus holds DNA. Mitochondria make ATP (energy). Ribosomes build proteins. The endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus assemble and package molecules. Lysosomes break down waste. In plants, chloroplasts do photosynthesis and the central vacuole stores fluid.

Each organelle is specialized — like organs in a body, but for the cell.
The mitochondrion is the organelle that produces most of a cell's ATP — its energy currency — by oxidizing glucose. Each cell has dozens to thousands. They have their own circular DNA, inherited only from your mother.
Cells break down glucose with oxygen to make ATP, the energy molecule. Three main stages: glycolysis (in cytoplasm), the Krebs cycle (in the mitochondrial matrix), and the electron transport chain (on the inner mitochondrial membrane).

One glucose yields about 30-32 ATP. Without oxygen, cells fall back on fermentation (much less efficient).
Plants take in CO₂ from air and water from soil, and use sunlight to combine them into sugar (glucose) and oxygen.

6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂

The light-dependent reactions happen in the thylakoid membranes (capturing light, splitting water). The Calvin cycle in the stroma builds sugar from CO₂.
DNA is a double helix — two strands twisted together, held by base pairs. The four bases are A, T, C, G. A always pairs with T, and C with G. Each strand is built from a sugar-phosphate backbone with the bases sticking inward.

The order of bases is the genetic code — a 3-billion-letter manual in every human cell.
RNA is DNA's single-stranded cousin. It uses uracil (U) instead of thymine (T) and has a slightly different sugar. Three main types: messenger RNA (carries the gene's instructions out of the nucleus), transfer RNA (brings amino acids), and ribosomal RNA (makes up ribosomes).

There are also many regulatory RNAs that control gene expression.
Transcription copies a gene's DNA sequence into messenger RNA. RNA polymerase unzips a small stretch of DNA, reads one strand, and assembles complementary RNA. The mRNA then leaves the nucleus to be translated into protein.

Only the bits of DNA being used at the moment get transcribed — that's why different cell types make different proteins.
Ribosomes read mRNA in triplets called codons. Each codon (like AUG, GCU, UAA) specifies one amino acid. Transfer RNAs bring matching amino acids, and the ribosome links them into a growing protein chain.

A start codon (AUG) kicks things off; one of three stop codons ends it.
Proteins are long chains of amino acids that fold into 3D shapes. Their shape determines their job — enzymes catalyze reactions, structural proteins build hair and muscle, antibodies fight infection, hemoglobin carries oxygen.

There are 20 standard amino acids; combinations create essentially infinite possible proteins.
Enzymes are protein catalysts that speed up specific biochemical reactions, usually by huge factors. Each enzyme has an active site shaped to fit a particular substrate, like a lock and key. Without enzymes, most of life's reactions would be far too slow to sustain you.
Mitosis makes two genetically identical daughter cells — used for growth and repair. Meiosis makes four genetically unique sex cells (gametes) with half the chromosomes, ready to combine with another gamete at fertilization.

Meiosis includes two rounds of division and a chromosome-shuffling step (crossing over) that creates genetic diversity.
Gregor Mendel showed that traits come in pairs of alleles (one from each parent), and dominant alleles mask recessive ones. A Punnett square tracks how alleles combine: cross two heterozygous (Aa) parents and you get 25% AA, 50% Aa, 25% aa.

Many human traits don't follow simple Mendelian rules, but it's still the foundation of genetics.
In any population, individuals vary. Some variations help survival or reproduction in a given environment. Those traits get passed to more offspring, so over generations the population shifts. Darwin's great insight.

It's the mechanism behind evolution — not a goal, just a statistical filter.
