Multiple independent lines point the same way: fossil sequences showing gradual change; DNA similarity matching evolutionary relationships; vestigial structures (whale leg bones, our appendix); biogeography (similar species on neighboring islands); direct observation in fast-reproducing species like bacteria and finches.

The theory of evolution by natural selection is one of the most thoroughly confirmed ideas in science.
Energy flows through ecosystems in steps. Producers (plants) make food from sunlight. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers. Secondary consumers (carnivores) eat them, and so on. Decomposers recycle everything.

Only about 10% of energy passes to each next level — that's why apex predators are rare.
A biome is a large region with characteristic climate and life. Major biomes include tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, temperate forest, taiga (boreal forest), tundra, grassland, and various aquatic biomes (freshwater, marine, coral reef).

Climate (temperature and rainfall) mostly determines which biome a region becomes.
The heart is a four-chambered pump. The right side receives oxygen-poor blood and pumps it to the lungs. The left side receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and pumps it to the rest of the body. Valves keep blood flowing one way only.

A pacemaker region called the SA node sets the beat — about 60-100 times a minute at rest.
Neurons signal each other with electrical pulses called action potentials. At rest, the inside of a neuron is negatively charged. When stimulated, sodium ions rush in and the voltage flips positive, then potassium ions flow out and it resets.

The pulse races down the axon and triggers the release of neurotransmitters at the other end.
Light enters through the cornea and pupil, gets focused by the lens onto the retina at the back of the eye. The retina has rod cells (for low light, no color) and cone cells (for color, in three types: red, green, blue). They convert light into electrical signals that travel along the optic nerve to the brain.

Your brain does most of the work — flipping the upside-down image, filling in gaps, and interpreting depth.
Sound waves vibrate the eardrum, which moves three tiny bones (the smallest in your body) that transmit the vibration to the fluid-filled cochlea. Hair cells in the cochlea bend with the fluid and fire signals to the brain. Different frequencies bend different parts of the cochlea — that's how you tell pitch.

Loud noise damages hair cells permanently — they don't grow back.
You have two immune systems. The innate one (skin, mucus, inflammation, certain white blood cells) attacks anything foreign immediately. The adaptive one (B and T cells, antibodies) learns specific pathogens and remembers them.

Vaccines work by training the adaptive immune system with a safe version of a pathogen so it's ready for the real thing.
Bacteria are tiny single-celled organisms — alive in every meaningful sense. They eat, grow, and reproduce on their own. Viruses are much smaller — really just genetic material in a protein coat. They can't reproduce alone; they hijack a host cell to make more of themselves.

Antibiotics kill bacteria but do nothing against viruses.
CRISPR-Cas9 is a precise gene-editing tool, originally a bacterial immune system against viruses. Scientists program a short guide RNA to match a target DNA sequence, and the Cas9 protein cuts the DNA at that exact spot. The cell's repair can then knock out a gene or insert a new one.

It's already used to treat sickle cell disease and is being trialed for many other genetic conditions.
Living things keep internal conditions steady — temperature, pH, blood sugar — even when the environment changes. This is homeostasis, achieved mostly by negative feedback loops: a sensor detects deviation, signals trigger correction, levels return to set point.

You sweat when hot, shiver when cold; your pancreas releases insulin to lower high blood sugar.
An ecosystem is all the living things in a place plus the nonliving environment they interact with — soil, water, sunlight, climate. Ecosystems can be tiny (a tide pool) or vast (the Amazon basin). Energy flows through them; matter cycles within them.
A gene is a stretch of DNA that codes for a protein (or a functional RNA). Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes scattered across 23 pairs of chromosomes. Many genes have multiple versions (alleles) that produce slightly different traits.
A chromosome is a long, tightly coiled molecule of DNA wrapped around proteins. Humans have 46 — 23 from each parent. They become visible when cells divide. Sex chromosomes (XX or XY in humans) determine biological sex.
Healthy ecosystems quietly do work that humans depend on: bees pollinate crops, forests filter water and store carbon, wetlands buffer floods, soil microbes recycle nutrients. Economists estimate the value at tens of trillions of dollars per year worldwide.

When ecosystems collapse, these services have to be replaced expensively (or not at all).
Photosynthesis takes CO₂ and water, uses light energy, and makes sugar and oxygen. Cellular respiration takes sugar and oxygen and breaks them down to release energy (ATP), producing CO₂ and water. Plants do both — they photosynthesize during the day and respire 24/7.

Net effect: plants are oxygen producers, but only when there's enough light.
The human genome has about 3.2 billion base pairs and roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes — fewer than scientists expected. Only about 1-2% of the genome codes for proteins; the rest regulates genes or has functions we're still figuring out.

The Human Genome Project completed a draft in 2003 and a truly complete sequence in 2022.
Cancer is uncontrolled cell growth. Normally cells divide on a tight schedule and die when they're supposed to. When key genes get damaged (oncogenes, tumor suppressors, DNA repair genes), cells can keep dividing, ignore stop signals, and invade other tissues.

It's not one disease but hundreds — defined by which cells went rogue and which mutations drove them.
Vaccines train your immune system to recognize a pathogen without making you sick. Some use weakened or killed germs; some use just a piece of the germ (like a protein); newer ones (mRNA) give your cells the recipe to make that piece. Either way, your body builds memory cells and antibodies that respond fast if you meet the real thing.

When enough people are vaccinated, even unvaccinated ones get protection from herd immunity.
Antibiotics target structures or processes unique to bacteria — like their cell wall or their distinct ribosomes — so they kill bacteria without harming your cells. They do nothing for viruses, which use your own cellular machinery.

Overuse breeds resistant bacteria, because sensitive ones die and the survivors reproduce. That's why doctors are careful with prescriptions.
Our solar system has the Sun at the center, eight planets, several dwarf planets (like Pluto, Eris, Ceres), about 200 moons, plus asteroids and comets. The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are rocky; the four outer ones (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are gas or ice giants.

The Sun holds 99.86% of the system's mass.
Stars form when clouds of gas and dust collapse under gravity. A main-sequence star (like the Sun) spends most of its life fusing hydrogen into helium. When the hydrogen runs out, it swells into a red giant.

Small stars end as white dwarfs. Bigger ones explode as supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes behind.
A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing — not even light — can escape once inside the event horizon. They form when massive stars collapse, or by other extreme processes.

The singularity at the center is where our physics breaks down; we don't really know what's there.
What's left after a massive star explodes as a supernova — a city-sized ball with more mass than the Sun. A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh billions of tons. Some spin rapidly and beam radio waves we detect as pulsars.
Galaxies are huge gravitationally bound systems of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter. Main types: spiral (like our Milky Way, with arms and a flat disk), elliptical (egg-shaped, mostly old stars), and irregular (no clear shape, often after collisions).

The observable universe holds an estimated 200 billion to 2 trillion galaxies.
About 13.8 billion years ago, the universe began as an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since. The Big Bang isn't an explosion in space — it's an expansion of space itself.

Key evidence: the cosmic microwave background (leftover heat), the proportions of hydrogen and helium, and the redshift of distant galaxies.
Faint microwave radiation filling the universe — the leftover heat from when the universe cooled enough for atoms to form, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. It's nearly uniform at about 2.7 K, with tiny ripples that grew into today's galaxies.
Distant galaxies are receding from us, and the farther away they are, the faster. Velocity equals Hubble's constant (H₀ ≈ 70 km/s per megaparsec) times distance. This is the observational basis for the Big Bang and an expanding universe.
We rarely see exoplanets directly. Two main methods: transit (the planet briefly dims its star as it passes in front), and radial velocity (the star wobbles slightly from the planet's gravity, shifting its spectral lines). Other methods include direct imaging, gravitational microlensing, and astrometry.

Kepler and TESS missions used transits to find thousands of planets.
A 1961 formula estimating the number of communicating civilizations in our galaxy. It multiplies factors like the rate of star formation, fraction with planets, fraction habitable, fraction that develop life, fraction that develop intelligence, fraction that broadcast, and how long they last.

Most terms have huge uncertainties, so estimates range from one civilization (just us) to millions.
If the universe is so vast and old, and many planets could host life, why haven't we found anyone? That's the Fermi paradox. Possible answers: intelligence is rare, civilizations destroy themselves, they don't broadcast, we haven't looked long enough, or they're avoiding us.

No answer is settled — but it's one of the best questions in science.
Galaxies rotate faster than the visible matter can explain — something invisible holds them together. That something is dark matter, roughly 5 times more abundant than ordinary matter. It doesn't emit, absorb, or reflect light. We've never directly detected a dark matter particle, only its gravitational effects.
The expansion of the universe isn't just continuing — it's speeding up. The mysterious cause is called dark energy, and it makes up about 68% of the universe's total energy content. Best guess so far: it's a property of space itself, possibly related to Einstein's cosmological constant.
Sometimes called the Goldilocks zone — the range of distances from a star where temperatures could allow liquid water on a planet's surface. Too close and water boils; too far and it freezes. Earth sits comfortably inside the Sun's habitable zone.
Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms Earth's surface. The surface re-emits energy as infrared. Greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, water vapor) absorb that infrared and re-radiate some back down, trapping heat.

Without greenhouse gases, Earth would average about -18°C (0°F). Adding more is shifting climate quickly.
Earth's outer shell is broken into about a dozen large plates that drift on the partly molten mantle below. Where they push together you get mountains and earthquakes (Himalayas, Andes). Where they pull apart, new crust forms (mid-ocean ridges). Where they slide past, you get faults (San Andreas).

Movement is slow — about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Rocks change form over geologic time. Igneous rocks form from cooled magma or lava. Weathering breaks them into sediment, which compacts into sedimentary rock. Heat and pressure transform any rock into metamorphic rock. Deep burial and melting return it to magma — and the cycle repeats.
From the surface up: troposphere (weather happens here, 0-12 km), stratosphere (ozone layer, 12-50 km), mesosphere (where meteors burn up, 50-85 km), thermosphere (auroras, ISS orbits here, 85-600 km), exosphere (fades into space).

Temperature doesn't simply drop with altitude — it dips, rises in the stratosphere (UV-warming ozone), dips again, then rises in the thermosphere.
Weather comes from uneven heating of Earth's surface by the Sun. Warm air rises, creating low pressure; cool air sinks, creating high pressure. Wind flows from high to low pressure, and Earth's rotation curves the path (Coriolis effect). Where warm wet air rises and cools, water condenses into clouds and falls as rain.

Fronts — boundaries between air masses — drive most storms.
Weather is what's happening in the atmosphere right now — today's rain, tomorrow's wind. Climate is the long-term average over decades. A cold day doesn't disprove warming any more than a hot day proves it.

Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get.
Earth's outer core is liquid iron flowing in complex patterns; that moving conductor generates the planet's magnetic field (the geodynamo). The field protects us from much of the solar wind and channels charged particles toward the poles, where they make auroras.

The magnetic poles drift, and the whole field flips polarity every few hundred thousand years on average.
Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, and plants (transpiration). It condenses in the cooler upper air into clouds. It falls as rain or snow (precipitation), runs off into rivers or sinks underground, and eventually returns to the ocean. The Sun powers the whole loop.

Every drop of water you drink has cycled through the planet many times.
A loop, not a checklist: observe something, ask a question, form a testable hypothesis, design an experiment to test it, analyze the results, draw conclusions, repeat. Other scientists try to reproduce your work; if they can't, your finding doesn't survive.

Real science is messier — it includes intuition, luck, dead ends, and arguments — but the loop is the core.
A hypothesis is a specific, testable guess. A scientific law is a concise description of what happens (often a formula) — like Newton's law of gravity. A scientific theory is a well-tested explanation for why things happen — like the theory of evolution or general relativity.

In science, a theory is the strongest kind of statement, not 'just a guess.'
Before research is published in a reputable journal, other experts in the field review it for errors and weaknesses — that's peer review. After publication, independent labs try to reproduce the results. A finding nobody can reproduce is not yet knowledge.

Many fields face a replication crisis: published results that don't hold up. This is uncomfortable but it's also science working — slowly self-correcting.
Two things going up together doesn't mean one causes the other. Ice cream sales and drowning both rise in summer — but ice cream doesn't cause drowning. Heat causes both. Correlation suggests a relationship; only careful experiments (or natural experiments) can establish causation.

Always ask: could a third factor cause both? Could the direction of causation be reversed?
In a single-blind study, participants don't know which treatment they got. In a double-blind study, the researchers measuring outcomes don't know either. Blinding controls for the placebo effect and for unconscious bias in scoring outcomes.

Without blinding, both patients and researchers tend to find improvement where their hopes lie — even when no real effect exists.
An atom is the smallest unit of an element with that element's chemical properties. It has a tiny dense nucleus of protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral), surrounded by a cloud of electrons (negative). The number of protons defines the element.
A molecule is two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds. Water (H₂O), oxygen gas (O₂), and DNA are all molecules. Some molecules contain just two atoms; biological molecules can contain millions.
An element is a pure substance made of one kind of atom — defined by its number of protons. There are 118 known elements; 94 occur naturally on Earth and the rest have only been made in labs. The periodic table organizes them by atomic number and chemical behavior.
Isotopes are variants of an element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon, but carbon-14 has two extra neutrons. Some isotopes are stable; others are radioactive and decay over time.
Newton described gravity as a force pulling masses together — stronger with bigger masses and weaker with distance squared. Einstein went deeper: mass and energy bend spacetime, and objects move along the straightest paths through that bend. Both descriptions agree wonderfully for everyday situations.

Near black holes or very fast motion, you need Einstein's version.
Every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to both masses and inversely proportional to their distance squared. G is the gravitational constant (6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²) — one of the hardest-to-measure constants in physics.
Light in a vacuum travels at exactly 299,792,458 meters per second — that's c. It's the same in every reference frame, no matter how fast you're moving. Nothing with mass can reach c, because the energy required becomes infinite.

The meter is actually defined by c: it's the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
A battery uses two different materials (electrodes) separated by an electrolyte. A chemical reaction at one electrode releases electrons (oxidation); the other electrode absorbs them (reduction). The electrons can only get from one to the other through an external circuit — and that's the current that powers your phone.

Rechargeable batteries reverse the reaction when you plug them in.
The Moon's gravity pulls Earth's oceans, raising a bulge on the near side. Surprisingly, there's also a bulge on the far side — because Earth itself gets pulled slightly toward the Moon, leaving the far ocean behind. The Sun adds a smaller effect.

As Earth rotates, any spot passes through both bulges per day — two high tides and two low tides.
The Moon is always half-lit by the Sun. We see different fractions of that lit side depending on the Moon's position in its orbit around Earth. New moon: the lit side faces away from us. Full moon: it faces toward us. Quarters and crescents are in between.

The cycle takes about 29.5 days.
Earth's axis is tilted 23.5° from vertical relative to its orbit. When your hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, sunlight hits more directly and days are longer — summer. When it tilts away, sunlight comes in at a shallow angle and days are shorter — winter.

Seasons aren't caused by distance to the Sun (Earth is actually closest in January).
A solar eclipse: the Moon passes between Sun and Earth, blocking the Sun. A lunar eclipse: Earth passes between Sun and Moon, throwing a shadow on the Moon. Solar eclipses are rarer for any given spot because the Moon's shadow on Earth is small.

The coincidence that the Moon and Sun look the same size in our sky is what makes total solar eclipses possible — and it's just a coincidence.
A state where a forward and reverse reaction happen at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stop changing. It's dynamic — both reactions keep happening, just balanced. Equilibrium can be shifted by changing concentration, pressure, or temperature.
A polymer is a long chain made of many repeating smaller units (monomers). Polymers can be natural (DNA, proteins, cellulose, rubber) or synthetic (polyethylene, nylon, PVC). Their properties depend on the monomer and the chain length.
Fission splits a heavy nucleus (like uranium-235) into lighter ones, releasing energy. Used in nuclear power plants and atomic bombs. Fusion joins light nuclei (like hydrogen isotopes) into a heavier one (helium), releasing far more energy. It powers the Sun and stars — but it's been very hard to harness on Earth.

Both release energy because intermediate-mass nuclei (around iron) are the most tightly bound.
Indicators are dyes that change color depending on pH. Litmus turns red in acid, blue in base. Phenolphthalein is colorless in acid, pink in base. Universal indicator shifts through a rainbow across the whole pH range — handy for quick measurement.

Many natural dyes (red cabbage, hibiscus, beet juice) work too.
Metabolism is all the chemical reactions that keep you alive — breaking down nutrients (catabolism) to release energy, and using that energy to build the molecules you need (anabolism). Enzymes catalyze nearly every step. Basal metabolic rate is how much energy you burn at rest.
Your diaphragm contracts and flattens, pulling air into the lungs. Air reaches tiny sacs (alveoli) surrounded by blood vessels. Oxygen diffuses into the blood; carbon dioxide diffuses out. Then the diaphragm relaxes and you exhale.

The drive to breathe comes mostly from rising CO₂, not falling oxygen.
Food gets mechanically broken in your mouth and stomach, and chemically broken by enzymes and acid. The small intestine absorbs nutrients into the blood. The large intestine reabsorbs water and houses huge populations of helpful bacteria. Waste leaves at the end.

The whole journey takes 24-72 hours.
About 86 billion neurons form the brain, communicating across trillions of synapses. The cerebrum (with two hemispheres) handles thought and voluntary movement. The cerebellum coordinates balance and fine motor control. The brainstem manages automatic functions like breathing and heartbeat.

Different regions specialize, but no thought happens in just one place — it's all networks.
Skeletal muscles are bundles of fibers containing parallel filaments of two proteins: actin and myosin. When a nerve signal arrives, calcium floods in and myosin grabs actin and pulls — like ropes ratcheting past each other. ATP supplies the energy.

Many tiny contractions add up to a strong pull.
Conduction: heat moves through a material by atomic collisions — a metal spoon heating up in soup. Convection: heat moves through a fluid as warm parts rise and cool parts sink — boiling water, atmospheric circulation. Radiation: heat travels as electromagnetic waves, needing no medium — sunlight crossing space.

Most real situations involve all three.
An object's color comes from which wavelengths of light it absorbs and which it reflects (or transmits). A red apple absorbs most wavelengths and reflects red. Pigments and dyes work by selectively absorbing parts of the visible spectrum.

Some colors come from structure instead of pigment — peacock feathers and soap bubbles use interference, not dyes.
Bats, dolphins, and submarines all send out sound pulses and time the echoes to map their surroundings. The shorter the pulse and higher the frequency, the finer the detail. Medical ultrasound uses the same idea — pulses above human hearing reflect off tissues and build an image.
Renewable sources replenish themselves on human timescales: solar (photovoltaic cells turn sunlight into electricity directly), wind (turbines convert moving air into rotation, then electricity), hydroelectric (falling water spins turbines), geothermal (heat from Earth's interior), and biomass.

They replace fossil fuels because they don't release stored ancient carbon into the atmosphere.
Carbon moves between atmosphere, oceans, land, and life. Plants pull CO₂ from the air; animals exhale it back. Decomposers release carbon from dead organisms. Oceans absorb and release CO₂. Over long timescales, rocks store carbon and volcanoes release it.

Burning fossil fuels adds ancient stored carbon to today's cycle faster than natural sinks can absorb it.
Deoxyribonucleic acid — a long, double-helix molecule that stores the genetic instructions for every known living organism. Built from four bases (A, T, C, G) whose sequence encodes everything from eye color to enzyme structure.
Change in the heritable traits of biological populations across generations. Driven mainly by natural selection, plus mutation, migration, and chance. It explains both the diversity of life and the unity (we all share ancestors and biochemistry).
Centripetal force is the real, inward force keeping something moving in a circle. Centrifugal force is the apparent outward push you feel when you're inside the rotating frame — your inertia trying to keep you going straight while something pulls you in.

From a non-rotating viewpoint, there's no centrifugal force; from the rotating viewpoint, it's a useful fiction.
Magnetism comes from moving electric charges — including the spin of electrons inside atoms. In most materials, electron spins cancel out. In iron, nickel, and cobalt, they can align in regions called domains. When most domains point the same way, the material is magnetized.

Heating a magnet jumbles the domains and weakens (or kills) the magnetism.
Speciation happens when one population splits into two that can no longer interbreed. The most common path: geographic separation, then independent evolution, until the two groups have diverged enough to be reproductively isolated even if they meet again.

It usually takes thousands to millions of years, but some plant species can form in a single generation through chromosome doubling.
A phylogenetic tree shows evolutionary relationships among species. Branches that share a recent common ancestor are close cousins; ones that diverged long ago are distant relatives. Modern trees are built mostly from DNA comparisons, sometimes combined with fossils.

All life appears to share a single common ancestor, deep in the past.
Stem cells can divide and turn into other cell types. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent — they can become almost any cell. Adult stem cells in tissues like bone marrow and skin are multipotent — they make a limited range of cell types. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are adult cells reprogrammed back to pluripotency.

They're a major hope for regenerative medicine.
Red blood cells have surface markers (antigens) — A, B, both (AB), or neither (O). You also have antibodies against any antigens you lack. Give someone the wrong type and their antibodies attack the donated cells. O-negative is the universal donor; AB-positive is the universal recipient.

The Rh factor (positive or negative) adds another layer of compatibility.
Renewable resources (sun, wind, water, geothermal) replenish themselves on human timescales. Nonrenewable resources (coal, oil, natural gas, uranium) formed over millions of years and we're using them up far faster than they re-form. Burning fossil fuels also releases carbon that had been stored for ages, driving climate change.
A mineral is a naturally occurring solid with a specific chemical composition and crystal structure — like quartz or halite. A rock is a mixture of one or more minerals. Granite, for example, is a mix of quartz, feldspar, and mica.
Surface currents are driven mostly by wind, deflected by Earth's rotation. Deeper currents are driven by differences in temperature and salinity — cold, salty water sinks and slowly moves around the globe in the thermohaline circulation, which takes centuries to complete a cycle.

Ocean currents redistribute huge amounts of heat, shaping climates.
The smallest unit of life that can function on its own — bounded by a membrane, filled with cytoplasm, and (in most cells) containing genetic material. Some organisms are single cells; you're made of about 30 trillion of them.
Stress is force per area applied to a material; strain is the fractional deformation that results. For small deformations, they're proportional — that's Hooke's law. The constant (Young's modulus) measures stiffness: steel is high, rubber is low.

Go too far and materials yield permanently, or break.
A huge collection of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter bound by gravity. Galaxies range from dwarf systems with millions of stars to giants with hundreds of billions. The Milky Way, our galaxy, has 100-400 billion stars.
By the IAU's definition: a body that orbits the Sun, is round under its own gravity, and has cleared its orbital neighborhood of other debris. Pluto fails the third test, which is why it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Asteroids are mostly rocky/metallic bodies, most living between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are mostly ice and dust — when they swing close to the Sun, the ice vaporizes and forms the famous tail. A meteor is a streak of light from a small body burning in the atmosphere; if a chunk survives to the ground, it's a meteorite.
A massive ball of plasma held together by its own gravity, hot enough at the core to fuse hydrogen into helium and release energy. Stars range from dim red dwarfs lasting trillions of years to brilliant blue giants that burn out in millions.
When something emitting light moves away from us, its light stretches to longer (redder) wavelengths — redshift. Coming toward us, it compresses to shorter (bluer) wavelengths — blueshift. Astronomers measure these shifts to figure out how fast stars and galaxies move, and to confirm the universe is expanding.

Cosmological redshift is slightly different: it comes from space itself stretching while light is in transit.
Telescopes collect light from a wide area and concentrate it. Refractors use lenses; reflectors use a curved mirror (most large telescopes are reflectors because mirrors are easier to make big). Space telescopes like Hubble and JWST avoid the blurring effects of Earth's atmosphere.

Radio telescopes use big dishes to collect radio waves instead of visible light.
Everything in the universe interacts through four forces: gravity (weakest but acts on everything over huge distances), electromagnetism (binds atoms together), the strong nuclear force (holds quarks and atomic nuclei together — strongest at short range), and the weak nuclear force (responsible for some radioactive decay).

Physicists have unified electromagnetism with the weak force; combining all four into one theory is still an open quest.
Protons and neutrons aren't fundamental — they're made of quarks (three each, of two flavors). The Standard Model of physics lists 17 fundamental particles: 6 quarks, 6 leptons (including the electron and neutrinos), 4 force-carrying bosons, and the Higgs boson.

It's spectacularly accurate but doesn't include gravity, dark matter, or dark energy.
An orbit is a path of one object continuously falling around another. The orbiting object has enough sideways speed that it keeps missing the central body as it falls. Newton imagined a cannonball fired hard enough horizontally to never hit the ground — that's an orbit.

Kepler showed orbits are ellipses (not perfect circles) with the central body at one focus.
Newton's second law links force, mass, and acceleration: the harder you push something, the faster it speeds up, but the heavier it is, the harder it is to get going. That's the idea behind F = ma. Pushing an empty shopping cart sends it rolling easily, while the same push on a fully loaded cart barely budges it because the extra mass resists the change. To get the same acceleration from a heavier object, you simply have to push harder.
Newton's third law says every force comes in a pair: when one object pushes on another, the second object pushes back just as hard in the opposite direction. When you jump, your legs push down on the ground and the ground pushes you up into the air. A rocket works the same way, throwing hot gas downward so the gas pushes the rocket upward. The two forces act on different objects, which is why they don't simply cancel out.
Friction is a force that resists sliding whenever two surfaces touch, caused by tiny bumps and grips between them snagging on each other. It always pushes against the direction of motion, which is why a ball rolling across grass slows down and stops. Friction can be annoying when it wastes energy, but it's also what lets your shoes grip the floor and your car tires hold the road. On smooth ice there's very little friction, so you slide much farther.
Acceleration is how quickly an object's velocity changes, whether it's speeding up, slowing down, or turning. Anytime your motion changes, you're accelerating. When a traffic light turns green and a car presses you back into the seat, that push is acceleration as the car gains speed. Slowing down to a stop is acceleration too, just in the opposite direction.
Speed tells you how fast something is moving, but velocity tells you how fast AND in which direction. So velocity carries more information than speed alone. A car driving in a circle at a steady pace has constant speed but constantly changing velocity, because its direction keeps changing. That changing velocity is exactly why you feel pulled to the side when a car turns.
Mass is how much 'stuff' an object is made of, and it never changes no matter where you go. Weight is the force of gravity pulling on that mass, so it depends on where you are. An astronaut has the same mass on the Moon as on Earth, but weighs much less there because the Moon's gravity is weaker. That's why they can bounce around in those famous low-gravity hops while carrying the very same body.
Free fall is when the only force acting on an object is gravity, so it accelerates downward without anything else holding it up. Surprisingly, gravity speeds up heavy and light objects at the same rate, so a hammer and a feather would land together if there were no air to slow the feather. Astronauts on the space station feel weightless because they and the station are both in free fall, endlessly falling around Earth together. The floating feeling comes from nothing pushing up on them.
Air resistance, also called drag, is a force that pushes back against anything moving through the air as it shoves air molecules out of the way. The faster you go and the bigger your surface, the more drag you feel. A parachute works by being huge, catching so much air that the upward drag nearly balances gravity and you drift down gently. It's also why a falling feather flutters slowly while a tight pebble drops fast.
In physics, work happens only when a force makes something move in the direction of the push or pull. If you push a heavy box across the floor, you do work because the box actually slides. But if you push hard against a brick wall and it doesn't budge, you've done zero work in the physics sense, no matter how tired your arms get. Holding a grocery bag still while standing also counts as no work, even though it feels like effort.
Energy is the ability to make things happen, the capacity to do work or cause change. A stretched rubber band, a hot cup of cocoa, a moving skateboard, and a battery all store energy in different forms, ready to be used. When you eat breakfast, you take in chemical energy from food, and your body converts it so you can run and play. Wherever something heats up, moves, glows, or grows, energy is doing the job behind the scenes.
Potential energy is stored energy that something has because of its position or condition, waiting to be released. A book sitting on a high shelf has gravitational potential energy because gravity could pull it down if it slipped off. The higher you lift something, the more potential energy it gains, which is why a roller coaster climbs a tall hill before its thrilling drop. A drawn bow and a compressed spring store potential energy too, ready to spring into motion.
Energy transformation is when one kind of energy turns into another kind, which is happening around us all the time. A flashlight changes chemical energy in its battery into electrical energy, then into light and a bit of heat. A toaster turns electrical energy into heat that browns your bread, and a plant turns sunlight into chemical energy stored in its leaves. Almost every machine and living thing is really just a clever device for transforming energy from one form into a more useful one.
Power is how fast work gets done or how quickly energy is used, not just how much. Two movers might carry the same heavy couch up the same stairs, but the one who does it in half the time is using more power. A sports car and an old truck might both reach the top of a hill, yet the sports car does it with much higher power because it gets there faster. So power is really about the rate of doing work, the difference between a quick sprint and a slow stroll.
Mechanical energy is the total energy an object has from its motion and its position added together, kinetic plus potential. A pendulum in a grandfather clock is a great example: at the top of its swing it's all potential, at the bottom it's all kinetic, but the mechanical energy stays roughly constant the whole time. A diver standing on a high board has mostly potential energy, which turns into kinetic energy as they fall toward the water. Whenever something can move or fall, it carries mechanical energy.
Friction is the rubbing force between surfaces that slide past each other, and it quietly turns useful motion energy into heat. Rub your hands together quickly and you'll feel them warm up, that warmth is kinetic energy being converted into heat by friction. This is why a ball rolling across grass slows down and stops, while one rolling on smooth ice keeps going much longer. No energy is truly lost, but friction spreads it out as heat that's hard to gather back up and reuse.
Thermal energy is the energy of the jiggling, bouncing motion of all the tiny particles inside something, and the faster they jiggle, the hotter it feels. A pot of boiling water has lots of thermal energy because its water molecules are zooming around wildly. When you warm your hands on a hot mug, thermal energy flows from the mug into your cooler skin until they even out. Adding thermal energy makes things hotter, and taking it away makes them colder.
Chemical energy is energy stored in the bonds between atoms inside a substance, ready to be released when those bonds rearrange. The food you eat, the gasoline in a car, a campfire log, and a battery all hold chemical energy. When you light a match, a chemical reaction breaks and reforms bonds, releasing that stored energy as heat and light. Your own body slowly unlocks the chemical energy in food to keep you warm and give you the get-up-and-go to move.
Elastic potential energy is stored in things that can stretch or squash and then snap back, like springs, rubber bands, and bows. When you pull back a slingshot, you're loading it with elastic potential energy, and letting go converts that into kinetic energy that launches the stone. A trampoline does the same trick: it stretches as you land, stores your energy, then springs you back up into the air. The more you stretch or compress something springy, the more energy it tucks away.
Work and energy are two sides of the same coin: doing work on something is exactly how you transfer energy to it. When you push a stalled shopping cart and it speeds up, the work you do becomes the cart's kinetic energy. When you lift a backpack onto a shelf, your work becomes its gravitational potential energy, stored up high. In short, energy is the currency, and work is the act of spending or earning it by pushing things into motion or up against a force.
Every cell is wrapped in a thin, flexible skin called the cell membrane, made of a double layer of fatty molecules. It acts like a security guard at a club door, letting some things in (food, oxygen) and keeping other things out or shoving waste out. Tiny protein 'doorways' embedded in the membrane open and close to control the traffic. Without this border, the inside of a cell would just dissolve into its surroundings like a drop of ink in water.
The nucleus is the cell's control center, a round compartment that stores the cell's DNA instruction manual. Think of it like the manager's office in a busy factory: the blueprints stay locked safely inside, and copies of just the needed pages get sent out to the workers. A protective wrapper called the nuclear envelope keeps the DNA tidy and shielded. Almost every plant and animal cell has one, but red blood cells famously toss theirs out to make room for carrying oxygen.
Mitochondria are tiny bean-shaped structures inside cells that act like little power plants, turning the food you eat and the oxygen you breathe into usable energy. They produce a molecule called ATP, which is the cell's rechargeable battery for everything from flexing a muscle to firing a thought. Cells that work hard, like the ones in your heart and thigh muscles, are packed with thousands of mitochondria. Strangely, they carry their own small loop of DNA, a clue that they were once free-living bacteria swallowed by an ancient cell.
Mitosis is how one cell splits into two identical copies of itself, which is how you grow and how a scraped knee heals over. First the cell makes a complete duplicate of all its DNA, then it lines the chromosomes up in the middle and pulls one full set toward each end before pinching apart. The goal is that both new cells get the exact same instruction manual, no pages missing. It's like photocopying a whole book, splitting the original and the copy into two stacks, then sliding each stack into its own new binding.
Meiosis is a special kind of cell division that makes egg and sperm cells, and it cuts the chromosome count in half so each one carries 23 instead of the usual 46. That way, when egg and sperm join, the new cell adds up to a full set of 46 again, half from each parent. Along the way, matching chromosomes swap chunks with each other in a shuffle called crossing over, which is why siblings are similar but never identical. It's like dealing two different hands from one shuffled deck, so no two kids get the exact same cards.
To build a protein, a cell first copies a single gene's recipe from its DNA into a portable message called RNA, a step known as transcription. That message travels out to a workbench called a ribosome, which reads the RNA three letters at a time and links together the matching building blocks, the amino acids, into a chain. The finished chain folds into a protein that does a job, like an enzyme that breaks down food. It's like a chef copying one recipe card from a locked master cookbook, carrying it to the kitchen, and following it step by step to cook a dish.
A mutation is a change in the letters of an organism's DNA, like a typo that creeps into a recipe when it's copied. Some happen by accident when a cell copies its DNA, and others are caused by things like UV rays from the sun. Many mutations do nothing at all, some cause problems, and a rare few turn out helpful, which is the raw fuel for evolution over many generations. A famous harmless example is the gene change that lets some adults keep digesting milk, while the cancer-causing ones happen when the typo lands in a gene that controls cell growth.
You inherit two copies of most genes, one from each parent, and sometimes those copies disagree on which version of a trait to show. A dominant version drowns out a recessive one, so it only takes one dominant copy to show up, while a recessive trait needs both copies to match. That's why two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child: each parent secretly carried one hidden blue (recessive) copy alongside their brown (dominant) one. It's like a vote where a single loud dominant voice wins unless both votes happen to be the quiet recessive one.
Chloroplasts are the green structures inside plant cells where photosynthesis happens, capturing sunlight to make sugar food for the plant. They're packed with a green pigment called chlorophyll, which is exactly why leaves and grass look green to your eyes. Inside, the plant combines sunlight, water from its roots, and carbon dioxide from the air, then releases the oxygen you breathe as a leftover. Like mitochondria, chloroplasts carry their own tiny DNA, hinting they were once free-living bacteria taken in by an early plant ancestor.
Muscles work by pulling, never pushing. Inside each muscle, thousands of tiny protein fibers slide past each other to make the whole muscle shorten, tugging on the bone it's attached to. Because a muscle can only pull, your body uses them in opposing pairs: when you bend your arm your biceps pulls tight and your triceps relaxes, and when you straighten it the triceps pulls and the biceps lets go. It's like two kids on opposite ends of a rope taking turns yanking.
When you breathe in, a dome-shaped muscle under your lungs called the diaphragm flattens down, making your chest bigger so air rushes in to fill the extra space. The air travels down to millions of tiny grape-like sacs in your lungs, where oxygen slips into your blood and carbon dioxide slips out to be breathed away. When the diaphragm relaxes, your chest shrinks and pushes the used air back out. It works like a bellows or an accordion gently squeezing and stretching.
You inherit traits because you get one copy of each gene from your mother and one from your father, mixing their instructions together. Some versions of a gene are 'dominant' and show up even with just one copy, while 'recessive' ones only appear if you get the same version from both parents. That's why two brown-eyed parents can sometimes have a blue-eyed child: both quietly carried a hidden recessive version. It's like each parent handing you a deck of cards and your traits being whichever cards happen to win.
Natural selection is the engine behind evolution: living things that happen to have traits suited to their surroundings tend to survive and have more babies, passing those handy traits on. Imagine beetles in a forest where some are green and some are brown; if hungry birds spot the green ones more easily, more brown beetles survive to breed, and over generations the whole group turns browner. Nobody plans it, the environment simply favors whatever works best. Given enough time, this steady sorting reshapes entire species.
Some parts of your body are leftovers from ancestors who needed them more than you do, called vestigial structures. The little muscles that let some people wiggle their ears, the tailbone at the base of your spine, and goosebumps that puff up body hair all trace back to relatives for whom they were useful. Goosebumps once fluffed up thick fur to trap warmth or look bigger to a threat, but on our thin hair they don't do much anymore. These leftovers are like clues that show how living things changed over time.
Skin is your body's largest organ and acts like a waterproof, self-repairing suit that keeps the good stuff in and the harmful stuff out. It blocks germs, holds in water so you don't dry out, and is packed with tiny sensors that let you feel heat, cold, pressure, and pain. It also helps control your temperature by sweating to cool you down and by tightening tiny blood vessels to hold in heat. When you get a cut, your skin springs into action and grows new cells to seal the gap.
Sleep is when your body and brain do their nightly cleanup and repair work. While you rest, your brain sorts through the day's events and locks important memories into place, which is why studying then sleeping helps you remember better than cramming all night. Your body also releases growth and repair signals, patches up worn tissues, and clears out waste that builds up in the brain while you're awake. That's why a missed night leaves you foggy and cranky, like a phone that never got recharged.
A food chain shows who eats whom, passing energy from one living thing to the next. It usually starts with a plant that makes its own food from sunlight, then a plant-eater, then a meat-eater. Picture a meadow: grass grows, a grasshopper munches the grass, a frog gobbles the grasshopper, and a hawk swoops down and eats the frog. Each link passes along energy that originally came from the sun.
A food web is a tangle of many food chains linked together, because most animals eat more than one thing and are eaten by more than one thing. It's a more honest picture of nature than a single straight chain. Think of a pond: a fish might eat insects, tadpoles, and algae, while that same fish gets eaten by a heron, a snake, or a big bass. All those crossing arrows make a web instead of a line.
Decomposers are the living things that break down dead plants, dead animals, and waste, recycling the nutrients back into the soil. Without them, the world would be buried in fallen leaves and dead bodies. The classic crew is fungi, bacteria, earthworms, and beetles. When you see a log in the forest slowly going soft and crumbly, decomposers are at work turning it back into food for new plants.
Plants need nitrogen to grow, but the nitrogen in the air is locked in a form they can't use. Special bacteria in the soil and on plant roots 'fix' that air nitrogen into a usable form, plants absorb it, animals get it by eating plants, and decomposers release it again when things die. It's a relay race where bacteria are the key runners. Bean and clover plants are famous for hosting these helpful bacteria in little bumps on their roots.
Pollination is how flowering plants make seeds: pollen from one flower has to reach the egg-making part of another flower. Many plants can't move, so they hire delivery helpers like bees, butterflies, birds, and the wind. When a bee crawls into a flower for sweet nectar, pollen sticks to its fuzzy body, and it dusts that pollen onto the next flower it visits. That tiny accident is why we get apples, almonds, and pumpkins.
Germination is the moment a seed wakes up and starts growing into a plant. A seed is like a tiny packed lunch with a baby plant and a food supply inside a tough coat. Give it water, warmth, and air and the seed swells, the coat splits, a root pushes down to drink, and a shoot reaches up for light. You can watch this yourself by putting a bean on a damp paper towel and waiting a few days.
A tropism is the way a plant grows toward or away from something in its surroundings, even though it can't walk. Growth toward light is called phototropism, and growth in response to gravity is gravitropism. A houseplant on a windowsill slowly leans its leaves toward the glass to catch more sunlight, and a root always heads downward no matter which way you plant the seed. The plant 'moves' by growing one side faster than the other.
Transpiration is how a plant pulls water all the way up from its roots to its highest leaves. Water evaporates out of tiny pores in the leaves, and as each water molecule leaves, it tugs the next one up behind it, like sipping through a long straw. This pull is strong enough to lift water dozens of feet up a tall tree with no pump at all. On a hot day a single big tree can breathe out hundreds of liters of water vapor, which is why a forest feels cool and humid.
Symbiosis is a close, long-term relationship between two different kinds of living things. Sometimes both partners win (mutualism), sometimes one wins while the other is unbothered, and sometimes one benefits while harming the other (parasitism). A clownfish living safely among a sea anemone's stinging arms while keeping the anemone clean is a friendly mutualism. A tick sucking blood from a dog is the unfriendly kind.
Bacteria are tiny single-celled living things, far too small to see without a microscope, and they live almost everywhere on Earth. Most are harmless or even helpful, and only a few make us sick. The bacteria in your gut help you digest food, and other bacteria turn milk into yogurt and cheese. They multiply by simply splitting in two, so one bacterium can become millions overnight if it has enough food and warmth.
Bacteria are complete living cells that can eat, grow, and reproduce on their own, while a virus is more like a set of instructions in a shell that can only copy itself by hijacking a living cell. That's why antibiotics work on bacteria but do nothing against a virus like the common cold. Think of bacteria as tiny self-running machines and a virus as a memory stick that does nothing until you plug it into a computer.
Fungi are their own kingdom of life, neither plant nor animal, that feed by soaking up nutrients from the stuff around them instead of making food from sunlight. Mushrooms, molds, mildew, and yeast are all fungi. The mushroom you see is just the fruit; most of the fungus is a hidden web of fine threads spreading through the soil or a log. Yeast, a tiny fungus, is what makes bread rise and turns grape juice into wine.
The Moon does not make its own light; we only see the half of it lit by the Sun, and the phases are simply how much of that lit half is facing us as the Moon orbits Earth. When the Moon is on the far side of us from the Sun we see its whole lit face (full moon), and when it sits between us and the Sun the lit side points away and it nearly vanishes (new moon). Hold a ball up near a single lamp and slowly walk it in a circle around your head; you will watch the bright part grow and shrink just like the Moon does over a month.
Deep underground it is hot enough to melt rock into a gooey liquid called magma, which is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises toward the surface. Trapped gases inside the magma expand as it climbs, and when the pressure gets too high it bursts out as an eruption of lava, ash, and gas. It works like shaking a fizzy soda and then popping the cap: the dissolved gas suddenly escapes and pushes everything out fast. Once the lava reaches the air it cools and hardens into new rock, slowly building the mountain higher.
Earth's crust is broken into giant slabs called tectonic plates that are always slowly pushing and grinding against each other. Where they catch and lock, stress builds up for years until the rock suddenly slips, releasing all that stored energy as shaking waves that travel through the ground. Bend a wooden ruler more and more until it snaps; the sudden release and buzz in your hands is a tiny version of an earthquake. The point underground where the slip starts is the focus, and the spot on the surface right above it is the epicenter.
The Sun constantly flings out a stream of tiny charged particles called the solar wind, and when these hit Earth our magnetic field funnels them toward the north and south poles. Up high they slam into gas atoms in the atmosphere and make them glow, painting curtains of green, pink, and purple light across the polar sky. It works on the same principle as a neon sign or an old TV screen: energized particles striking gas make it light up, and the color depends on which gas gets hit. That is why the aurora is mostly seen near the poles, where the magnetic field guides the particles down.
Earth's air is not all the same; it is stacked into layers that get thinner as you go up. The bottom layer, the troposphere, is where we live and where weather happens; above it the stratosphere holds the ozone that blocks harmful sunlight and is where jets like to cruise; higher still the mesosphere burns up most meteors, and the thin thermosphere is where the aurora glows and many satellites orbit. Think of it like a layered cake where each layer has its own job and the air gets sparser toward the top. By the time you reach space there is so little air left there is no clear line, it just fades away.
Sound is a wave made of tiny pushes and pulls passing through a material like air, water, or wood. When something vibrates, it squeezes the air molecules next to it, and those bump into the next ones, passing the squeeze along like a stadium crowd doing the wave. Your eardrum feels those pushes arrive and your brain turns them into what you hear. That is also why there is no sound in outer space: with no air molecules to bump into each other, the wave has nothing to travel through.
Pitch is how high or low a sound seems, and it comes from frequency: how many times the wave wiggles back and forth each second. A fast-vibrating object, like a thin guitar string or a tiny whistle, makes a high pitch, while a slow-vibrating one, like a thick bass string or a tuba, makes a low pitch. You can hear this when you fill a glass with water and tap it: as the water rises and shortens the vibrating air, the tap climbs higher. The faster the wiggle, the higher the note.
Loudness depends on amplitude, which is how big the wave's push-and-pull is. A gentle tap on a drum makes small vibrations and a soft sound, while a hard whack makes much bigger vibrations and a loud boom, even though the pitch stays the same. Think of it like waves on the ocean: tall waves carry more energy than little ripples. The bigger the vibration, the more energy reaches your ear, and the louder it feels.
An echo is a sound wave bouncing off a hard surface and coming back to your ears. When you shout toward a canyon wall or a big empty gym, the wave hits the surface, reflects, and travels back, so you hear your own voice a moment later. The delay happens because sound takes time to make the round trip out and back. If the wall is too close, the reflection returns so fast it blends with your original shout and you do not notice it as a separate echo.
The Doppler effect is why a passing ambulance siren sounds higher as it speeds toward you and suddenly drops lower once it zooms past. As the source moves toward you, each new wave is sent from a little closer, so the waves bunch up and the pitch rises; as it moves away, the waves stretch out and the pitch falls. The actual siren never changes its note, only how the waves reach you does. Police use the same idea with radar to measure how fast a car is going.
Resonance happens when you push something at just the right rhythm and its vibrations build up bigger and bigger. Everything has a natural frequency it likes to wiggle at, and matching that rhythm pumps in energy efficiently. The classic example is pushing a child on a swing: small pushes timed to the swing's natural back-and-forth send it higher and higher, while badly timed pushes do almost nothing. The same trick lets a singer rattle a wine glass by holding exactly the right note.
A standing wave forms when a wave reflects back on itself and the two waves lock into a steady pattern that seems to stay put, with some spots always still and others always swinging. A plucked guitar string is the perfect example: the wave bounces between the two fixed ends, and only certain patterns fit neatly, which is why the string sings one clear note instead of noise. Shortening the string by pressing a fret fits a faster pattern and raises the pitch. Wind instruments do the same thing with standing waves of air inside a tube.
Wavelength is the distance from one peak of a wave to the next peak, like measuring from the top of one ocean swell to the top of the following one. Long wavelengths and short wavelengths carry the same wave at the same speed, but they pack their wiggles differently: short wavelengths mean more wiggles crammed into the same space. For sound, a short wavelength goes with a high pitch and a long wavelength goes with a low, rumbling one. It is one of the basic rulers we use to describe any wave.
Waves come in two basic flavors depending on which way the material wiggles compared to the way the wave travels. In a transverse wave, the material moves up and down across the direction of travel, like flicking a rope and watching a hump race down it while the rope itself only goes up and down. In a longitudinal wave, the material squeezes and stretches along the same direction the wave moves, like a Slinky you push and let bunch up. Sound is longitudinal, while the waves on water and on a rope are transverse.
Sound travels fast, but not instantly, and it moves quicker through materials whose molecules are packed close together so they can pass the push along sooner. That is why sound zips faster through water than air, and faster still through steel: tightly packed molecules hand off the vibration almost immediately. You can feel this gap during a thunderstorm, where you see the lightning flash right away but hear the thunder seconds later, because light reaches you almost instantly while sound lags behind. Counting the seconds between them tells you roughly how far away the storm is.
When two waves overlap, they add together: where two peaks meet they pile into a bigger wave (constructive), and where a peak meets a dip they can cancel out into stillness (destructive). You can see it when two stones dropped in a pond send ripples that cross and form a crisscross pattern of taller bumps and flat spots. Noise-canceling headphones use destructive interference on purpose, creating a wave that is the exact opposite of incoming noise so the two erase each other. The result is quiet, built out of two sounds combined.
Human ears can only catch a certain band of frequencies, and sounds above or below that band exist but stay silent to us. Ultrasound is pitched too high for people to hear, which is how dog whistles call a dog without bothering you and how doctors image a baby before birth by bouncing high-frequency pulses off it. Infrasound is too low for us, the deep rumble that elephants and whales use to signal each other across great distances. Both are real waves, just outside the window our ears were built to notice.
When you play the same note on a guitar and a piano, they sound clearly different even at the identical pitch, and that flavor of a sound is called timbre. It comes from harmonics: along with the main note, an instrument quietly adds a stack of faster, fainter notes, and the particular mix of those extras gives each instrument its signature. A flute leans on a pure, simple blend, while a trumpet piles on bright, buzzy harmonics. Your ear hears all of them at once and recognizes the instrument the way you recognize a friend's voice.
Reflection happens when light bounces off a surface instead of passing through or being absorbed. On a smooth, shiny surface like a mirror or still pond, the light bounces in an orderly way, so you see a clear image. The angle the light comes in at equals the angle it leaves at, which is why a mirror flips your image left-to-right but keeps it sharp. On a rough surface like paper, light scatters in every direction, so you see the surface but not a reflection of yourself.
Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one material into another, like from air into water or glass. Light travels slower in water than in air, and that change in speed makes it change direction at the surface. This is why a straw in a glass of water looks broken or bent at the waterline, and why a pool always looks shallower than it really is. Lenses in glasses and cameras work by bending light through refraction.
White light is actually a mixture of all the colors blended together. When white light enters a glass prism, each color bends by a slightly different amount because each color travels at a slightly different speed in glass. Red bends the least and violet bends the most, so the colors fan out and you see a rainbow band on the wall. This splitting of light into its colors is called dispersion, and it is the same effect that paints rainbows in the sky after rain.
A rainbow forms when sunlight passes through millions of tiny raindrops still floating in the air. Each raindrop acts like a little prism: light bends as it enters, bounces off the back of the drop, and bends again as it leaves, splitting white sunlight into its colors. Because every color leaves the drop at a slightly different angle, you see a curved band of red on the outside and violet on the inside. That is also why a rainbow always appears in the part of the sky opposite the sun, when the sun is behind you.
Objects do not really 'have' color the way they have weight; they have color because of which light they reflect and which they absorb. White light contains all colors, and when it hits a leaf, the leaf absorbs most colors but reflects green light back to your eyes, so it looks green. A red apple absorbs all colors except red, which it bounces back to you. A black object absorbs nearly all the light, while a white object reflects almost all of it, which is why dark clothes feel hotter in the sun.
A shadow forms because light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around solid objects. When something blocks the light, it leaves a dark region behind it where the light cannot reach, and that dark patch is the shadow. The shadow's size and shape depend on the angle of the light: a streetlight directly overhead makes a short shadow, while the low evening sun stretches your shadow out long across the ground. Move closer to the light source and your shadow grows larger, because you block a wider cone of the light.
Light waves normally vibrate in every direction as they travel, but polarized light vibrates in only one direction, like a rope shaken straight up and down. A polarizing filter acts like a picket fence with vertical slots, letting through only the light wobbling the right way and blocking the rest. Polarized sunglasses use this trick: glare bouncing off water or a car hood is mostly horizontal, so the vertical filter blocks it and the glare disappears. That is why fishermen wear them to see fish below a shiny water surface.
When light traveling inside a material like glass or water hits the boundary at a steep enough angle, instead of escaping it bounces completely back inside, trapped like a ball ricocheting in a tube. This is called total internal reflection, and it happens once the angle passes a critical point. Fiber-optic cables use it to carry internet and phone signals as pulses of light that zigzag down a thin glass thread for miles without leaking out. The same effect makes the underside of a swimming pool's surface look like a mirror when you look up from below.
Diffraction is the way light bends and spreads out when it passes through a narrow opening or around the edge of an object. The smaller the gap compared to the wave, the more the light fans out, like water ripples spreading after passing through a gap in a dock. Tiny closely-spaced grooves can split light into colors by diffraction, which is why the back of a CD or DVD flashes rainbow colors when you tilt it under a light. The same effect lets you see faint colored fringes when you squint at a distant streetlight.
A luminous object makes its own light, while a non-luminous object only shines because it reflects light from something else. The Sun, a candle flame, and a glowing screen are luminous: they are the original source of the light. The Moon, a book, and your own face are non-luminous; you can only see them because light from the Sun or a lamp bounces off them into your eyes. This is why the Moon goes dark during an eclipse: when Earth blocks the sunlight, there is nothing left for the Moon to reflect.
Materials are sorted by how much light passes through them. Transparent things like clear glass and air let almost all light pass straight through, so you can see clearly through them. Translucent things like frosted glass, wax paper, or thin curtains let some light through but scatter it, so you see a blurry glow instead of a sharp image. Opaque things like wood, metal, and your hand block light completely, which is why they cast solid shadows and you cannot see what is behind them.
Electric charge is a basic property of matter that comes in two flavors: positive and negative. Like charges push apart and opposite charges pull together, which is why a balloon rubbed on your hair makes the hair stand up and reach toward the balloon. The hair gave up tiny particles called electrons to the balloon, so the balloon turned negative and the hair turned positive, and opposites attract. Almost everything is normally balanced, with equal positive and negative, so we don't feel it until rubbing shuffles some charge around.
Static electricity happens when extra charge piles up on something and just sits there instead of flowing away. When you shuffle across a carpet in socks, your shoes scrape electrons off the fibers and your body collects a surplus of negative charge. Touch a metal doorknob and all that built-up charge suddenly leaps across the gap as a tiny spark, and you feel the zap. It's worst on dry winter days because moist air normally lets the charge drain off your skin before it can build up.
Electric current is the flow of electric charge through a material, usually electrons moving through a wire. A good picture is water flowing through a pipe: the current is how much charge streams past a point each second, just like how many liters of water rush by. When you flip a light switch, you open a path that lets current flow from the wall, through the bulb, and back, and the bulb glows. We measure current in amperes, or amps for short.
Voltage is the push that drives electric current through a circuit, like the water pressure that forces water through a hose. The bigger the voltage, the harder the charge is shoved along, which is why a 9-volt battery can do more than a single small battery. Sticking your tongue on a 9-volt battery tingles because that pressure pushes a little current through your wet skin. Voltage is really a difference between two points, which is why a battery has a plus end and a minus end.
Resistance is how much a material fights against electric current trying to flow through it. Think of a wide smooth pipe versus a narrow pipe stuffed with gravel: water flows easily through one and struggles through the other. A thin or poor-conducting wire has high resistance, so charge bumps into atoms as it squeezes through, and that bumping heats the wire up. That heating is exactly how a toaster glows and how an old light bulb makes light. Resistance is measured in ohms.
A circuit is a complete loop that lets electric current flow from a power source, through whatever you want to power, and back again. If the loop is broken anywhere, the flow stops, which is exactly what a switch does when you turn off a lamp. A simple flashlight is a perfect example: a battery, a wire, and a bulb all connected in a ring, and a switch that opens or closes the loop. No complete loop means no current and no light.
There are two main ways to wire several things into a circuit. In a series circuit everything sits on one single loop, so the current has only one path; old holiday lights worked this way, which is why one dead bulb made the whole string go dark. In a parallel circuit each device gets its own branch back to the source, so the current splits and each part can run on its own. Your home is wired in parallel, which is why turning off the kitchen light doesn't shut off the TV in the living room.
Conductors are materials that let electric charge move through them easily, while insulators hold their charge tightly and block the flow. Metals like copper are great conductors because some of their electrons are free to roam, which is why wires are made of metal. Rubber, plastic, and glass are insulators, which is why the wire to your phone charger has a soft plastic coating you can safely hold. The metal carries the current and the plastic keeps it from leaking into your hand.
An electromagnet is a magnet you can switch on and off using electric current. When current flows through a coil of wire, it creates a magnetic field around the coil, and wrapping the wire around an iron nail makes that field much stronger. Flip the switch off and the magnetism vanishes instantly. This is how the giant magnets at a junkyard lift cars and then drop them on command, and it's also what makes the buzzer in a doorbell snap back and forth.
Temperature measures how fast the tiny particles in something are jiggling on average, while heat is the total energy that flows from a hotter thing to a colder one. They are not the same: a sparkler burns at a much higher temperature than a bathtub of warm water, yet the bathtub holds far more heat because it has so many more particles. Think of temperature as how energetic each particle is, and heat as the energy actually moving around. That is why touching the sparkler's tiny spark barely hurts, but climbing into a hot bath warms your whole body.
Conduction is heat moving through a material by direct contact, as fast-jiggling particles bump into their slower neighbors and pass energy along the line. Metals conduct heat quickly because their loose electrons carry energy fast, while wood and plastic conduct slowly. This is why a metal spoon left in hot soup soon gets too hot to hold near the handle, while a wooden spoon stays cool. It is also why metal feels colder than wood at room temperature: the metal whisks heat out of your hand faster, even though both are the same temperature.
Convection is heat carried by the actual movement of a fluid like air or water. When part of a fluid heats up it expands, becomes less dense, and rises, while cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place, setting up a circulating loop called a convection current. You can watch this in a pot of soup as warm broth rises in the middle and cooler broth sinks at the edges. The same process makes a hot-air balloon float, drives weather, and is why the air near the ceiling of a room is warmer than the air near the floor.
Thermal radiation is heat that travels as invisible infrared light, needing no material to pass through, which is how the Sun's warmth crosses empty space to reach Earth. Every warm object glows with this infrared light, and the hotter it gets the more it radiates, eventually glowing in visible colors like the orange of a stove burner. You feel radiation directly when you hold your hands toward a campfire and sense the warmth even before the heated air reaches you. Dark, dull surfaces both emit and absorb radiation well, which is why a black car gets hotter in the sun than a white one.
The first law of thermodynamics is conservation of energy applied to heat: energy is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another or moved around. If you add heat to a gas, that energy either raises the gas's internal energy, makes the gas do work by pushing outward, or both. A pressure cooker shows this nicely, as the heat you add becomes hotter, faster-moving steam particles that push hard on the lid. There is no free lunch, which is why no machine can put out more energy than is put into it.
The second law of thermodynamics says heat naturally flows from hotter things to colder things, never the other way on its own, and that the disorder of the universe, called entropy, always tends to increase. A hot cup of coffee always cools to room temperature, but a room-temperature coffee never spontaneously heats itself back up by pulling warmth from the air. To force heat to go the unnatural direction, like cooling the inside of a fridge, you must spend energy with a pump. This one-way tendency is also why a shuffled deck never reshuffles itself into order.
Most materials expand when heated and shrink when cooled, because adding heat makes their particles jiggle harder and push each other a little farther apart. The effect is small but real, which is why bridges and railway tracks are built with small gaps so they have room to grow on hot days without buckling. You can use it on purpose too: running a stuck metal jar lid under hot water makes the lid expand a touch more than the glass, loosening its grip. Liquids expand as well, which is the trick behind an old-fashioned thermometer where the colored liquid climbs the tube as it warms.
Specific heat capacity is how much energy it takes to raise the temperature of a given amount of a substance by one degree, and different materials are very different. Water has an unusually high specific heat, so it warms up and cools down slowly, soaking up a lot of energy for only a small temperature change. That is why beach sand can scorch your feet at midday while the ocean stays cool, even though the sun shone equally on both. Water's stubbornness is also why coastal towns have milder weather and why a hot-water bottle stays warm in your bed for hours.
Latent heat is the hidden energy a substance absorbs or releases while changing state, such as melting or boiling, without its temperature changing at all. While ice melts, every bit of added heat goes into breaking the bonds holding the solid together, so a glass of ice water stays near freezing until the last ice cube is gone. The same happens at a rolling boil: the water stubbornly stays at boiling temperature while the added heat is spent turning liquid into steam. This is also why sweating cools you, as your body's heat is carried away to evaporate the sweat rather than warming you further.
Evaporative cooling happens because the fastest, most energetic particles in a liquid are the ones that escape as vapor, leaving the slower, cooler particles behind. Since the average energy of what remains drops, the liquid and whatever it touches get cooler. This is exactly how sweating works: as your sweat evaporates it carries heat away from your skin, which is why a breeze or a fan feels so refreshing on a hot day. It is also why stepping out of a swimming pool into the wind gives you a sudden chill, even when the air is warm.
Absolute zero is the lowest temperature anything can ever reach, the point where particles have given up essentially all of the energy they can lose and their jiggling slows to the bare minimum. It is the bottom of the Kelvin temperature scale, which scientists start from zero because there is genuinely nothing colder. You can keep cooling something closer and closer to it, but you can never quite get there, a bit like trying to reach the finish of a race where each step only covers half the remaining distance. Near this extreme cold, materials behave in strange ways, like helium turning into a liquid that can creep up the walls of its container.
A heat engine turns heat into useful motion by letting heat flow from a hot place to a cold place and grabbing some of that energy as work along the way. In a car engine, burning fuel creates a hot, high-pressure gas that pushes a piston down, and that push eventually turns the wheels. No engine can convert all the heat into work, though, because the second law of thermodynamics forces some energy to be dumped into the cooler exhaust, which is why your car has a radiator and tailpipe getting rid of waste heat. The bigger the temperature gap between the hot source and the cool exhaust, the more work the engine can squeeze out.
A refrigerator is a heat engine run in reverse: instead of letting heat flow downhill on its own, it spends electrical energy to pump heat uphill, from the cold inside to the warmer kitchen. It does this with a special fluid that absorbs heat from the food compartment as it evaporates, then is compressed and releases that heat outside through coils on the back, which is why those coils feel warm. The food gets cold not by adding cold but by removing heat and carrying it elsewhere. An air conditioner and a home heat pump use the very same trick, just moving heat in or out of your house instead of a fridge.
An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons at its center, with electrons whizzing around it in fuzzy regions called orbitals. The nucleus is incredibly small compared to the whole atom — if an atom were the size of a sports stadium, the nucleus would be a pea on the center spot, and the rest is mostly empty space.
