That empty space is why solid things feel solid only because of the electric forces between electrons, not because atoms are packed tight.
An orbital isn't a neat planet-like path — it's a 3D region where an electron is most likely to be found at any moment. Because of quantum rules, you can never pin down exactly where an electron is, so we describe it as a blurry cloud of probability, denser where the electron is more likely to turn up. It's a bit like a hummingbird hovering near a flower: it's somewhere in that fuzzy buzzing zone, but snap a photo and you can't predict the exact spot.
In the quantum world, an electron in an atom can only have certain fixed energy amounts — never the in-between values. When it jumps from a higher level to a lower one, it spits out the leftover energy as a single packet of light, and the size of that packet sets the light's color. It's like climbing stairs instead of a ramp: you can stand on step 1 or step 2, but never halfway between, and the glow of a neon sign comes from electrons making exactly these stepped jumps.
When light hits certain metals, it can knock electrons right out of the surface — but only if the light's color (its frequency) is high enough, no matter how bright a low-frequency light is. This showed that light arrives in individual energy packets called photons, and a single dim blue photon can do what a flood of red ones cannot. Solar panels and the automatic doors that 'see' you walk up both rely on light kicking electrons loose this way.
Because a particle's location is a spread-out probability rather than a pinpoint, there's a small chance it can show up on the far side of a barrier it shouldn't have enough energy to cross. It's as if you rolled a ball at a hill too gently to get over the top, yet now and then it simply appears on the other side. This isn't a loophole or a trick — it's why the Sun can fuse hydrogen and why flash memory in your phone can store data by letting electrons leak through thin walls.
Before you measure a quantum object, it can be in a blend of multiple possibilities at once — not secretly one or the other, but genuinely both until the moment you look. Measuring forces it to 'pick,' collapsing the blend into a single definite outcome. Schrödinger's famous thought experiment imagines a cat that's both alive and dead until the box is opened, a deliberately absurd way to highlight how strange this rule is when stretched to everyday objects.
A regular computer bit is always a 0 or a 1, but a qubit can sit in a superposition of both at once, and many qubits can be entangled so their states are linked. This lets a quantum computer explore a huge number of possibilities in parallel, which can crack certain problems — like factoring giant numbers or simulating molecules — far faster than ordinary machines. Picture a maze: a normal computer tries one path at a time, while a quantum one explores many routes together before the answer 'snaps' into focus.
A laser pumps energy into a material so many of its atoms hold electrons in raised energy states at once, then one passing photon triggers them all to release identical photons in a chain reaction called stimulated emission. The result is light that's a single color and perfectly in step, like a marching band stepping in unison instead of a crowd shuffling randomly. That coherence is why a laser pointer stays a tight dot across a room while a flashlight beam spreads and fades.
Every type of particle has a mirror-image partner with the opposite electric charge — the electron's twin, for example, is the positron. When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate and convert entirely into energy, usually a burst of light. This isn't only science fiction: PET scanners in hospitals work by detecting the tiny flashes made when positrons from a tracer meet the body's electrons.
Einstein started from two simple ideas: the laws of physics look the same for anyone moving steadily, and light always travels at the same speed no matter how fast you chase it. Holding the speed of light fixed forces space and time themselves to stretch and squeeze depending on motion, so moving clocks run slow and moving rulers shrink. The effects are tiny at car or even jet speeds, but they're real — fast-moving particles created in the upper atmosphere survive long enough to reach the ground only because their internal clocks run slow.
GPS satellites carry precise clocks, and relativity bends those clocks two ways at once: their speed makes them tick slightly slow, while the weaker gravity high above Earth makes them tick slightly fast. The gravity effect wins overall, so without correcting for it, the satellites' clocks would drift and your phone's location would be off by miles within a day. Engineers build the relativity math right into the system, making it one of the most practical proofs that Einstein was right.
An ordinary light microscope can never reveal an atom, because you can't see detail smaller than the wavelength of the light you're using — like trying to feel the bumps on a coin while wearing thick mittens. Electrons, when sped up, behave as waves with a far shorter wavelength than visible light, so an electron microscope can resolve features thousands of times finer. That's how scientists capture images of individual atoms arranged in a crystal.
Protons in a nucleus all carry positive charge and should repel each other, yet they stay packed together because the strong nuclear force glues them tight over very short distances. The energy needed to rip a nucleus apart — or released when one forms — is its binding energy, and a tiny bit of the particles' mass is 'spent' to provide it. This mass-to-energy trade is exactly what powers both the Sun's fusion and a nuclear reactor's fission.
Atoms are built from three main particles. Protons carry a positive charge and live in the nucleus; neutrons have no charge and sit in the nucleus alongside them; electrons carry a negative charge and zip around the outside. Think of the nucleus as a heavy ball at the center of a stadium and the electrons as fast fans circling the upper seats. Protons and neutrons are about the same weight, while electrons are so light they barely add to the total.
The atomic number is simply the count of protons in an atom's nucleus, and it acts like the atom's ID badge. Every carbon atom has exactly the carbon number of protons, and the moment that count changes, you have a different element entirely. It's like a house number on a street: change the number and you're at a different house. That single value is also why each element gets its own spot on the periodic table.
The periodic table lists every known element in order of atomic number, reading left to right and top to bottom. The rows are called periods and the columns are called groups, and the layout isn't random: elements in the same column tend to behave in similar ways. It works a bit like organizing a library, where similar books end up on the same shelf. That's why the table predicts chemistry so well, putting reactive metals on one side and unreactive gases on the other.
A period is a horizontal row of the periodic table, and a group is a vertical column. Elements in the same group share the same number of outer electrons, which is why they react in similar ways, like a family with the same habits. Going across a period, atoms gain one more proton and electron at each step. So the table is really a grid where your position tells you a lot about how an element will behave.
Atomic mass tells you roughly how heavy an atom is, and it comes mostly from the protons and neutrons in the nucleus since electrons weigh almost nothing. The value on the periodic table is an average across an element's natural isotopes, weighted by how common each one is. That's why it often lands on a messy decimal instead of a tidy whole number. It's like averaging the weights of a class where most kids weigh one amount and a few weigh more.
Electrons don't pile up randomly; they settle into layers around the nucleus called shells, with each shell holding only so many electrons before the next one fills. The inner shells fill first because they sit at lower energy, like seats closer to a warm fire filling up before the back rows. The outermost electrons matter most for chemistry because they're the ones that meet other atoms. Knowing how full that outer shell is tells you a lot about how an atom will react.
Valence electrons are the electrons in an atom's outermost shell, and they're the ones that do the work in chemical reactions. Atoms tend to gain, lose, or share these outer electrons to reach a stable, full outer shell. It's a bit like people at a party reaching out to shake hands; the outer electrons are the hands that connect one atom to another. An atom's number of valence electrons largely decides which other atoms it will bond with.
Most elements on the periodic table are metals, found on the left and middle, while nonmetals cluster on the upper right. Metals tend to be shiny, bend without breaking, and carry electricity well, which is why wires and pans are made of them. Nonmetals are often dull, brittle, or even gases, and they're poor at conducting, like the sulfur in a match head or the oxygen you breathe. A few in-between elements called metalloids share traits of both and show up in computer chips.
An ion is an atom that has gained or lost one or more electrons, leaving it with an electrical charge. Lose electrons and you get a positive ion; gain electrons and you get a negative ion, because the proton and electron counts no longer balance. Table salt is made of charged sodium and chlorine ions clinging together, and the salty tang on your tongue comes from ions dissolved in saliva. Ions are also what let your nerves send signals and batteries push current.
A chemical bond is the connection that holds atoms together, and atoms form bonds to reach a more stable arrangement of their outer electrons. In one common type, atoms share electrons, like two friends sharing a pair of headphones; in another, one atom hands electrons to another and the resulting charges attract. These bonds are why two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom lock into a water molecule. Breaking and remaking bonds is exactly what happens whenever something burns, rusts, or cooks.
An ionic bond forms when one atom hands an electron over to another atom instead of sharing it. The atom that loses an electron becomes positively charged and the one that gains it becomes negatively charged, and the opposite charges pull together like magnets. Table salt is the classic example: a sodium atom gives an electron to a chlorine atom, and the resulting ions lock into a tidy crystal grid. That grid is why salt forms hard little cubes you can see if you look closely.
In a covalent bond, two atoms share a pair of electrons instead of one giving them away. By sharing, both atoms get to act like they have a full, stable set of electrons, so neither has to lose out. Picture two kids sharing a jump rope, each holding one end so the rope stays between them. The oxygen you breathe is two oxygen atoms sharing electrons, and the bonds in DNA, plastics, and sugar all work this way too.
A polar bond is a covalent bond where the two atoms share electrons unequally, so one end of the bond is a little negative and the other a little positive. This happens when one atom pulls on the shared electrons harder than the other. In water, oxygen tugs the electrons closer than the hydrogens do, giving water a slightly negative side and a slightly positive side. That lopsidedness is why water can stick to itself, climb up a paper towel, and dissolve so many things.
A chemical reaction is a change where atoms break old bonds and form new ones, turning starting substances (reactants) into different substances (products). The atoms themselves are never destroyed; they just get rearranged into new combinations. When you toast bread, heat triggers reactions that turn pale, soft starches into brown, crunchy, tasty molecules. The bread can't un-toast because new bonds have formed.
An exothermic reaction releases energy, usually as heat, so it warms its surroundings; an endothermic reaction absorbs energy, so it cools things down. Whether heat comes out or goes in depends on how much energy it takes to break the old bonds versus how much is freed making the new ones. A campfire is exothermic, throwing off heat and light. An instant cold pack is endothermic, getting chilly as a reaction inside soaks up heat from your sore muscle.
Activation energy is the starting push a reaction needs before it can get going, even if it will release energy once it does. It's the hump the reactants have to get over before rolling downhill into products. A match is loaded with energy, but it won't burst into flame until you scratch it and the friction gives that first kick of heat. Once over the hump, the fire keeps itself going.
Acids are substances that release hydrogen ions into water and tend to taste sour, while bases accept those ions and often feel slippery. They sit at opposite ends of a scale, and most everyday substances land somewhere in between. Lemon juice and vinegar are acids, which is why they make your mouth pucker, while baking soda and soap are bases. When an acid and a base meet, they cancel each other out in a reaction called neutralization.
Neutralization is the reaction that happens when an acid and a base combine and cancel out each other's extremes, usually producing water and a salt. The acid's hydrogen ions pair up with the base's partner ions, leaving a much milder mixture behind. If you've ever taken an antacid for a sour stomach, you've used neutralization: the base in the tablet tames the stomach acid that was causing the burn. Adding baking soda to a vinegar spill does the same thing.
The pH scale is a ruler from 0 to 14 that tells you how acidic or basic something is. Numbers below 7 mean acidic, 7 is neutral like pure water, and numbers above 7 mean basic. Each step on the scale is a big jump, so a lemon at around 2 is far more acidic than coffee at around 5, not just a little. You can test pH at home with a strip of paper that changes color, the same way pool owners check their water.
Neutralization is what happens when an acid and a base meet and undo each other's strength. The hydrogen ions from the acid pair up with the partners from the base, and together they form water plus a salt. This is why a baking soda paste can soothe a bee sting, since the mild base calms the acid the sting left behind. Heartburn relief works the same way, with a chalky antacid neutralizing the extra acid in your stomach.
Matter usually shows up in three everyday states: solid, liquid, and gas. In a solid the tiny particles are packed tightly and barely move, so it keeps its shape, like an ice cube. In a liquid the particles slide past each other, so it flows and takes the shape of its container, like water in a glass. In a gas the particles zip around freely and spread out to fill any space, like the steam rising off a hot kettle.
Melting and freezing are two sides of the same coin, and both are about how much the tiny particles in a substance are jiggling. When you heat a solid, its particles vibrate harder until they break loose and start sliding, and the solid turns into a liquid. Cool a liquid down and the particles slow until they lock into place, turning it back into a solid. You watch both happen with an ice cube melting in your drink and water freezing into ice cubes in the freezer.
Evaporation is when a liquid quietly turns into a gas without boiling, because the fastest-moving particles at the surface escape into the air. That is why a wet sidewalk dries up on a sunny day even though it never reaches boiling. Condensation is the reverse: when that gas cools, the particles slow down and clump back into a liquid. You see it as the foggy drops on the outside of a cold glass of lemonade on a warm day.
When something dissolves, its particles break apart and spread out evenly among the particles of a liquid, making a clear mixture called a solution. The dissolved stuff does not vanish, it just hides between the water molecules, which is why a glass of sugary water tastes sweet even though you cannot see the sugar. Warm water dissolves many things faster because its lively particles bump and break the solid apart more quickly. That is why sugar disappears faster in hot tea than in iced tea.
A physical change rearranges or moves a substance without making anything new, so you could undo it. Melting an ice cube or tearing paper are physical changes, since it is still water and still paper. A chemical change turns substances into something brand new with different properties, and it is usually hard to reverse. Baking a cake or burning a log are chemical changes, because you cannot turn the cake back into raw eggs and flour.
Rust forms when iron meets oxygen and water and slowly reacts to make a new, flaky orange substance called iron oxide. This is a chemical change, so the strong shiny metal becomes weak and crumbly over time. That is why an old bike left out in the rain gets a rough orange coating, while one kept dry stays smooth. Painting or oiling metal works by blocking the oxygen and water so the reaction cannot get started.
A mixture is just different substances mingled together without joining chemically, so you can usually separate them again. A bowl of trail mix or a glass of salty water are mixtures, and you could pick out the raisins or boil away the water to get the salt back. A compound is when atoms actually bond into a single new substance with its own properties, like water itself, which is hydrogen and oxygen locked together. You cannot pick the hydrogen out of water with your fingers the way you can pick peanuts out of trail mix.
When you pour vinegar onto baking soda, the acid in the vinegar reacts with the base in the baking soda and makes a brand-new gas called carbon dioxide. That gas needs somewhere to go, so it pushes up and out as the foamy bubbles you see erupting in a homemade volcano. It is a chemical change, because the fizzing leaves behind something different from what you started with. The same gas is what makes bread and cake rise and puff up in the oven.
Solubility is how much of a substance can dissolve in a liquid, and for most solids it goes up when the liquid is warmer. Heat makes the liquid's particles move faster and bump the solid apart more eagerly, so more of it can squeeze in. That is why you can stir a heap of sugar into hot tea but the same amount just sinks and sits in iced tea. Let the sweet hot tea cool slowly and some sugar may even creep back out as tiny crystals.
Sublimation is the unusual trick where a solid turns straight into a gas without ever becoming a liquid in between. It happens because the particles gain enough energy to break free all at once instead of loosening into a puddle first. The clearest example is dry ice, the frozen form of carbon dioxide, which never melts into a liquid but instead fogs away as a chilly gas. The same thing slowly happens to ice cubes left forgotten in the freezer, which shrink over time even though they never get wet.
In incomplete dominance, neither allele fully masks the other, so the heterozygote shows a blended in-between trait rather than one parent's. Classic example: a red snapdragon crossed with a white one gives pink flowers, because half the usual red pigment is made. A Punnett square of two pinks (Rr x Rr) predicts 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, so here the genotype ratio and the phenotype ratio match exactly.
In codominance both alleles are fully expressed at the same time, so the heterozygote shows both traits side by side rather than a blend. A roan cow with a red-and-white speckled coat is a good example: it has both pure red hairs and pure white hairs, not pink ones. This is different from incomplete dominance, where the two alleles average into a single new appearance like pink.
Some genes have more than two possible alleles in the population, even though any one person still carries only two. The ABO blood gene has three alleles: A and B are codominant with each other, while O is recessive to both. So a parent with IA IB blood is type AB, and a child who inherits one O allele from each parent is type O even if grandparents were A and B.
A dihybrid cross tracks two different traits at the same time, like seed shape and seed color in peas. Each parent can pass four allele combinations, so the Punnett square has sixteen boxes instead of four. When you cross two parents heterozygous for both traits, the classic phenotype ratio that comes out is nine showing both dominant traits, three and three showing one dominant each, and one showing both recessive.
A test cross reveals whether an organism showing a dominant trait is homozygous or heterozygous, since both look identical on the outside. You cross the mystery individual with a homozygous recessive partner and watch the offspring. If any offspring show the recessive trait, the mystery parent must have carried a hidden recessive allele; if all offspring show the dominant trait, it was almost certainly homozygous dominant.
A carrier is someone who has one copy of a recessive allele but does not show the trait because their other allele is dominant. They are healthy themselves yet can pass the recessive allele to their children. If two carriers have a child, a Punnett square predicts a one-in-four chance the child inherits both recessive copies and shows the trait, which is how conditions like cystic fibrosis can appear in families with no visible history.
Sex-linked genes sit on the X or Y chromosome, so they are inherited along with biological sex. Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele on it, such as the one for red-green color blindness, shows up with no second copy to mask it. Females have two X chromosomes and usually need both copies to be recessive, which is why X-linked recessive traits appear more often in males.
A polygenic trait is controlled by many genes acting together, so instead of a few distinct categories you get a smooth range of outcomes. Human height and skin color work this way, which is why a class of people forms a bell-shaped spread rather than just tall or short. A single Punnett square cannot capture this, because each gene adds a small amount to the total effect.
Pleiotropy is when a single gene affects several seemingly unrelated traits at once. The same gene change can ripple into many body systems because its protein is used in more than one place. In sickle cell disease, for example, one altered gene changes the shape of red blood cells, which in turn affects oxygen delivery, pain, organ function, and even resistance to malaria.
Epistasis is when one gene masks or overrides the effect of a completely different gene. A common example is coat color in Labrador retrievers: one gene decides whether the pigment is black or brown, but a second gene can switch pigment off entirely and produce a yellow lab regardless of what the first gene says. So a dog can carry black-coat alleles yet still be yellow because the masking gene won out.
When you cross two heterozygotes for one trait, such as Bb crossed with Bb, the four-box Punnett square gives one BB, two Bb, and one bb. Because both BB and Bb show the dominant trait, three of the four boxes look dominant and only one looks recessive, producing the famous 3:1 phenotype ratio. The genotype ratio underneath is actually 1:2:1, which is hidden because the heterozygotes look just like the dominant homozygotes.
Genes that sit close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited as a package, which is called linkage, so they break the usual independent-assortment rules behind Punnett squares. During the formation of egg and sperm cells, matching chromosomes can swap matching segments in a process called crossing over, which shuffles alleles and can separate even linked genes. The closer two genes are on a chromosome, the less often crossing over splits them apart.
The genotype is the actual set of alleles an organism carries, while the phenotype is the trait you can observe, such as eye color or height. The same phenotype can come from different genotypes, because a dominant trait shows up whether you have one or two dominant alleles. That is exactly why a Punnett square's genotype ratio of 1:2:1 collapses into a 3:1 phenotype ratio, and why two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child.
At mid-ocean ridges, two plates pull apart and hot rock rises from the mantle to fill the gap, cooling into fresh seafloor that pushes the older crust outward on both sides. This means the ocean floor is youngest right at the ridge and gets steadily older the farther away you look. Picture a conveyor belt: new material is added in the middle and carried sideways, slowly widening the ocean over millions of years. This is part of why the Atlantic Ocean is still getting a little wider every year.
Where two plates collide and one is denser, the heavier plate bends and sinks beneath the lighter one back down into the mantle. As the sinking slab heats up, it releases water that lowers the melting point of the rock above it, feeding chains of volcanoes near the boundary. Think of pushing one edge of a floating rug under another until it slips below the surface. This is why volcanoes and deep ocean trenches often line up along the same coastlines.
A transform fault is a boundary where two plates grind horizontally past each other instead of pulling apart or colliding, so no crust is created or destroyed. The rough surfaces snag and build up strain until they suddenly slip, which is what produces earthquakes there. It is like two bricks sliding past one another with their gritty faces catching, then jerking free. The San Andreas Fault in California is a famous example separating two plates moving in opposite directions.
A convergent boundary is where two plates move toward each other, and what happens depends on what kinds of crust meet. Ocean-meets-ocean or ocean-meets-continent leads to subduction and volcanic arcs, while continent-meets-continent crumples both edges upward because neither is dense enough to sink. The result can be towering mountain ranges, deep trenches, or strings of volcanoes. It is like two cars in a head-on collision: the metal has nowhere to go but up and outward.
A divergent boundary is where two plates move away from each other, letting hot mantle rock rise and create brand-new crust in the gap. Under the ocean this builds mid-ocean ridges, and on land it forms rift valleys where the ground stretches, thins, and drops down between cracks. Imagine slowly pulling apart a stretched piece of taffy until the middle thins and tears. East Africa is being torn apart this way right now and may eventually split off into a new sea.
Plates don't just drift randomly; two forces do most of the pushing and pulling. Ridge push happens because the elevated, hot rock at a mid-ocean ridge slides downhill and shoves the plate away, while slab pull happens when a cold, dense subducting slab sinks and drags the rest of the plate behind it like a tablecloth slipping off a table. Slab pull is generally considered the stronger of the two. Underlying mantle convection helps, but these edge forces dominate the motion of a plate.
A hotspot is a fixed column of unusually hot rock rising from deep in the mantle that melts through the plate above it, creating volcanoes far from any plate boundary. Because the plume stays roughly in place while the plate slides over it, it punches out a trail of volcanoes, with the oldest ones carried farthest away and the active one sitting over the plume now. Think of holding a candle under a sheet of paper you slowly drag across it, leaving a line of scorch marks. The Hawaiian island chain formed exactly this way.
A Wadati-Benioff zone is the sloping band of earthquakes that traces a subducting slab as it dives deeper into the mantle. The quakes get progressively deeper the farther you move inland from the trench, mapping out the angle and path of the descending plate even though we can't see it directly. It is like dropping a marked stick into murky water and tracking it only by the bubbles rising along its length. These deep quake patterns gave early scientists some of the first clear proof that whole slabs really sink into the mantle.
Isostasy is the idea that the rigid plates float on the denser, slowly flowing mantle beneath them, finding a balance like ice cubes bobbing in water. Thicker or lighter crust rides higher and also pushes a deeper root down below, which is why tall mountain ranges have thick crustal roots underneath them. When a heavy ice sheet melts away, the land it was pressing down slowly rebounds upward over thousands of years. Parts of Scandinavia and Canada are still rising today for exactly that reason.
An accretionary wedge is a pile of seafloor sediment and rock that gets scraped off a subducting plate and plastered onto the edge of the overriding plate. As the lower plate dives down, the soft material on top is shaved off and stacked into a wedge-shaped, folded heap near the trench. Picture a snowplow pushing snow into a growing ridge in front of its blade. Over time these wedges can grow large enough to become dry land or even contribute to building coastal mountains.
A triple junction is a point where three tectonic plate boundaries meet, so three plates share a single corner. The boundaries can be any mix of ridges, trenches, and transform faults, and some combinations are stable and stay put while others slowly migrate over time. Think of the spot where three slices of a pie all come to a point in the center. The Afar region in East Africa sits near such a junction, where rifting in several directions is pulling the crust apart at once.
The Wilson cycle describes the long-term life story of an ocean basin: continents rift apart, a new ocean opens and widens through seafloor spreading, then subduction begins, the ocean closes, and finally the continents collide to raise mountains. The cycle can take hundreds of millions of years to run its course before starting over. It is like a slow breath in and out, with oceans being born, growing, and disappearing again. The Atlantic is currently in its opening stage while remnants of older closed oceans are recorded inside mountain belts like the Appalachians.
A sonic boom is the loud crack you hear when an object travels faster than the speed of sound. The object outruns its own pressure waves, so those waves pile up into a single sharp shock front shaped like a cone trailing behind it. When that cone sweeps over your ears, all the built-up pressure arrives at once as a bang. A supersonic jet doesn't boom only when it 'breaks the barrier' — it drags the boom along the ground the whole time it's flying that fast.
The Mach number is an object's speed divided by the local speed of sound, so Mach 1 means moving exactly as fast as sound travels in that air. The 'sound barrier' isn't a wall — it's the sharp rise in air resistance that happens as an aircraft approaches Mach 1, because the air can't get out of the way fast enough and pressure waves stack up in front. Above Mach 1 the craft is supersonic and outruns its own sound. Because the speed of sound drops in colder, thinner high-altitude air, the same true speed can be a higher Mach number up high than at sea level.
Human hearing spans an enormous range of sound intensities, so loudness is measured on the decibel scale, which is logarithmic rather than linear. Each increase of about ten decibels represents roughly ten times more sound intensity, even though our ears perceive it as only 'about twice as loud.' That's why a whisper and a jet engine can be described with numbers that look close together but differ by trillions in actual energy. It also means two identical sound sources together are only about three decibels louder than one, not double the decibel number.
When two sounds of slightly different frequencies play together, they drift in and out of step, alternately reinforcing and cancelling each other. The result is a slow throbbing in loudness called a beat, and the number of throbs per second equals the difference between the two frequencies. Musicians use this to tune instruments: as two strings get closer in pitch, the beats slow down, and when the wobble disappears entirely the notes match. You can hear it as a 'wah-wah-wah' pulse when two people hum almost-but-not-quite the same note.
Diffraction is the way waves bend around edges and spread out after passing through gaps, and sound does it readily because its wavelengths are large — often comparable to the size of everyday doorways and walls. That bending is why you can hear someone talking in the next room even when you can't see them around the corner. Low, long-wavelength sounds like bass diffract more than high, short-wavelength sounds, which is part of why you mainly hear the thumping bass from a party down the street while the crisp treble is lost.
Sound travels faster in warmer air, so when air temperature changes with height, sound waves bend toward the cooler, slower layers. On a sunny day the ground is hot and the air above is cooler, so sound bends upward and away from a listener, making distant sounds fade quickly. At night the ground cools and a warm layer sits above, so sound bends back down toward the ground and carries much farther. That's why a train horn or distant voices can sound surprisingly clear across a lake on a calm evening.
Acoustic impedance describes how much a material resists being set into vibration by a sound wave, and it depends on the material's density and the speed of sound within it. When a sound wave hits a boundary between two materials with very different impedances, most of the energy reflects instead of crossing over. That's why sound made in air mostly bounces off a water surface rather than entering it, and why ultrasound machines use a gel to bridge the impedance gap between the probe and your skin so the sound can get inside.
Reverberation is the lingering wash of sound that remains after a source stops, made of countless reflections bouncing off walls, floors, and ceilings and arriving at your ears slightly delayed. Unlike a distinct echo, these reflections blur together into a smooth tail because each surface sends sound back many times. Hard, bare rooms reverberate a lot and sound boomy, while curtains, carpet, and furniture absorb the energy and deaden it. Concert halls are tuned for just enough reverberation to make music feel rich without smearing the notes together.
The Doppler effect for sound is not perfectly symmetric: it matters whether the source is moving or the listener is, because sound travels through air, which acts as a fixed reference medium. A moving source bunches up the actual wave crests in front of it, while a moving listener simply runs into or away from crests faster. At everyday speeds the two cases give almost the same pitch shift, but the underlying math differs slightly. This is unlike the Doppler effect for light, where only the relative motion matters because light needs no medium.
Doppler radar bounces radio waves off a moving target and measures how the reflected wave's frequency has shifted, using that shift to calculate the target's speed toward or away from the device. A police speed gun does this to a passing car, while weather radar uses it to see how fast rain and wind are moving inside a storm, revealing rotation that can signal a tornado. Because it relies on the Doppler shift, it measures only the part of the motion along the radar beam, so a car crossing sideways would barely register.
For light from very fast-moving sources, the ordinary Doppler shift is modified by special relativity, because the source's clock runs slow from the observer's point of view. This adds an extra time-dilation factor on top of the usual frequency change, and it even produces a transverse Doppler shift — a redshift you see when the source moves straight across your line of sight, where classical theory predicts no shift at all. Astronomers must use these relativistic formulas when measuring the speeds of distant galaxies and fast jets of matter near black holes.
The speed of sound in a material depends on two competing properties: its stiffness, which speeds sound up, and its density, which slows it down. Solids like steel are extremely stiff, so even though they are dense, sound races through them many times faster than through air. This is why you can hear a distant train sooner by pressing your ear to the rail than by listening through the air. It also explains why sound is faster in water than in air but slower in lead than in aluminum, since stiffness usually wins out over density.
Active noise-cancelling headphones use a tiny microphone to listen to incoming sound, then play back a matching wave that is exactly inverted — its peaks line up with the noise's troughs. When the two waves meet, they undergo destructive interference and largely cancel, leaving near silence. This works best on steady low-frequency drones like an airplane engine, because the headphones can predict and invert that smooth wave; sudden, high-pitched sounds are too quick and irregular to cancel cleanly. It's the same wave-cancelling idea as beats, but aimed at erasing sound rather than making it pulse.
The old lock-and-key idea pictured an enzyme's active site as a rigid slot the substrate slips into. The induced-fit model is closer to reality: the active site is flexible and reshapes itself slightly around the substrate once it arrives, gripping it and straining its bonds toward the reaction. It is less like a stiff lock and more like a hand closing around a ball it has just caught.
Many enzymes can't work alone and need a non-protein helper called a cofactor. Cofactors that are metal ions (like zinc or iron) lock into the enzyme, while organic helpers are called coenzymes, several of which your body builds from vitamins. The bare protein is the apoenzyme; add its cofactor and you get the active holoenzyme. This is one reason vitamin deficiencies can stall whole chunks of your metabolism.
A competitive inhibitor is a molecule shaped enough like the real substrate to slot into the active site, where it just sits and blocks the substrate from binding. Because it competes for the same spot, flooding the cell with more substrate can outcompete it and restore the reaction. Many drugs work this way, jamming an enzyme's active site so its normal job slows down.
Some enzymes have a second binding spot away from the active site called an allosteric site. When a regulator molecule docks there, it bends the whole protein into a different shape, turning the active site on or off without touching it directly. This lets cells dial enzymes up or down on the fly, like a thermostat that responds to how much product has already piled up.
In a chain of reactions where each enzyme hands its product to the next, the final product often loops back and switches off the first enzyme in the line. That way the cell stops spending raw materials the moment it has made enough, then resumes when stocks run low. It is the same logic as a factory that pauses the assembly line once the warehouse is full.
Every enzyme has a sweet spot of temperature and pH where its precise folded shape works best. Push the heat or acidity too far and the protein unravels, a permanent change called denaturation that wrecks the active site. It is exactly what happens when you fry an egg: the heat denatures its proteins, and they never go back to clear and runny.
Glycolysis is the opening act of breaking down sugar: a chain of enzymes splits one glucose into two smaller pyruvate molecules right in the cell's cytoplasm. It spends a little energy up front to gain more back, netting a small amount of ATP plus electron carriers for later stages. Crucially it needs no oxygen, which is why it is the oldest and most universal energy trick in life.
Also called the Krebs cycle, this is a loop of reactions in the mitochondria that finishes pulling apart the carbons from food. Each turn strips off carbon dioxide you breathe out and loads up electron carriers that feed the next stage. Think of it as the spinning gear that doesn't make much energy directly but charges up the batteries the cell will cash in afterward.
This is where cells make the bulk of their ATP. Electron carriers charged up earlier dump their electrons into a row of proteins in the mitochondrial membrane, and the energy released pumps protons to one side. Those protons then rush back through a turbine-like enzyme that spins to crank out ATP, a process called chemiosmosis. Oxygen sits at the very end to grab the spent electrons, which is the whole reason you need to breathe.
ATP synthase is a tiny molecular motor embedded in the mitochondrial membrane. Protons crowded on one side flow back through it like water through a dam, physically spinning part of the enzyme. That rotation snaps a phosphate onto ADP to build ATP, the cell's rechargeable energy battery. It is one of the few cases in biology where you can literally call a protein a spinning turbine.
When oxygen runs short, cells can't finish the usual energy chain, so they fall back on fermentation to keep glycolysis running. In your muscles, hard sprinting builds up lactic acid this way, contributing to that burning, tired feeling. Yeast does a different version, turning sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, which is exactly how bread rises and beer brews.
Your metabolism runs two opposite directions at once. Catabolism breaks big molecules down into smaller ones and releases energy, like digesting a meal into usable fuel. Anabolism spends that energy to build big molecules up, like knitting amino acids into the muscle you grow after a workout. Tearing down and building up are constantly traded off depending on whether you've just eaten or are running on reserves.
When you haven't eaten and blood sugar dips, your liver builds fresh glucose from non-sugar sources like amino acids and lactate. It is roughly glycolysis run in reverse, but it uses a few different enzymes to push past the steps that normally only flow one way. This is what keeps your brain, a glucose hog, fueled through an overnight fast or a long stretch without food.
Deposition is when a gas turns straight into a solid without ever passing through the liquid stage, the exact reverse of sublimation. The vapor particles lose energy and lock into a solid arrangement all at once instead of first puddling into a liquid. Frost on a cold window or on the grass is the classic example: water vapor in the air freezes directly onto the chilly surface as delicate ice crystals.
The triple point is the single, exact combination of temperature and pressure where a substance can exist as solid, liquid, and gas all at the same time, in balance. At that precise point ice, water, and steam can sit together in the same container without any one of them winning out. It is so reliable and reproducible that scientists long used water's triple point to help define the temperature scale itself.
Push a substance past its critical point, a special temperature and pressure, and the difference between liquid and gas simply disappears, leaving a single state called a supercritical fluid. It can flow and fill a container like a gas but dissolve things like a liquid, blurring the usual boundary. Supercritical carbon dioxide is used industrially to decaffeinate coffee beans, since it soaks out the caffeine but leaves no harmful residue behind.
Heat a gas hot enough, or zap it with strong energy, and electrons get torn away from their atoms, leaving a glowing soup of charged particles called plasma. Because it is full of free charges, plasma conducts electricity and bends to magnetic fields in ways an ordinary gas cannot. You meet it every day in lightning, neon signs, and the flickering glow of the Sun, which is itself an enormous ball of plasma.
A Bose-Einstein condensate is an exotic state that forms when certain atoms are cooled to a whisker above absolute zero, the coldest temperature possible. At that point the atoms slow almost to a standstill and merge into one shared quantum blob, all behaving as a single entity rather than as separate particles. It is the opposite extreme from plasma: where plasma is matter at scorching energy, this is matter at the very bottom of the cold.
Inside a liquid every molecule is pulled in all directions by its neighbors, but at the surface there are no neighbors above, so those molecules pull sideways and inward, forming a kind of stretchy skin. This is why water beads up into round droplets and why a gently placed paper clip or a water strider can rest on the surface without sinking. It also pulls small drops into the most compact shape possible, a sphere.
Viscosity is a liquid's resistance to flowing, set by how strongly its particles cling to and drag past one another. Thick, sticky liquids like honey or syrup have high viscosity and ooze slowly, while thin liquids like water have low viscosity and pour fast. Warming a liquid usually lowers its viscosity, which is why honey runs much more easily after you heat it.
A liquid boils when its escaping vapor pushes hard enough to match the air pressure pressing down on it, so lower air pressure lets it boil at a lower temperature. On a high mountain the thinner air means water boils well below its sea-level temperature, so cooking takes longer because the water is cooler. A pressure cooker does the opposite: it traps steam to raise the pressure, letting water get hotter than usual and cook food faster.
Supercooling is when a very pure, undisturbed liquid is chilled below its normal freezing point yet stays liquid, because it has no speck or jolt to trigger the first crystals. Freezing usually needs a starting point such as a dust grain or a scratch, and without one the molecules cannot get organized. A bottle of very clean water can sometimes be cooled below freezing and then snap into ice the instant you tap it or drop in a single crystal.
Inertia is the lazy streak in everything: an object keeps doing what it's already doing unless a force changes it. A still object stays still, and a moving one keeps moving in a straight line. The more mass something has, the more inertia it has, so heavy things are harder to start or stop.
Newton's first law says an object won't change its motion unless a force pushes or pulls it. No force? Then a resting thing stays at rest and a moving thing keeps gliding at the same speed and direction. Forces are what make things speed up, slow down, or turn.
When several forces push on one object, you add them up (counting direction) to get the net force. That single combined force decides what happens. If the forces cancel out, the net force is zero and motion doesn't change. If they don't cancel, the object accelerates in the leftover direction.
Balanced forces are evenly matched, so they cancel and the object's motion stays the same. Unbalanced forces don't cancel, leaving a net force that changes the motion, making the object speed up, slow down, or change direction. Only unbalanced forces cause acceleration.
Static friction holds a still object in place and must be overcome before it starts sliding. Once it's moving, kinetic friction takes over and is usually a bit weaker. That's why something is harder to get moving than to keep moving.
Air resistance is friction from air pushing back on things moving through it. The faster you go and the bigger your surface facing the air, the stronger it gets. It's why a feather flutters down slowly while a rock drops fast, and why parachutes work.
Mass is how much stuff is in an object and never changes no matter where you are. Weight is how hard gravity pulls on that mass, so weight changes with gravity. On the Moon your mass stays the same, but you weigh about six times less because the Moon's gravity is weaker.
Speed tells you how fast something moves. Velocity tells you how fast AND which direction. So two cars going 50 km/h have the same speed, but if one heads north and one heads south, they have different velocities. Direction is the key difference.
Circular motion is when something travels along a curved path around a center point. Even at constant speed, it's always accelerating because its direction keeps changing. A force pointing toward the center is what keeps bending the path into a circle.
When you throw something, it moves forward and falls down at the same time. Its forward motion stays steady while gravity pulls it down faster and faster, bending the path into a smooth curved arc. That curve is why everything thrown eventually comes back down.
The normal force is the push a surface gives back to an object resting on it, pointing straight away from the surface. It's why you don't sink through the floor: the floor pushes up just as hard as gravity pulls you down, balancing things out.
Tension is the pulling force carried along a rope, string, or cable when it's stretched tight. It pulls equally on whatever is attached at both ends. A rope can only pull, never push, so tension always points along the rope away from the object.
Hooke's law says a spring's pull-back force grows in step with how far you stretch or squash it. Pull twice as far and it pulls back twice as hard. This works only up to a point; stretch too far and the spring bends out of shape and stops obeying the rule.
Power is how fast energy is used or work is done. Doing the same job quickly takes more power than doing it slowly. Two engines might do the same total work, but the more powerful one finishes sooner. Power is measured in watts.
Insulation slows the flow of heat by using materials that conduct poorly, often trapping pockets of air. Trapped air is a great insulator because it doesn't move heat easily. That's why fluffy coats, foam, and double windows keep warmth where you want it.
A wave is a traveling disturbance that carries energy from place to place without moving the material itself very far. The water or rope just wiggles up and down or back and forth while the energy moves through it. Sound, light, and ripples are all waves.
In a transverse wave, the material wiggles up and down (or side to side) while the wave travels at a right angle to that wiggle. Light and the wave you make by shaking a rope are transverse. The crests and troughs are the high and low points.
In a longitudinal wave, the material squishes and stretches back and forth in the same direction the wave travels, making compressions and rarefactions. Sound is the classic example, pushing air particles forward and back.
Frequency is how many wave cycles pass a point each second, measured in hertz. High frequency means lots of fast wiggles; low frequency means few slow ones. For sound, higher frequency means higher pitch.
Amplitude is how big a wave is, measured from the calm middle to a peak. Bigger amplitude means more energy. For sound that means louder; for light it means brighter. The wiggle's height, not its spacing, sets the amplitude.
Wave speed is how fast a wave's energy travels through a material. It depends mostly on what the wave is moving through, not on how hard you make the wave. Sound zips faster through water and solids than through air.
Reflection is when a wave bounces off a surface instead of passing through. Light reflecting lets you see things and makes mirrors work; sound reflecting makes echoes. The wave bounces off at the same angle it hit, like a ball off a wall.
Refraction is the bending of a wave as it passes from one material into another and changes speed. Light slows down entering water and bends, which is why a straw in a glass looks broken at the surface.
Diffraction is how waves spread out and bend around edges or through gaps. It's why you can hear someone around a corner even when you can't see them: sound waves bend around the corner more easily than light does.
When two waves overlap, they add together. Crests meeting crests make a bigger wave (constructive), while a crest meeting a trough can cancel out (destructive). This combining is called interference and explains everything from louder spots to noise-canceling headphones.
Sound is a wave made of vibrations traveling through a material, usually air. A vibrating object pushes and pulls the air, sending ripples of pressure to your ears. No material means no sound, which is why space is silent.
Pitch is how high or low a sound seems, and it depends on the sound wave's frequency. Fast vibrations make high-pitched sounds; slow vibrations make low ones. Tightening or shortening a string raises its pitch by speeding up its vibration.
Loudness is how strong a sound seems, and it depends on the sound wave's amplitude, or how much energy it carries. Bigger vibrations move more air and sound louder. Loudness is measured in decibels, and very loud sounds can damage your ears.
An echo is sound that bounces off a far surface and comes back to you a moment later. The delay happens because sound takes time to travel there and back. You need a hard surface far enough away to hear the return clearly.
Ultrasound is sound too high-pitched for humans to hear, above about 20,000 hertz. It bounces off objects and echoes back, so machines use it to make pictures inside the body or measure distances. Bats and dolphins use it naturally to navigate.
Echolocation is finding things by sending out sounds and listening for the echoes that bounce back. The timing and direction of the returning echoes reveal where objects are and how far away. Bats and dolphins use it to hunt and navigate in the dark.
Visible light is the part of the electromagnetic spectrum our eyes can detect, made of all the colors from red to violet. Each color is light of a different wavelength. Mixed together they look white, and they all travel at the same blazing speed.
Objects have color because they absorb some light wavelengths and reflect others. The colors that bounce back are what you see. A red apple reflects red light and soaks up the rest; a black object soaks up almost everything, reflecting little.
A prism splits white light into a rainbow because each color bends by a slightly different amount as it slows down in the glass. Violet bends most and red least, fanning the colors apart. This separating of light is called dispersion.
Rainbows form when sunlight enters raindrops, bends, bounces off the back, and bends again on the way out, splitting into colors. Each raindrop sends one color toward your eyes, and millions of drops together paint the full arc.
Infrared is invisible light with wavelengths just longer than red. Warm objects give it off, so cameras that 'see' infrared can spot heat in the dark. TV remotes use infrared to send signals to your television.
Ultraviolet is invisible light with wavelengths just shorter than violet, carrying more energy than visible light. Too much from the Sun causes sunburn, which is why sunscreen blocks it. Some animals, like bees, can actually see UV patterns on flowers.
You see when light bounces off objects, enters your eye, and lands on the retina at the back. Special cells turn that light into signals your brain reads as images. Without light there's nothing to bounce, which is why you can't see in total darkness.
A shadow forms where an object blocks light from reaching a surface. Because light travels in straight lines, it can't bend around solid things, leaving a dark patch shaped like the blocker. Move the light closer and the shadow grows bigger.
Materials handle light in three ways. Transparent ones like clear glass let light pass straight through so you see clearly. Translucent ones like frosted glass scatter light so things look blurry. Opaque ones like wood block light completely, casting solid shadows.
Resistance is how much a material fights the flow of electric current. High resistance slows current down and often turns electrical energy into heat. Thin or long wires resist more, while thick short ones resist less, like wide pipes letting water flow freely.
In a series circuit, parts are connected one after another in a single loop, so the same current flows through every part. If one part breaks, the whole circuit stops, like old holiday lights where one dead bulb killed the whole string.
In a parallel circuit, parts sit on separate branches, each with its own path for current. If one branch breaks, the others keep working. That's why your home is wired in parallel: one switched-off lamp doesn't darken the whole house.
Conductors let electric current flow easily because their electrons move freely; metals like copper are great conductors. Insulators block current because their electrons are locked in place; rubber and plastic are good insulators, which is why wires are coated in them.
A battery stores chemical energy and turns it into electrical energy on demand. Inside, chemical reactions push electrons out one end and pull them in the other, driving current around a circuit. When the chemicals are used up, the battery goes dead.
Magnetism is a force that pulls or pushes certain metals like iron. Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Opposite poles attract and like poles repel. The invisible region where the force acts is called a magnetic field.
An electric motor turns electrical energy into spinning motion. Current flowing through a coil makes it an electromagnet, and a nearby magnet pushes and pulls it so the coil spins around. That spin powers fans, toys, and electric cars.
A generator is like a motor run backward: instead of using electricity to make motion, it uses motion to make electricity. Spinning a coil near a magnet pushes electrons along the wire, creating current. Power plants spin huge generators to make our electricity.
Electricity can be dangerous because the human body conducts current, and even a small amount can hurt your heart or burn you. Water makes it worse by helping current flow. That's why you keep electrical things away from water and never poke metal into outlets.
Fuses and circuit breakers protect wiring from too much current. If the current gets dangerously high, a fuse melts or a breaker trips, instantly cutting the circuit before wires overheat and start a fire. Breakers can be reset; fuses must be replaced.
Grounding gives stray electric current a safe path straight into the earth instead of through a person. Appliances have a third prong connected to ground, so if something inside goes wrong, the current rushes harmlessly into the ground rather than shocking you.
Lightning is a giant spark of static electricity. Clouds build up huge amounts of charge as ice and water bump around inside them. When the charge gets strong enough, it leaps as a brilliant bolt to another cloud or the ground, heating the air so fast it bangs as thunder.
Simple machines are basic tools that make work easier by changing the size or direction of a force. The six classics are the lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, and screw. They don't reduce total work, but they spread it out so it feels easier.
A lever is a stiff bar that pivots on a point called a fulcrum. Pushing down on one end lifts a load on the other. By placing the fulcrum cleverly, a small effort over a long distance can move a heavy load a short distance.
A pulley is a wheel with a rope over it that changes the direction of your pull. Pulling down to lift something up is easier than pushing up. Combining several pulleys lets you lift heavy loads with much less force, spread over more rope.
An inclined plane is a ramp that lets you raise something by pushing it up a gentle slope instead of lifting it straight up. It takes less force, but you push over a longer distance, so the total work stays about the same.
A wedge is like a moving ramp with a sharp edge that splits or pushes things apart. As you drive it in, it turns your forward push into a strong sideways force. Knives, axes, and door stops are all wedges.
A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a rod into a spiral ridge. Turning it many times pulls it deep into material with great gripping force, while you only have to apply a gentle twisting effort. That's how it holds things tightly together.
A wheel and axle is a big wheel attached to a smaller rod (the axle). Turning the large wheel a little makes the axle turn with extra force, or turning the axle spins the wheel fast over a distance. Doorknobs and steering wheels use this idea.
Gears are toothed wheels that lock together so one turns the next. A small gear driving a big one trades speed for turning force; a big gear driving a small one trades force for speed. That's how bikes and clocks adjust their power and pace.
Air pressure is the weight of the atmosphere pressing on everything from all directions. You don't usually feel it because it pushes evenly. Differences in air pressure drive winds and let straws and suction cups work by letting outside air push things along.
Buoyancy is the upward push a liquid or gas gives to objects in it. The fluid pushes up with a force equal to the weight of the fluid the object shoves aside. If that push beats the object's weight, it floats; if not, it sinks.
Whether something floats depends on its density compared to the liquid. If an object is less dense than water, it floats; if it's denser, it sinks. Density is how much mass is packed into a space, so a light, spread-out object floats while a heavy, compact one sinks.
A pendulum is a weight that swings from a fixed point. Gravity pulls it back toward the middle, so it swings past and back over and over. Surprisingly, the length of the string, not the weight, sets how long each swing takes.
Speed tells you how much distance something covers in a certain time. Go farther in the same time and your speed is higher. We measure it in units like kilometers per hour or meters per second. Average speed smooths out the fast and slow parts of a trip.
Near Earth's surface, gravity speeds up every falling object at the same rate, about 9.8 meters per second faster each second. Heavy or light, they fall the same if air resistance is ignored. That steady speed-up is why falling feels faster the longer you drop.
Weight is the force of gravity pulling on an object's mass. It points straight down toward Earth's center. Because it depends on gravity, the same object weighs less on the Moon and would weigh more on a bigger planet, even though its mass never changes.
A force is a push or a pull that can start motion, stop it, change its direction, or change an object's shape. Forces have both strength and direction. You can't always see them, but you see their effects whenever something speeds up, slows, or bends.
Drag is the resisting force a fluid like air or water puts on something moving through it. It grows fast as you speed up and pushes opposite to your motion. Smooth, pointy shapes have less drag, which is why race cars and fish are streamlined.
Thrust is the forward push that drives vehicles like rockets, planes, and boats. It comes from pushing something backward, so by Newton's third law the vehicle is pushed forward in return. Rockets throw hot gas down to thrust themselves up.
Lift is the upward force that holds an airplane in the air. A wing's shape and tilt make air move faster over the top and push more underneath, creating an upward force. When lift beats the plane's weight, it rises.
An object is in equilibrium when all the forces on it cancel out, giving zero net force. It can be sitting still or moving at a steady speed in a straight line. Either way, nothing changes its motion because the forces are perfectly balanced.
The center of mass is the balance point of an object, where its weight is evenly spread. If you support an object right under its center of mass, it balances. When this point sits over the base, the object is stable; if it tips past the edge, it falls.
Something is stable when it's hard to tip over, which happens with a low center of mass and a wide base. Tall, top-heavy objects tip easily because a small lean pushes their center of mass past the edge of the base. Race cars are low and wide to stay stable.
Torque is the turning power of a force. Pushing farther from the pivot point makes more torque, so it's easier to spin or twist something. That's why a long wrench loosens a tight bolt better than a short one, and why door handles sit far from the hinges.
Weightlessness is the floating feeling you get in free fall, when nothing is pushing up against gravity. Astronauts in orbit aren't beyond gravity; they're falling around Earth along with their spacecraft, so there's no support force and everything floats.
The law of reflection says light bounces off a smooth surface at the same angle it arrived. A ray coming in steeply leaves just as steeply on the other side. Smooth mirrors keep the rays neat so you see clear images; rough surfaces scatter them.
A lens is a curved piece of clear material that bends light to focus it. Convex lenses bulge out and bring light together to magnify or focus; concave lenses curve in and spread light apart. Glasses, cameras, and your own eye all use lenses.
A laser makes a tight, straight beam of light where all the waves march in perfect step at a single color. That's different from a flashlight, whose light spreads out and mixes colors. Lasers stay narrow over long distances and pack lots of energy into a small spot.
Fiber optic cables carry information as flashes of light down thin glass strands. The light bounces along inside the fiber by total internal reflection, staying trapped even around bends. This lets data travel fast over huge distances with little loss.
You hear when sound waves enter your ear and vibrate the eardrum. Tiny bones pass the vibration to a fluid-filled spiral that turns it into nerve signals your brain reads as sound. Louder sounds vibrate the eardrum harder; higher pitches vibrate it faster.
Solar panels turn sunlight straight into electricity. Light hitting special materials in the panel knocks electrons loose, and that flow of electrons becomes current. The brighter the sunlight, the more electricity the panel makes.
Friction turns motion energy into heat. As surfaces rub, their tiny bumps scrape and grab, making particles jiggle faster, which we feel as warmth. That's why brakes get hot, sticks can start fires, and your hands warm up when you rub them.
Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle, so it needs a material like air, water, or solids to travel through. In the vacuum of space there are almost no particles, so sound has nothing to move through and can't travel at all.
Light is the fastest thing in the universe, traveling about 300,000 kilometers every second. Nothing can go faster. It's so fast that light from the Sun, 150 million kilometers away, reaches us in about eight minutes.
Rubbing two materials together can transfer electrons from one to the other. The one that gains electrons becomes negatively charged and the one that loses them becomes positively charged. This is how you build up static electricity that makes hair rise or balloons stick.
A speaker turns electricity into sound. An electric signal flows through a coil that becomes an electromagnet, pushing and pulling against a magnet so the cone vibrates. Those vibrations shake the air, sending out the sound waves you hear.
A microphone does the opposite of a speaker: it turns sound into electricity. Sound waves vibrate a thin part inside, and that motion creates a matching electric signal. The signal can then be recorded, amplified, or sent far away.
Mitochondria are tiny bean-shaped parts inside cells that make energy. They take in food and oxygen and turn them into a fuel the cell can use, called ATP. That's why people call them the powerhouse of the cell. Busy cells like muscle cells have lots of them.
Ribosomes are tiny machines in the cell that build proteins. They read the instructions copied from DNA and link together building blocks called amino acids, one by one, like stringing beads. Proteins do almost every job in the body, so ribosomes are very busy.
Cytoplasm is the jelly-like goo that fills the inside of a cell. It holds all the tiny parts in place and lets them float and move around. Many of the cell's chemical jobs happen right in this jelly.
Plant cells have a tough outer layer called the cell wall, just outside the membrane. It's stiff and strong, giving the plant its shape and helping it stand up straight. Animal cells don't have one, which is why animals are soft and bendy.
A vacuole is a storage bubble inside a cell. It holds water, food, or waste until the cell needs it. Plant cells usually have one big vacuole full of water that helps keep the plant firm and crisp.
Plant and animal cells share many parts, like a nucleus and mitochondria. But plant cells also have a stiff cell wall, green chloroplasts for making food, and one big water-filled vacuole. Animal cells are softer, can't make their own food, and have smaller vacuoles.
Cell division is how one cell becomes two. The cell copies its DNA, then splits down the middle, giving each new cell a full set of instructions. This is how you grow bigger and how cuts heal up.
Your body has many kinds of cells, each shaped for a special job. Nerve cells are long and stringy to carry messages, red blood cells are round to carry oxygen, and muscle cells can squeeze and stretch. Different shapes help them do their jobs well.
When many cells of the same kind work together, they form a tissue. Muscle tissue moves your body, and skin tissue covers and protects you. Tissues are a step up from single cells in how your body is built.
An organ is a body part made of different tissues working together to do a big job. Your heart pumps blood, your lungs take in air, and your stomach digests food. Each organ has its own important role.
Organs that team up to do a big job form an organ system. The digestive system breaks down food, and the circulatory system moves blood. Many systems working together keep your whole body running smoothly.
Your skeleton is the frame of bones inside your body. It holds you up, gives you shape, and protects soft parts like your brain and heart. Bones also make blood cells inside the soft marrow in their centers.
Muscles move your body by pulling on bones. They can only pull, not push, so they work in pairs: one pulls a bone one way, and another pulls it back. When a muscle gets a message from the brain, it squeezes shorter.
The nervous system is your body's message network. Your brain, spinal cord, and nerves send fast signals to control your body. When you touch something hot, nerves zip the message to your brain so you pull your hand away.
A neuron is a special nerve cell that carries messages as tiny electric signals. It has long branches to pass signals to the next neuron. Billions of them connect together to make your brain think and your body move.
A reflex is a super-fast reaction your body does without thinking. When you touch something sharp, your spinal cord sends the pull-away signal before your brain even notices. Reflexes protect you from danger in a flash.
Digestion is how your body breaks food into tiny pieces it can use. It starts in your mouth, where chewing and spit begin the job. Then food travels to the stomach and intestines, where it's broken down and the good stuff is soaked up into your blood.
The stomach is a stretchy bag that mashes and mixes your food. It makes strong acid that breaks food into a thick liquid and kills germs. After a couple of hours, it sends the mush on to your intestines.
The intestines are long, coiled tubes where most digestion finishes. The small intestine soaks up nutrients from food into your blood. The large intestine takes back water and turns what's left into waste.
The liver is a large organ that cleans your blood and stores energy. It filters out harmful stuff, makes a juice called bile to help digest fat, and keeps your blood sugar steady. It's one of your body's hardest workers.
Breathing brings oxygen into your body and pushes out waste gas. When you breathe in, air goes down your windpipe into your lungs. There, oxygen passes into your blood and carbon dioxide passes out to be breathed away.
Your lungs are two spongy organs that pull oxygen out of the air. Inside are millions of tiny air sacs where oxygen slips into your blood. A muscle below your lungs, the diaphragm, pulls down to suck air in.
The circulatory system moves blood around your body in tubes called blood vessels. Your heart pumps the blood, which carries oxygen and food to every cell. It also picks up waste to be cleaned out.
Blood is a red liquid that carries oxygen, food, and warmth around your body. Red blood cells carry oxygen, white blood cells fight germs, and tiny platelets help cuts stop bleeding. The watery part, called plasma, carries everything along.
Blood vessels are the tubes that carry blood around your body. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, and tiny capillaries connect them. Together they reach every part of you.
Your immune system is your body's defense team against germs. White blood cells hunt down and destroy bacteria and viruses that make you sick. When you get better after being sick, your immune system did the work.
White blood cells are the germ-fighters in your blood. Some swallow up bacteria, and others make special weapons called antibodies that stick to invaders. When you're sick, your body makes extra to win the fight.
Your two kidneys are blood filters about the size of your fists. They clean waste and extra water out of your blood and turn it into pee. This keeps the right amount of water and salt in your body.
Skin is your body's largest organ and its outer shield. It keeps germs out, holds water in, and helps you feel touch, heat, and cold. It even helps cool you down by making sweat.
Your brain is the boss of your body and the home of your thoughts. It controls your movements, holds your memories, and lets you feel and think. It sends and gets messages through the nerves all over your body.
Your senses tell your brain about the world around you. Sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch each use a special body part to send messages to your brain. Together they help you understand and stay safe.
Your eyes work like little cameras. Light bounces off things and enters your eye, where a lens focuses it onto the back wall. Special cells there turn the light into signals your brain reads as pictures.
Sounds are tiny waves moving through the air. Your ear catches them, and they make a thin skin called the eardrum wobble. That wobble turns into signals your brain understands as sound.
Your tongue is covered in tiny bumps holding taste buds. They sense flavors like sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and savory and tell your brain. Smell helps too, which is why food seems flavorless when your nose is stuffy.
Smelling happens when tiny bits float off objects into the air and reach your nose. Special cells high in your nose catch these bits and send signals to your brain. That's how you can smell cookies baking from another room.
Teeth break food into smaller pieces so you can swallow and digest it. Sharp front teeth cut, pointed teeth tear, and flat back teeth grind. Teeth are coated in enamel, the hardest stuff in your whole body.
When you're young, your bones grow longer at soft areas near their ends called growth plates. New bone is added there as you get taller. Around the end of your teens, these plates harden and you stop growing taller.
Food gives your body energy and the building blocks to grow and repair. Your body breaks food down and uses it to power your muscles, brain, and every cell. Without food, you'd run out of energy and couldn't grow.
Your cells need oxygen to turn food into energy. Without oxygen, your mitochondria couldn't make the fuel your body runs on. That's why you can't hold your breath for long; your cells get hungry for oxygen fast.
Sweating cools you down when you get too hot. Your skin lets out salty water, and as it dries off your skin, it carries heat away. That's why you sweat when you run around or when it's hot outside.
Hair grows from tiny pockets in your skin called follicles. New cells push up from the bottom, and the part you see is actually dead and that's why a haircut doesn't hurt. Hair helps keep your head warm and protects your skin.
Your body keeps itself at a steady warm temperature, around 37 degrees Celsius. Your cells make heat as they work, and your body adjusts to stay just right. If you're too hot you sweat, and if you're too cold you shiver.
A fever is when your body gets warmer than usual, often because you're fighting germs. Your body turns up the heat on purpose because many germs don't like it warm. A fever is a sign your immune system is at work.
DNA is the instruction book inside every cell that tells your body how to grow and work. It's a long, twisted ladder shape, and the rungs spell out a code. This code decides things like your eye color and height.
DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder, called a double helix. The two long sides twist around each other, and rungs made of paired chemicals connect them. This twist lets a huge amount of code pack into a tiny cell.
A gene is a short section of DNA that holds instructions for one feature, like the color of your hair. You have thousands of genes, each carrying a small piece of the plan for your body. Together, all your genes make you who you are.
A chromosome is a tightly packed bundle of DNA inside a cell. People have 46 of them, arranged in 23 pairs. Packing DNA into chromosomes keeps the long strands neat and easy to copy when cells divide.
You get your genes from your parents, half from each. That's why you might have your mom's nose or your dad's eyes. These passed-down instructions are why families often share looks and traits.
You get two copies of each gene, one from each parent. Some genes are strong, or dominant, and show up even if there's just one copy. Others are quiet, or recessive, and only show when both copies match.
A trait is a feature you can see or measure, like hair color, height, or whether you can roll your tongue. Many traits come from your genes, but some are also shaped by how you live. Traits are what make each person unique.
Identical twins come from one fertilized egg that splits into two. Because they start from the same cell, they share the same DNA. That's why they look so much alike, though tiny differences can still appear.
Each person gets a special mix of genes from their parents, shuffled in a new way. With so many ways to combine genes, almost no two people are exactly alike. Even how we grow up adds to our differences.
Plants make their own food using sunlight, in a process called photosynthesis. Their green leaves catch sunlight and mix water from the roots with a gas from the air to make sugar. They also release oxygen, which we breathe.
Roots are the part of a plant that grows underground. They drink up water and minerals from the soil and anchor the plant so it doesn't fall over. Some roots, like carrots, also store food for the plant.
The stem holds a plant up and connects its parts. Inside are tiny tubes that carry water up from the roots and food down from the leaves. The stem lifts leaves toward the sunlight they need.
